fundamental.thesis: Redington is one of India's largest IT and mobility distributors, with operations across India, the Middle East, Africa and Turkey. It is tagged Industrials here, but it is really a thin-margin, working-capital-heavy distribution business, so the order-book sector card does not apply. On the latest officially extracted quarter, Q1 FY27, revenue grew 34.6% YoY to ₹34,922 cr and PAT rose 94.6% to ₹453 cr. Revenue growth has re-accelerated from +15.7% in Q3 FY26 and +22.1% in Q1 FY26. PAT margin is stable-to-improving but razor-thin, at 1.3% versus 1.1–1.4% across the window. The Q2 FY27 results are filed but not yet extracted; the unverified yfinance figure of ₹41,405 cr revenue and ₹541 cr PAT suggests the momentum continued. Valuation uses EV/EBITDA and P/E against the broad market, because there are no tight distribution peers and the IT-services P/E band does not fit. At 9.4x EV/EBITDA and 14.3x trailing / 10.1x forward P/E, it sits at P9–P13 of the broad market, which is cheap. Sell-side EPS estimates were raised 6.7% over 30 days. The biggest risk is cash conversion: FY26 CFO/PAT was only 0.16x, so profits are being absorbed by receivables and inventory.

Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq, CaratLane, Mia; about 8.5% share of organised retail) and also leads in watches (27% analog share) and is the number two organised eyewear chain, with 3,758 stores. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹20,533 cr, up 25.1% YoY, which is faster than the first half overall (H1 ₹41,970 cr, +19.1%, so Q1 was about +13-14%), helped by studded jewellery growing 32%, jewellery same-store growth of 15%, and margin gains in watches (+27% revenue) and eyecare (+28%). However, the H1 PAT of ₹4,170 cr (+88.6%, 9.9% margin) is boosted by one-offs: ₹536 cr of customs duty benefits and a ₹671 cr reduction in the Damas option liability. H1 operating cash flow was negative at -2.68x PAT (FCF -₹11,585 cr), almost certainly from building up gold inventory. Q2 PAT was not extracted, so the latest-quarter margin cannot be confirmed. On valuation, trailing P/E is 74.3x and forward P/E is 49.4x, which sits inside the 60-100x premium band the sector card sets for top consumer franchises, so I grade it fair. The peer screen does show it as expensive (EV/EBITDA 48x vs a 21.9x median, P94), but that peer set is mostly autos and is not a like-for-like comparison. The biggest risks are that jewellery buyer count was flat YoY, so growth depends on bigger ticket sizes and gold prices, and that the earnings are both inflated by one-offs and not yet turning into cash.

Hindalco is a global aluminium and copper producer: it makes primary aluminium in India, owns Novelis (the world's largest maker of rolled aluminium products) and runs a large copper business, so its earnings swing with LME metal prices. Q2FY27 revenue hit a record ₹91,708 cr, up 38.8% YoY, faster than Q1's +32.0%. PAT reached a record ₹7,533 cr, up 58.9%, but PAT growth slowed from +75.2% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 17.7% to 15.0% quarter on quarter as the Novelis Oswego fire costs hit. The PAT jump was also helped by about 150 bps from a lower tax rate. For a cyclical, the right yardstick is EV/EBITDA. At 9.3x, Hindalco is cheap against its broad Materials peers (P7, median 17.9x), but that median is pushed up by paint makers. Against the 5–8x mid-cycle range for metal producers, it is somewhat rich for a business near peak LME prices. Trailing P/E of 18.2x sits inside the 12–22x band, forward P/E is 10.3x, and the stock is at 85% of its 52-week range, so overall valuation is fair, not cheap. The main worry is that strong profits are not yet turning into cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.19x PAT, free cash flow was -₹16,519 cr, and net debt/EBITDA rose to 1.80x from 1.23x a year ago, with capex set to rise further in FY28.

fundamental.thesis: Bank of Baroda is one of India's largest public-sector banks, with about ₹15L cr of advances. Domestic loans grew 13.5% and international loans grew 39.7%. Q2FY27 total income rose 19.8% YoY to ₹41,966 cr and net profit rose 35.8% YoY to ₹6,532 cr, a PAT margin of 15.6%. The jump came after a very weak Q1FY27 (PAT of ₹1,278–1,783 cr; the sources disagree), so H1FY27 profit is still down 16.5% YoY. The underlying picture is mixed: asset quality is improving (GNPA fell from 1.99% to 1.78%, NNPA from 0.50% to 0.37%, provision coverage is 94.7%), but net interest margin keeps slipping (2.89% in FY26, 2.77% in Q1, 2.74% in Q2), CASA fell to 36.4% and fee income fell 8.5%. That suggests treasury gains and lower costs drove part of the Q2 beat, not core lending spread. For a lender I graded valuation on price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E: at 0.81x book with a 12.7% trailing ROE (19.3% annualised in Q2), the stock is cheap in absolute terms and against peers. It ranks P7 on P/B (median 1.5x) and P21 on trailing P/E (6.8x vs a 16.8x peer median). Part of that discount is the usual PSU-bank discount, so cheap here does not mean mispriced. The biggest risk is that margins keep sliding while credit costs rise (0.55% vs 0.29% a year ago), making the Q2 profit spike a one-off rather than the new run-rate. Data caveats: the Q3FY26 and H1FY26 rows in the trend table look like a much smaller entity (deposits ₹1.5L cr), so the pre-computed trajectory signals are unreliable. Live data also has errors (a 322% dividend yield, and the 52-week position does not match the price implied by the analyst target), so I lowered conviction.

Samvardhana Motherson is a global auto-parts supplier (wiring harnesses, polymer modules, vision systems) operating in 47 countries. Its revenue is driven mainly by the European, US and China car cycles rather than India: Europe is 35% of revenue, North America 22% and India 24%. Revenue growth has sped up from about +11% in FY26 to +17% in Q1 FY27 and +27% in Q2 FY27, reaching a record ₹38,280 cr, and normalised PAT rose 37% YoY to ₹1,175 cr (about 3.1% margin). But much of this growth came from acquisitions: wiring harness revenue rose 68% after the deals, while global light-vehicle production fell 2.3%. EBITDA margin also slipped from 9.5% in FY26 to 8.8% (9.0% to 8.8% YoY), even though booked business hit a record USD 106bn with 19% EV exposure. This is a capital-intensive business, so EV/EBITDA is the main yardstick: at 13.9x it is 27% below the peer median of 19.1x (P20, cheap). On other measures it looks less cheap: trailing P/E of 39.3x is near the peer median but above the 18–28x auto range, and P/B of 4.1x does not match a 10.1% ROE. Forward P/E of 22.1x prices in strong earnings growth, and the stock sits at 88% of its 52-week range, so overall the valuation is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that acquisition-led growth hides weak organic demand in Europe, where Modules & Polymer Products grew only 4%, while copper, aluminium and polymer costs rise 23–44% YoY and keep squeezing margins.

The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

Using P/B with ROE as the yardstick for a lender, valuation is fair: P/B of 1.86× with ROE of 13.2% (14.7% annualised in H1) sits between the cheap (<1.5×) and expensive (>3×) markers, the 14.84× trailing P/E is shown for reference and appears to rest on FY26 profit, and the 'cheap vs peers' verdict is discounted because it compares against the broad market rather than banks. The biggest risk is that loans (+26%) are outgrowing deposits (+21%) with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 93%, which could squeeze funding costs and hide credit stress in a fast-growing, unseasoned book.

Aadhar Housing Finance is a mid-sized affordable housing lender with an AUM of ₹32,643 cr, spread across 632–644 branches in 23 states, and it focuses on small-ticket home loans averaging about ₹11.3 lakh. In Q2 FY27 revenue grew 16.8% YoY to ₹1,048 cr and PAT grew 15.7% to ₹308 cr. Growth is steady but slowing a little: revenue growth slipped from +17.1% in Q1 to +16.8%, PAT growth eased from +19.0% to +15.7%, and AUM growth has cooled from 20% to 18%. Even so, PAT margin rose from 28.3% to 29.4% and ROA is holding at a healthy 4.2%. This is a lender, so I graded it on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE) rather than P/E. At 2.8x book with ROE around 15–16%, it sits between the desk's cheap band (below 1.5x with ROE above 12%) and expensive band (above 3x with ROE below 12%), so I call it fair. The stock looks cheaper on a P/E-only view (19.6x trailing against a 35x broad-market median, and 13.0x forward), and analysts are uniformly bullish, but their next-year earnings estimates have been trimmed slightly. The main thing to watch is loan quality: gross bad loans rose from 1.08% at FY26 to 1.35% now, while only about 35% of bad loans are covered by provisions, which leaves little cushion if more borrowers default.

fundamental.thesis: Firstsource Solutions (FSL) is a mid-cap BPS/digital-services provider servicing Banking, CMT, and Healthcare verticals for global clients, with a growing $1m+ client roster (45 accounts), six consecutive quarters of 4+ large-deal wins, and 11 straight quarters of QoQ revenue growth — the deal pipeline signals reasonable near-term revenue visibility for its scale. The dominant risk is that CC revenue growth has halved over four quarters, the 27.5% voluntary attrition rate constrains margin expansion headroom, and a 66% concentration in cyclical Banking+CMT verticals leaves earnings vulnerable to any corporate IT/BPS budget tightening.

Elgi Equipments makes air compressors (92% of revenue) and automotive service equipment, with about half its sales coming from outside India, mainly North America and Europe. It is a product-cycle business, not an order-book one. H1 FY27 revenue grew 19.7% YoY to ₹2,196 cr and PAT grew 11.9% to ₹232 cr. Q2 is derived as H1 minus Q1, using the reported YoY rates to back out last year's figures, so these numbers are approximate: Q2 revenue is about ₹1,134 cr (+17% YoY) and PAT about ₹129 cr (+6% YoY). That is a slowdown from Q1's +22.5% revenue and +20.7% PAT growth, and PAT growth is now falling well behind sales, partly because of ₹11 cr of restructuring charges in H1. Valuation is fair but towards the rich end. Trailing P/E is 44.3x, at the top of the 28–45x Industrials band. EV/EBITDA is 32x, 37% above the broad-market median of 23.3x, and P/B of 8.5x is backed by a 21% ROE. The stock is ranked P64–P75 against peers and sits at 86% of its 52-week range, so upside is limited even though forward P/E (33x) and upward estimate revisions (+2.7% in 30 days) point to earnings growth. The main risk is margin. EBITDA margin dipped to 14.6% in Q1, and if margins keep shrinking while the stock is priced near its high, the multiple could fall.

fundamental.thesis: Great Eastern Shipping is India's largest private shipping company, running tankers, dry-bulk carriers and gas carriers plus an offshore-rig and vessel arm (Greatship). The system tags it as Industrials, but it is really a freight-rate-driven shipping business, so the order-book framework on the Industrials sector card does not fit. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹3,830 cr (+56.8% YoY) and PAT was ₹2,578 cr (+137.4%), with PAT margin rising from 39.9% to 57.0% over the trend window and cash conversion steady at about 0.97x CFO/PAT. However, Q2 FY27 alone (₹1,825 cr revenue, derived from H1 minus Q1 at ₹2,005 cr) was lower than Q1, so freight rates may be starting to peak. For a capital-intensive cyclical, EV/EBITDA and P/B with ROE are the right valuation measures: at 4.7x EV/EBITDA, 1.19x P/B and 18.8% ROE, with net cash (net debt/equity -0.45 per the filing; the 6.41 debt/equity in the data feed looks like a percentage misread, and the 330% dividend yield is a data error), the stock is cheap against the broad market (P2-P6). Some of that discount is normal for shipping, which typically trades at low multiples near cycle peaks. A forward P/E above the trailing P/E (7.2x vs 6.9x) shows the market expects earnings to fall. The ongoing ₹900 cr buyback, capped at ₹1,530 per share, supports the price. The biggest risk is a fall in tanker and gas-carrier freight rates, which would shrink earnings quickly from record margins while the company is spending heavily on second-hand vessels (₹1,541 cr capex in H1).

Gland Pharma makes sterile injectables. It sells mainly to US partners (the US is 64% of revenue) and has a fast-growing contract-manufacturing (CDMO) arm. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 23.3% YoY to ₹1,834 cr and PAT grew 58.3% to ₹291 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from +6.0% in Q2FY26 to +20-23% over the last three quarters, helped by US growth of 42% and CDMO growth of 31%. PAT margin is 15.9%, up from 12.0% a year ago, but it slipped from Q1's 18.0% as PAT fell from ₹317 cr to ₹291 cr. Part of the YoY jump comes from a weak base quarter, and quarter-on-quarter revenue grew only 2%. Using the pharma P/E yardstick, the trailing P/E of 35.3x sits inside the 28-40x sector band, and EV/EBITDA of 20.1x is 14% below the median. The forward P/E of 24.1x shows earnings growth is already expected, while P/B of 3.5x on a modest ROE of 10.5% caps the upside, so I grade it fair. The biggest risks are the heavy reliance on the US, where a review of generic-drug tariffs is pending, weakness in India and the rest of the world (down 42% and 21% YoY), and conflicting data that lowers confidence: the 92% dividend yield and the 2.74 debt/equity look like data errors, and the analyst target of about ₹3,249 does not match the ₹1,574-2,396 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: ACME Solar is a mid-sized renewable power producer (IPP) with 2,990 MW running and about 5,080 MW under construction, and its 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs) are mostly with central-government buyers like NTPC. Such a company grows through new capacity and the spread between its returns and its cost of debt, and the new BESS (battery storage) and FDRE (round-the-clock renewable) projects are its growth engine. H1 FY27 revenue rose 78.2% YoY to ₹1,745 cr and PAT rose 105% to ₹504 cr. YoY growth has sped up from +59% (FY26) to +63% (Q1) to +78% (H1), and PAT margin rose from 19.9% to 24.7% to 28.9%. Within H1, the September quarter works out to roughly ₹791 cr revenue (below Q1, which fits the monsoon dip in solar output) but higher PAT of about ₹269 cr. Operating capacity barely moved in Q1 (+3.5% YoY), so near-term growth now depends on commissioning, which has started: 66.68 MW of solar plus BESS units went live in early November, and a 400 MW FDRE PPA was signed with NTPC. Valuation is fair: I graded it on EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for capital-heavy businesses. fundamental.thesis: PG Electroplast is a contract manufacturer of room air-conditioners, washing machines, TVs and plastic components for consumer-durable brands, so its earnings depend on brand outsourcing volumes and seasonal cooling demand rather than consumer pricing power. fundamental.thesis: TBO Tek runs a B2B travel-distribution platform that connects travel agents worldwide to hotel and airline inventory, and since the Classic Vacations acquisition it also has a North American leisure arm. Q2 PAT was not available from the filings, and the revenue scale in the trend table does not match the yfinance rows, so treat the absolute figures with some caution. On valuation, the sector card says platform names should be judged on EV/EBITDA and growth delivery, not P/E alone: at 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81 vs the broad market) and 68.4x trailing P/E (P83), with the stock at 88.8% of its 52-week range, the shares look expensive even though the forward P/E of 33.5x assumes strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes perfection while FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days and governance issues are piling up: an unprovisioned ED/FEMA penalty of about ₹22 cr, an ₹8.1 cr employee fraud at an overseas subsidiary, and ₹8.9 cr of FX losses.

Oil India is a state-owned upstream oil and gas producer in the Northeast, and through its Numaligarh refinery stake it also has large refining exposure (refining is about 69% of H1 revenue in the consolidated results). Q2 FY27 numbers are worked out as H1 minus Q1 from the filings: revenue was about ₹11,915 cr (+29.9% YoY vs ₹9,175 cr) and PAT about ₹2,521 cr (+141% YoY vs ₹1,044 cr), helped by a 20% rise in crude production. Growth is still strong but slowed from Q1's +47.3%, and PAT margin fell back from 31.2% in Q1 to about 21.2%. I graded valuation with the sector card's PSU-upstream yardstick (P/E plus dividend yield, backed by EV/EBITDA for a capital-heavy business). Trailing P/E is 10.3x, inside the 8–14x Energy band; forward P/E is 6.9x, EV/EBITDA 8.3x and P/B 1.18x with 12.7% ROE. Earnings estimates were raised about 13% over 90 days, and the stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range. That makes it fair and policy-priced rather than truly cheap: the discount to the wider market reflects lasting government-policy risk. The main risks are a windfall-tax style grab of high crude realisations, and about ₹7,800 cr of contingent tax claims (₹5,284 cr GST/service tax on royalty plus ₹2,485 cr Assam land tax), of which ₹4,858 cr is already deposited under protest.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. Q2FY27 revenue grew a strong +26.2% YoY to ₹4,762 cr, but PAT collapsed -39.8% YoY to ₹112 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from ~13–14% (FY26/Q3FY26) to just 9.5% today — this is the defining trajectory: top-line accelerating while margins are structurally compressing, driven by commodity cost headwinds from the West Asia conflict and the Camso acquisition integration costs; the DSCR of 0.84× (below the 1.0× sustainability floor) and a current ratio of 0.67× flag tightening liquidity. Valuation looks outright cheap: EV/EBITDA at 7.4× sits at P5 vs the broad market (median 23.3×), trailing P/E of 20.2× is at P23 vs peers and -43% below market median — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock screens as cheap, but the multiple compression is warranted given the margin collapse, and forward P/E of 15.1× implies the market expects earnings recovery, which is far from assured. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

fundamental.thesis: Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

Endurance Technologies is a two-wheeler and four-wheeler component maker (castings, suspension, braking, transmission). H1 FY27 revenue was ₹9,159 cr, up 31.6% YoY. Our own split, subtracting Q1 (₹4,348 cr, +29.6%) from H1, gives Q2 revenue of about ₹4,811 cr, up roughly 33%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E, as suits a capital-intensive utility. On those, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 15.4x (inside the 10–18x utilities range), EV/EBITDA is 10.5x and the stock sits around the 12th–15th percentile of the market. But both figures are based on trailing earnings that are falling fast, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 50–59% in 90 days. So I grade it fair, and the low multiples may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that IGL cannot raise CNG and PNG prices to cover higher gas costs (in a politically sensitive Delhi market, with crude near $91 and rising), so margins stay crushed.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue grew +12.8% YoY to ₹1,075 cr — a clear acceleration from +5.4% in Q1FY26 — with PAT rising faster at +22.9% to ₹395 cr and PAT margin expanding to 36.7% from 25.3%; the EBITDA margin, however, contracted to 54.7% from 62.5% quarter-on-quarter, the residential segment effectively shut down at -92% YoY, and FY26 full-year CFO/PAT of 0.34× signals that a large portion of reported earnings is not yet converting to operating cash. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

fundamental.thesis: SBI Card is India's #2 credit-card issuer, a mono-line lender with about 18.5% share of cards and 18.2% of spends, earning on revolver interest and fees. In Q2FY27 revenue was Rs 5,302 cr, up 3.2% YoY, and growth has slowed steadily from +10.1% in FY26 to +7.0%, +3.4% and now +3.2%. PAT jumped 74.8% YoY to Rs 778 cr (margin 14.7%, up from 10.5% in FY26), but that came from falling credit costs off a weak base, not from growth: receivables fell 2% YoY and card spends grew only 3%, while gross NPA improved from 2.41% to 1.90% and net NPA from 1.04% to 0.77%. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book against ROE, not P/E), 3.6x book against a 14.7% trailing ROE (18.4% in the latest quarter) is fair to slightly rich: it ranks P78 on P/B and P67 on trailing P/E among credit-services peers, though the stock sits near its 52-week low, the 16.3x forward P/E is below the 26x trailing, and FY EPS estimates were raised about 7% over 30 days. The main risk is that profit growth is coming from credit-cost relief while the loan book shrinks, and that lever runs out once asset quality normalises.

Prestige Estates is a Bangalore-based developer with residential, office, retail and hospitality businesses across several major cities, and it is consolidating its assets, recently buying out Allure Developers and Gloind Vintage Infra. In H1 FY27, revenue was flat at ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY), and net profit fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr (owners' share down 36.4%, EPS down 36.3% to ₹10.68). EBITDA fell 5.7% while finance, land and contractor costs all rose. The upbeat 'expanding margin' signal is not reliable: the FY26 and 9M FY26 rows in the trend table (₹1,269 cr and ₹861 cr) look badly under-extracted, and the filings pack gives no pre-sales or collections figures. On the yardsticks the sector card prefers, EV/EBITDA of 21.6x is close to the market median (P46) and P/B is 4.0x (P44), so the stock looks fair, not cheap. The 55x trailing P/E means little for a developer, but a 4x P/B on an 8% ROE is a demanding price. On the positive side, operating cash flow was ₹1,311 cr (2.5x PAT), and CPPIB's up-to-₹30,000 cr commitment to the hospitality arm (₹15,000 cr first tranche closed in October 2026) gives the group fresh growth capital. Even so, sell-side earnings estimates are being cut steadily (FY EPS -5.8% over 30 days and -8.2% over 90 days) while 19 of 21 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before the stock is re-rated lower.

fundamental.thesis: KPIT Technologies is a mid-cap software engineering specialist for global carmakers, focused on vehicle features, middleware and connected services, and it depends heavily on its strategic clients (84.6% of Q4 FY26 revenue). Q2 FY27 revenue rose 6.5% YoY to Rs 1,691 cr, with growth slowing from +12.0% in Q4 FY26 (the table's Rs 17,110 cr for Q4 is a units error; about Rs 1,711 cr reconciles to FY26), while PAT fell 28.6% to Rs 121 cr and PAT margin slipped from 9.5% in Q4 to 7.1%, although EBITDA margin recovered to 17.8% from an implied 14-15% in Q1, and deal wins of USD 213 mn are only about 1.2x quarterly revenue. fundamental.thesis: Godrej Properties is an asset-light residential developer that has doubled its national market share from 2.4% in CY21 to 4.8% in CY25. Its FY26 operating base looks healthy: bookings were ₹34,171 cr (+16% YoY), collections ₹19,965 cr (+17%) and new project additions ₹42,100 cr (+59%). Reported H1 FY27 numbers are weaker: revenue rose 107.8% YoY to ₹2,441 cr, but PAT fell 49.8% to ₹495 cr (12.6% margin). That PAT includes a ₹309 cr non-cash fair-value gain, so underlying profit is roughly ₹186 cr. Operating cash flow was negative at ₹-724 cr, and net debt rose from ₹7,607 cr in Q1 to ₹8,111 cr. The trend table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so the 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are not reliable, and H1 FY27 bookings and collections are not in the data, which leaves a gap in the metrics that matter most here. I graded valuation on enterprise value to pre-sales (bookings) and P/B against ROE, not P/E, because reported profit here lags actual sales by 2–4 years. Enterprise value is about ₹59,500 cr, or roughly 1.7× FY26 bookings. P/B is 2.68× against ROE of 10%, and the stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range, so it looks fair, leaning slightly cheap. The biggest risk is that cash generation weakens while debt rises in a risk-off market.

Reliance Power is a leveraged private power producer with about 5.3 GW of operating capacity, anchored by the Sasan coal plant (around 92% load factor) and Rosa. Unlike the regulated-return utilities such as NTPC and POWERGRID, its earnings depend on keeping a debt-heavy balance sheet afloat. H1 FY27 revenue fell 1.9% YoY to ₹3,786 cr, after +3.8% in Q1 FY27 and +12.2% in Q2 FY26, so growth is slowing; PAT fell 28.2% to ₹95 cr (2.5% margin). The implied Q2 FY27 figures (about ₹1,830 cr revenue, down roughly 7% YoY, and about ₹30 cr PAT) look weaker still, though the periods in the table may not be on the same basis. Judged on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive power business, the stock looks cheap at 8.3x (P8 vs the broad market) with P/B of 0.69x and a price at 13% of its 52-week range. That cheapness reflects real distress, not mispricing: net debt is about ₹12,208 cr at 24x EBITDA, and interest coverage is only 0.14x (EBIT ₹110 cr vs interest ₹775 cr). Operating cash flow of ₹1,550 cr and debt falling from ₹14,812 cr to ₹13,802 cr are real positives. But auditors flagged material going-concern uncertainty at the RSTEPL and SMPL subsidiaries (SMPL's lenders have started insolvency proceedings), UPPCL has deducted a disputed ₹158 cr from bills, and ₹303 cr of warrants lapsed, so this looks more like a possible value trap than a clean value buy for a midcap book.

fundamental.thesis: P&G Hygiene & Health Care is a debt-free, cash-rich standalone FMCG company with leading brands in feminine hygiene (Whisper) and over-the-counter healthcare (Vicks), and it earns a very high return on equity (about 115%) because it pays out most of its profit. Growth has stalled. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,145 cr, roughly flat against ₹1,150 cr a year ago (-0.4%), after Q1FY27 fell 5%. Q2 PAT fell 7% to ₹196 cr, and H1FY27 PAT is down 19.9% to ₹322 cr on flat H1 revenue of ₹2,037 cr. The H1 EBITDA margin fell about 590 bps, from 27.0% to 21.1%, and the filings give no volume growth figure to show whether underlying demand is holding. On valuation I used trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers: at 35.2x trailing P/E and 24.8x EV/EBITDA it is the cheapest of its Household & Personal Products peers, about 20% below the peer medians of 43.8x and 31.0x, and below the 40-60x FMCG range. With the stock near its 52-week low (8% of the range), that grades as cheap. The sector card warns that a cheap FMCG stock usually signals a structural problem. Here that looks like profits shrinking on flat sales, and analysts have cut EPS estimates by 5.7% over 90 days, so the discount may be earned rather than a mispricing. Cash conversion is solid (CFO/PAT 1.16x in H1) and there is a net cash buffer of about ₹700 cr, which caps downside risk.

fundamental.thesis: Belrise Industries is a mid-cap auto ancillary manufacturer supplying structural and chassis components to OEMs across 2Ws, PVs, and CVs, now diversifying into aerospace/defence via the £13.2 mn Chester Hall (UK) acquisition and the $5.65 mn Hyva India tipper body deal. At a trailing P/E of 41.1× versus the auto sector median of 18–28× (auto ancillaries carry no structural premium that justifies this gap), the stock is expensive; EV/EBITDA of 18.1× is below the broad-market median but sits against a deteriorating margin trend, and the stock trading at 95.7% of its 52-week range with EPS estimates revised down -11.9% over 90 days signals derating risk rather than re-rating potential. The dominant risk is a compounding stack of high leverage (D/E 29.1), margin compression, multiple pending NCLT amalgamation schemes, dual near-term acquisition integrations, and a RISK_OFF macro backdrop with FII outflows and rising crude — all of which strain the premium multiple at a time when the earnings growth that could justify it is being revised lower.

fundamental.thesis: Hyundai Motor India is a large passenger-vehicle maker with a net-cash balance sheet (filing net debt/EBITDA -0.88x, which overrides the 5.48 debt/equity figure in the data feed), and it is starting a new product cycle with the Bayon launch and a mass-market EV planned for Q4 FY27. Q2 FY27 revenue growth accelerated from -0.5% to +18.5% YoY (Rs 20,696 cr, on record volumes of 219,072 units, up 15%), but PAT still fell 23.9% to Rs 1,196 cr and EBITDA margin dropped about 440 bps YoY to 9.5% on commodity costs; this rests on Q1 and Q2 FY27 only, because the FY26 and Q3 FY26 rows look wrong in scale and the H1 EBITDA margin does not reconcile, so the pre-computed trend signals are unreliable. Using the OEM P/E band from the sector card (18-30x) as the yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 36.2x trailing earnings with EV/EBITDA of 21.2x; the 23.8x forward P/E is within the band, but it relies on a margin recovery while current-year EPS estimates have been cut 13.8% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that volume growth keeps failing to reach profit if commodity costs stay high, which would leave the expected earnings rebound and the bullish 26-of-29 analyst buy ratings exposed.

Techno Electric is a midcap power-infrastructure EPC contractor, mainly building transmission and distribution projects, and it is shifting into data centres. That puts it in the government-led grid-capex upcycle described in the sector card, but this pack has no order book or order inflow figures to check that against. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 26.9% YoY to ₹1,738 cr and PAT grew only 4.9% to ₹252 cr (17.1% on continuing operations). Revenue growth has slowed from the +43% to +67% range of earlier periods, and margins have slipped: PAT margin went from 17.5% to 14.5% and EBITDA margin from 21.2% to 19.3%. Q2 alone (H1 minus Q1, about ₹1,108 cr revenue and ₹159 cr PAT) points to faster execution. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses. At 19.4x it is about 17% below the broad-market median of 23.3x. Trailing P/E of 26.2x sits just under the 28–45x Industrials band and forward P/E is 16.7x, but because the stock is near its 52-week low, sell-side estimates are being cut and earnings convert poorly to cash, I call it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is earnings quality: operating cash flow was only 0.19x PAT in H1 and -1.24x in FY26, and about ₹590 cr of Afghanistan receivables plus ₹212 cr in arbitration claims are tied up. The ₹2,030 cr net cash pile softens that risk.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). The quality of that growth is mixed: offtake rose +7.6% to 384.2 MT while production fell -2% to 321 MT, so part of the growth came from selling down inventory, which fell 49% to 130.3 MT. Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: ICICI Lombard is one of India's largest private general insurers, with about 10.3% of the motor market and a fast-growing health book (retail health +64% YoY), offset by a shrinking commercial lines segment (-8.1%). In H1 FY27, gross direct premium rose only 5.4% YoY to Rs 15,110 cr (gross premium written +9.6% to Rs 16,562 cr) while PAT fell about 14% to Rs 1,350 cr, because the claims ratio worsened from 72.3% to 77.4%, the expense ratio rose to 74.5% and the combined ratio reached 107%, so profits now lean on investment income. Judged on the insurer yardstick of price-to-book against return on equity (not P/E or EV/EBITDA), a P/B of 5.45x for a ROE of 15.5-17.9% is expensive: the stock sits at the 91st percentile of financials on P/B and the 79th on trailing P/E (31.8x vs a 17.5x median), and the forward P/E of 23.8x assumes an earnings rebound that analysts have been trimming (-3% FY EPS revisions over 90 days). The biggest risk is that claims inflation in motor and health keeps the combined ratio above 105% and the expected rebound never arrives, which would leave little room to justify the premium multiple.

fundamental.thesis: InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) is India's largest airline, with a 442-aircraft fleet, and its results are driven mainly by fares, fuel costs and the rupee rather than the order-book measures in the Industrials sector card. Q2FY27 revenue growth accelerated over the available periods from +4.7% in Q1FY26 to +25.9% (Rs 23,364 cr), but this was fare-led (yield +34.3%) while passengers fell 4.7% and load factor fell 2.2 points to 80.3%; the Rs 1,879 cr net loss narrowed from Rs 2,582 cr, including about Rs 1,155 cr of forex losses, with unit revenue (Rs 5.76) still below unit cost (Rs 6.22) and fuel cost per unit up 68.9%. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick because trailing P/E is unavailable on losses, valuation is fair rather than cheap: 16.4x is 51.7% below the 34.0x peer median and forward P/E is 21.0x, but those peers are mostly capital-goods and auto companies, the forward multiple relies on a recovery while current-year EPS estimates have been cut 18.9% in 90 days, and P/B of 27.1x is the highest in the group. The biggest risk is that crude (USD 96.61 and rising) and a weak rupee keep costs above fares while softer passenger demand limits further fare increases, although Rs 39,929 cr of free cash provides a cushion against Rs 87,303 cr of debt including leases; the H1FY27 PAT and margin figures do not reconcile with Q1 and Q2, so this view relies on the quarterly numbers.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Green Energy is India's largest renewable power producer. H1 minus Q1 implies Q2 revenue of about ₹4,258 cr, faster than Q1's +16.6%, but Q2 PAT margin of about 17.5% is below Q1's 22.2%. The 'expanding margin' signal compares half-year, full-year and nine-month figures, so it is not like-for-like and overstates the improvement. This is a capital-intensive business, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, and on that basis it is expensive. EV/EBITDA is 31.8x against a utilities peer median of 11.6x, the highest in the group. Price-to-book is 12.7x while ROE is only 7.6%, and the stock sits at 93.6% of its 52-week range. Sell-side earnings estimates have been cut 14.5% over 90 days even though 9 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower. The main risk is the balance sheet: net debt is 5.6x run-rate EBITDA, gross debt is ₹1.12 lakh cr and H1 free cash flow was -₹7,141 cr, so the equity depends on capacity coming online on time and on cheap refinancing. That is happening while US yields are at 5% and the rupee is weakening.

The biggest risk is that the 39.8x forward P/E assumes about 29% EPS growth while FY estimates have been cut 3.1% in the last 30 days, and the 136% dividend yield and 4.61 debt/equity readings look unreliable, so they were not used to judge income or leverage.

fundamental.thesis: Shree Cement is a large Indian cement maker with a growing UAE business and is expanding toward a long-term capacity target of 80 MT. Revenue growth accelerated from +4.0% in Q3FY26 to +23.9% in Q2FY27 (Rs 5,897 cr, on 14% higher consolidated volumes), but PAT fell 15.2% to Rs 263 cr, while EBITDA margin dropped from 23.8% in Q1FY27 to 17.2% and EBITDA per tonne fell 8% YoY to Rs 966, near the low end of the Rs 900-1,100 healthy range. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick, the stock looks expensive at a snapshot 30.4x versus a 17.9x peer median (P80), and its 48.6x trailing P/E is well above the 37.3x peer median and the 12-22x Materials benchmark; however, TTM EBITDA from the filings implies only about 18x EV/EBITDA, so the grade leans more on P/E and is held with moderate confidence despite the stock sitting near its 52-week low (19% of range). The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit as fuel costs stay high with crude rising, a concern reflected in FY EPS estimates being cut 14.1% in 30 days despite a mostly bullish rating mix, while the snapshot's 66% dividend yield and 38.15 debt/equity are treated as data errors (the filings show debt/equity of 0.08).

fundamental.thesis: Yes Bank is a mid-sized private bank (₹4.69 lakh cr assets, ₹2.73 lakh cr advances) still rebuilding after its 2020 rescue, with improving asset quality (GNPA 1.5% to 1.3%, NNPA 0.3% to 0.2%, PCR 81.9%) but only a 35.1% CASA ratio and a high 63% cost-to-income ratio. The latest extracted figures are FY26 (Q2FY27 results and the earnings call are filed but not in our data, so these numbers are stale). FY26 revenue grew just +1.5% to ₹36,928 cr, while PAT jumped +43.6% to about ₹3,512 cr off a low base, and Q4 NII grew +15.9% with advances up 11.1% and NIM rising to about 2.6-2.7%. Using the bank yardstick of price-to-book versus return on equity, a P/B of 1.47x is at the peer median (P50) but rich for a 7.1% ROE, which is well below the cost of equity and implies a fair P/B nearer 0.6-0.9x even on a recovery case, so I grade it expensive; trailing P/E of 20.6x also sits at P79 vs peers (median 16.8x). The biggest open risk is the 2026-10-24 Supreme Court judgment on the 2020 AT1 bond write-off, whose outcome is not in our data and could be material to capital, compounded by 10 of 13 analysts rating it a sell and EPS estimates being cut about 2-3% over 30-90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Max Financial Services is the listed holding company for Axis Max Life Insurance, a large private life insurer in which it owns 80.01%. Q2FY27 revenue rose 18.5% YoY to ₹11,601 cr, with premium income of ₹10,187 cr, while PAT of ₹100 cr jumped from a very low ₹5.91 cr base but fell from ₹118 cr in Q1, taking PAT margin from 1.6% to 0.9%; the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly and 9-month periods, Q4FY26 and FY26 data are missing, and H1 revenue of ₹17,484 cr does not match Q1 plus Q2 (₹18,876 cr). The right yardstick for a life insurer is P/EV, but neither P/EV nor VNB margin or APE growth was provided, so the 'expensive' grade is provisional and rests on peer multiples: forward P/E of 102.3x vs a 46.0x median, P/B of 20.3x vs 6.8x, and EV/EBITDA of 69.1x vs 58.8x, with the 682.7x trailing P/E given little weight because accounting profit understates life insurer economics. The biggest risk is paying a top-of-peer-group price without evidence of new-business value growth, while the planned merger into Axis Max Life still needs IRDAI and shareholder approvals, and the peer table's labelling conflict and the consensus upside figure (+54.8% stated, about +14% implied by a price near ₹1,618) both need checking.

Alkem is mainly an India branded-generics drug maker: about 68% of sales come from India, it ranks No. 1 in trade generics and No. 3 by prescriptions, and it leads in anti-infectives. Its US generics, biotech (Enzene) and newly acquired MedTech (Occlutech) businesses are smaller. In Q2FY27, revenue grew 13.8% YoY to ₹4,552 cr and EBITDA margin rose to 22.5% from 20.5% in Q1. Consolidated PAT, however, fell 14.4% YoY to ₹667 cr, a 14.7% margin, because of a higher tax rate and a high base: Q2FY26 included a ₹14.3 cr one-off gain. Two parts of the growth story are weaker than the headline: India sales grew 9.5%, below the overall Indian drug market's 13.8% even though chronic medicines did well, and US sales growth slowed sharply to 2.4% from 20.3% in FY26. I graded valuation on P/E against peers plus EV/EBITDA. The stock trades at 27.4x trailing and 23.1x forward earnings, about 25% below the peer median of 36.4x (P31) and just under the sector's 28–40x band. EV/EBITDA is 20.2x, close to the peer median (P46). With the price mid-way in its 52-week range, I call it fair rather than cheap. Biggest risk: the Daman plant's Aug-2026 US FDA OAI status (official action indicated) on top of mid-teens US price erosion, while analysts have cut EPS estimates 3.1% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Oberoi Realty is a Mumbai (MMR) ultra-luxury residential developer that is also building a rental income base (offices, malls and hotels), and it runs a very clean balance sheet: debt/equity is 0.14x, interest coverage is 13.6x and net debt is only ₹830 cr. H1FY27 revenue rose 7.4% YoY to ₹2,972 cr and PAT rose 10.4% to ₹1,305 cr. However, Q1 alone was +31.7% (₹1,301 cr), so the implied Q2 revenue of about ₹1,671 cr is roughly 6% below last year, and implied Q2 PAT of about ₹761 cr is flat. The headline 'accelerating' signal therefore hides a slowdown in Q2, although this is normal for a developer that recognises revenue only when projects are handed over. Following the sector card, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B rather than P/E: EV/EBITDA is 17.6x (about 25% below the broad-market median) and P/B is 3.5x for a 42% PAT-margin business, with the stock mid-way in its 52-week range, which I grade as fair. Conviction is held back because the key forward metrics (pre-sales/bookings, collections and the launch pipeline) are missing from the data provided. I also ignored two obvious data errors: the 45% dividend yield and the 15.77 debt/equity figure.

fundamental.thesis: Aavas Financiers is a mid-sized affordable housing lender with AUM of Rs 24,801 cr across 443 branches in 15 states. Revenue growth has slowed steadily from +15.7% in Q1 FY26 to +12.9% in Q1 FY27 and +10.4% in Q2 FY27 (about Rs 736 cr, derived as H1 minus Q1), while PAT growth fell from +23.0% to +10.7% (about Rs 182 cr); PAT margin has held at around 24-25% for five quarters, and gross NPA is flat YoY at 1.24%, though up from 1.22% in Q1 FY27. On the P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders, valuation is fair at 2.3x book (about 2.2x on the latest Rs 5,398 cr net worth) with ROE of 13.9%; I gave no weight to the 'cheap' peer verdict because it compares Aavas with the broad market rather than lenders, or to the +41% consensus upside because market cap and 52-week position imply a price near Rs 1,468, or only about 7% upside to the Rs 1,577 target. The biggest risk is that growth keeps slowing while expectations stay high: taken at face value, the 12.56x forward P/E implies about 31% earnings growth, against about 11% delivered last quarter, and NIM, credit-cost and guidance data were not available to support that step-up.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC is a ₹33,750 cr mid-cap asset manager whose earnings depend mainly on equity assets under management (AUM) and fund flows. Revenue growth is weak at +3.9% YoY to ₹526 cr in Q2 FY27 (+3.5% in Q1, +9.5% in FY26), with AUM up only 4%, while PAT swung from +11.7% to ₹309 cr in Q1 to -8.4% to ₹221 cr in Q2; the Q1-to-Q2 margin drop from 66.9% to 42.0% is overstated because Q1 included ₹162 cr of other income and the two revenue figures may not be like-for-like. AUM-linked valuation cannot be calculated because absolute AUM is not provided, so using P/E as a proxy, the stock looks expensive at 34.6x trailing earnings, near its 52-week high (99.4% of range), with weak growth and FY EPS estimates cut 15.6%; the 'fair' peer reading (P48) is a weak signal because it uses the broad market rather than AMC peers, and the market cap and 52-week position imply a price near ₹1,167, above the ₹1,103 mean target despite the feed's +35.3% upside. The biggest risk is that a risk-off market hits AUM and flows while ₹69-75 cr of annual ESOP cost weighs on earnings, leaving little valuation cushion.

fundamental.thesis: Canara HSBC Life Insurance (CANHLIFE) is a bancassurance-focused life insurer distributed primarily through the Canara Bank and PNB branch networks, giving it a structural reach advantage over standalone agency-model peers; however, for a life insurer the correct valuation yardstick is P/EV (Price-to-Embedded Value), not P/E, and P/EV data is absent from this pack. Revenue growth has been strong at +25% YoY in FY26 (peaking at +31.6% at 9M before settling), but PAT has grown only +8.5% as PAT margin contracted from 1.6% (H1 FY26) to 1.3% (FY26 full year), meaning topline momentum is not converting to bottom-line expansion — a concerning quality signal; crucially, H1 FY27 results were filed on 9-Oct-2026 but remain unextracted, leaving the current trajectory blind. As the best available proxy, P/B at 8.29× against a TTM ROE of only 8.1% is clearly expensive (P/B < 1.5 + ROE > 12% = cheap; this is the inverse), and broad-market peer rank at P94 on trailing P/E (107×, +205% vs median 35×) and P98 on forward P/E confirm top-decile expensiveness with no margin of safety. The single biggest risk is that thin, contracting PAT margins (1.3%) combined with a ₹287.5 cr NCD issuance signalling capital needs leave the earnings base fragile — any claims spike, cost overrun, or distribution slowdown would disproportionately impair an already leverage-heavy, low-ROE profile in a RISK_OFF macro regime where Financials are macro-underweight.

Cummins India is the market leader in diesel and gas engines and gensets in India, and its high-horsepower power-generation business is strongly tied to data-centre demand: data centres were 40% of the power-gen mix in Q1 FY27, up from 23% a year earlier. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 10.7% YoY to ₹6,727 cr, but PAT fell 8.9% to ₹1,116 cr and EBITDA fell 11.4%, so the PAT margin dropped about 340bps to 15.9%; working back from Q1 (₹3,375 cr, +18%), Q2 revenue growth appears to have slowed to roughly +4% while PAT kept falling, so the 'accelerating' trajectory flag is misleading. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an industrial, the stock trades at 50.3× against a peer median of 34.0× (P71), with forward P/E at P76 and P/B at P94, so it is expensive vs peers even though its net cash (₹2,196 cr), 29.5% ROE and 0.91× CFO/PAT show a high-quality business. The main risk is that the market prices data-centre growth with no room for error while margins and earnings estimates head the other way: FY EPS estimates were cut 2.4% in 30 days and next-FY estimates 3.2% in 90 days, even though 17 of 22 analysts rate it a buy.

IFCI is a government-controlled development finance institution, and its core lending book is almost entirely impaired. The KPIs extracted from the just-filed H1 FY27 results show gross NPA at 99.23%, net NPA at 95.55% and capital adequacy at negative 18.42%, so the business does not have a working lending franchise and earns mostly from subsidiaries and treasury. The newest revenue and profit figures are from FY26, because the H1 FY27 income lines did not extract. FY26 revenue was ₹2,069 cr, up 2.5% YoY, after growth slowed from +13.4% in H1FY26 to -0.3% in Q3FY26. FY26 PAT was ₹181 cr (+5.7%), and the PAT margin has narrowed from 13.6% in H1FY26 to 8.7%. Loan growth was -23.6% in FY26 and return on assets fell from 1.27% to 0.69%. Using the sector card's yardstick for lenders (price-to-book against sustainable return on equity), the stock is expensive. It trades at 2.43x book and 119x trailing earnings (96th percentile of the broad market) while earning a return on assets below 1% with negative capital, which is far from the 'P/B under 1.5 with ROE over 12%' level that would make a lender cheap. The forward P/E of 23x relies on an earnings recovery that the filings do not support. The biggest risk is that the stock's price depends on government support and possible restructuring or capital infusion rather than on earnings, so the price can swing sharply on policy news in either direction.

fundamental.thesis: Cholamandalam Financial Holdings is a holding company. Gold-loan AUM grew 92.5% YoY, and gross NPA fell from 2.96% to 1.56% by Q1FY27, but much of the PAT jump comes off the very weak FY26 base, when Asirvad credit costs were high. Using P/B against ROE (the right yardstick for a lender), the stock trades at 1.7x book: that is fair if the annualised H1FY27 ROE of 15.2% holds, but on the trailing ROE of 7.0% it looks full. The forward P/E of 11.0x (P12 vs the market) suggests the recovery is mostly priced in, and with the stock at 86% of its 52-week range, upside from here is limited. The biggest risk is that very fast gold-loan growth, with gold prices now falling, could strain loan-to-value cushions and asset quality, and the Q2 press release does not disclose NPA or provision data to check this.

fundamental.thesis: Shipping Corporation of India is India's largest state-owned shipping company, running tankers, liner, bulk carriers and offshore vessels. It is a freight-rate-driven, capital-intensive cyclical, so the Industrials order-book sector card does not really apply. H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr, faster than Q1 FY27 (+40.3% revenue, +74.9% PAT) and FY26 (+3.1% revenue). PAT margin widened to 28.9% from 20.5% a year ago, cash backed the profit (CFO/PAT 1.10x), and tankers led the growth (+62.5%, 44% PBIT margin), helped by Middle East disruption. On the yardsticks for a capital-intensive lender-funded shipper, EV/EBITDA and P/B, the stock looks cheap: P/B is 1.69x and trailing P/E is 10.65x against a broad-market median of about 35x. The live EV/EBITDA (35x), forward P/E (94x), dividend yield (424%) and debt/equity (29.45) readings look broken and were not used. My rough check puts EV/EBITDA near 5x on trailing EBITDA of about ₹3,500 cr. But these are probably peak-cycle, geopolitics-boosted earnings, and the stock is already at 66% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that tanker rates fall back as Middle East disruption eases. On top of that come stress in the LNG joint ventures (₹240 cr ILT-3 provision; auditors flag going-concern doubts at ILT-1/2/3), board committees still short of SEBI listing-rule requirements, and a government stake sale stuck since 2020.

Schneider Electric Infrastructure is a mid-cap maker of electrical distribution and grid equipment (transformers, switchgear, automation), positioned to benefit from India's power-transmission and data-centre capex cycle. Revenue growth picked up to +19.8% YoY in Q2FY27 (₹779 cr, from +4.8% in Q1FY27), but profit moved the other way: PAT fell 43.3% YoY to ₹30 cr, PAT margin dropped from 8.0% to 3.8%, EBITDA margin fell from 13.6% to 8.4%, and H1 operating cash flow turned negative (-₹29 cr vs +₹84 cr a year ago) as inventory built up. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for order-book industrials, the stock trades at 76.6x against a broad-market median of 23.3x (P96). Trailing P/E is 146.8x, far above the 28–45x industrials range, and the stock sits at 86% of its 52-week range, so it is clearly expensive. The biggest risk is that the market is paying a supercycle multiple while margins and cash conversion are getting worse. Sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 30% over 30 days and 44% over 90 days even though all 3 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating. No order-book or order-inflow figures were provided, so revenue visibility cannot be confirmed.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Motors (TMCV) is India's largest commercial vehicle maker, with 36.2% domestic share in H1 FY27 and 55.7% in heavy trucks, and it holds net cash of Rs 15,900 cr before the Iveco deal. Revenue growth accelerated from +16.1% in Q3 FY26 to +19.3% in Q1 FY27 and +36.3% in Q2 FY27 (Rs 25,338 cr on 42% wholesale volume growth), but EBITDA margin slipped from 11.3% to 10.9% YoY and PAT fell from Rs 2,556 cr in Q1 to Rs 1,253 cr in Q2 (5.0% margin) after a Rs 708 cr fair-value loss; management guides to tapering growth and a 150-200 bps commodity headwind in Q3, so the pre-computed 'expanding' PAT margin signal and the 17.1% Q1 EBITDA margin (it conflicts with 10.9% for both H1 and Q2) should not be relied on. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 16.8x is 28% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P30), and forward P/E of 18.5x sits at the low end of the 18-28x auto range with estimates up 10.1% over 90 days, but the trailing P/E of 49.5x (distorted by fair-value losses) and P/B of 11.8x (P87) limit the cheapness case, and the peer set is a broad-market fallback rather than true CV peers. The biggest risk is the Iveco acquisition, whose final tender outcome, funding and integration burden are not visible in the data provided and could erode the net cash position just as the CV cycle's growth rates are guided to slow, while the auditor resignation filed on 2026-10-31 remains unexplained here.

Tega Industries makes mining consumables (mill liners, wear parts) and equipment. With the Molycop acquisition closed on 1 June 2026, it is now a much larger, more leveraged global grinding-media and consumables group. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹1,720 cr, but only one month of Molycop is included, so it can't be compared with Q1FY26's ₹372 cr. The legacy Tega business grew revenue 21% YoY and consumables grew 36%. However, equipment revenue fell 44%, consolidated EBITDA margin dropped to 15.3% (from about 20% a year ago), one-time costs were about ₹1,900 cr, and earlier FY26 PAT had already fallen 28.9%. Results for Q2FY27, the first quarter that could show a fuller Molycop contribution, were filed on 8 Nov but are not yet in our trend data, so the most recent quarter is still unclear. Valuation looks expensive on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive order-book business: 51.7x, which ranks at P90 against the broad market (median 23.3x). The trailing P/E of 88.8x is far above the 28–45x industrials range, and ROE is only 5.9%. The biggest risk is the heavy acquisition debt (about ₹11,200 cr of group debt, with ₹110–120 cr of FY27 finance cost guided) combined with sharp sell-side EPS cuts (FY estimates down about 51% in 30 days).

fundamental.thesis: Titagarh Rail Systems is a mid-cap maker of railway wagons and metro/passenger coaches, so its revenue depends on executing its Indian Railways and metro orders. fundamental.thesis: Nuvoco Vistas is an East- and North-focused cement and ready-mix concrete (RMC) maker with about 35 MTPA of target capacity. It is a mid-tier player in a sector where UltraTech and Adani now control about 45% of capacity. Using the filings trend table (the yfinance rows are inconsistent and were ignored), Q2FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹2,790 cr, up from +9.0% in Q1, and cement volumes grew 9% YoY against 5% in Q1. Profit quality is thinner than the headline suggests. PAT rose 78% YoY, but only to ₹65 cr, a 2.3% margin. EBITDA margin fell to 14.7% from 18.3% in Q1 and 15.1% a year ago. Implied EBITDA per tonne is about ₹875, below the healthy ₹900–1,100 band and down from roughly ₹1,080 in Q1. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, not P/E. At 8.6x (P8 of the broad market, no close peers in the universe), with P/B of 1.09x, forward P/E of 20.5x against trailing 31x, and the price at 18% of its 52-week range, the stock looks cheap against typical cement multiples. Much of that discount is justified by an ROE of only 3.7% and high debt. The biggest risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is ₹5,028 cr, current ratio is 0.57x, free cash flow was -₹246 cr in H1 because of capex, and legal disputes are pending: the ₹490 cr CCI penalty and about ₹454 cr of West Bengal incentive provisions. These come on top of rising crude and a weak rupee pushing up fuel and freight costs.

NMDC is India's largest iron-ore miner and a state-run business (PSU) with ₹8,188 cr of net cash; it is a global price taker, so I graded it on EV/EBITDA and the cost cycle rather than on P/E. Growth has stalled: revenue growth slowed from +27.0% in H1FY26 to +2.4% in H1FY27 (₹13,433 cr), and H1 PAT slipped 0.6% to ₹3,645 cr. Q2FY27 alone, worked out as H1 minus Q1, shows revenue of about ₹6,638 cr (about +4% YoY) and PAT of about ₹1,669 cr (about -2% YoY), while H1 EBITDA fell 15.3% YoY as royalty and levies rose to about 47% of revenue. EV/EBITDA of 7.8x sits at the top of the 5-8x range typical for mid-cycle cyclicals, while trailing P/E of 10.4x is below the 12-22x sector range and at P6-P7 versus the broad market, so the stock looks fair rather than cheap. With earnings estimates being trimmed slightly (-0.5% to -1.5%) and no growth trigger in sight, the low multiple looks justified. Several fields look unreliable and I ignored them: the 397% dividend yield is impossible, the 18.8 debt/equity contradicts the net cash position, and the consensus implied price does not match the 52-week range position. The biggest open risk is the ₹16,189 cr Karnataka mineral-tax contingent liability.

fundamental.thesis: Sai Life Sciences is a mid-sized Indian contract research and manufacturing company (CRDMO) serving global pharma. It is moving clients from one-off projects to multi-year relationships covering discovery, development and manufacturing, which should benefit from the China+1 shift. Growth has slowed: H1 FY27 revenue rose 17% YoY to ₹1,213 cr and PAT rose 19% to ₹172 cr, against +29% revenue and +109% PAT in FY26 and +27% revenue in Q3 FY26. Q2 FY27 alone was better at ₹659 cr (+23% YoY), and management expects a stronger second half as new capacity ramps up. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy CDMO, the stock is expensive at 40.6x (P83 vs the broad market). Trailing P/E of 73.5x is well above the 28–40x pharma range, P/B is 10.3x against a 15.1% ROE, and the price sits at 93% of its 52-week range. Analysts raising estimates (+5–6% over 90 days) and a forward P/E of 49x show strong growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that the ₹621 cr H1 capex and new capacity fill up slower than the lumpy CDMO contract pipeline needs, which would squeeze margins further while the stock trades at a premium.

fundamental.thesis: Sapphire Foods runs KFC and Pizza Hut restaurants in India and Sri Lanka (974 stores as of Q1 FY26) and is being merged into Devyani International at 177 DIL shares for every 100 SAPPHIRE shares, so the stock now largely trades as a proxy for DEVYANI. The latest extracted figures are stale (FY26; the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-22 are not in the dataset). They show revenue growth slowing from +13.0% (Q4FY25) to about +8% in every period since, PAT moving from a small profit to a loss of about -1.0% of revenue, and same-store sales of 0% at KFC and -8% at Pizza Hut. That means growth is coming almost entirely from new stores, not from more sales per store. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because the company is loss-making, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: 27.8x is only slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3x (P61), which is fair for a QSR operator. Forward P/E of 96x (P99) and next-year EPS estimates cut by 21% in 30 days show earnings are not catching up with the price. The biggest risk is weak same-store sales combined with falling earnings estimates ahead of a merger swap that ties the stock's value to Devyani's own derating risk.

fundamental.thesis: CIE Automotive India makes forged, cast and machined components for auto OEMs, with about two-thirds of revenue from India and the rest from Europe (it reports on a calendar year, so 9M26 means Jan–Sep 2026). Revenue for 9M26 rose 12.1% YoY to ₹7,866 cr and PAT rose 16.8% to ₹729 cr. India grew 14.7% while Europe grew only 7.4%. Growth is steady but edging down: from +13.0% in H1 to +12.1% for 9M, which implies about +10% in Q3 on its own. EBITDA margin also slipped from 16.7% in H1 to 16.1% for 9M. I graded valuation on P/E, the yardstick the sector card uses for auto names. Trailing P/E is 20.0x, in the lower half of the sector's 18–30x band, and forward P/E is 15.9x, so the market expects earnings to grow. EV/EBITDA is 18.9x against a broad-market median of 23.3x. That makes the stock fair, leaning cheap, but the peer ranking (P22 on P/E) compares it with the whole market, not auto peers, so I put less weight on it. The main risks are weak cash conversion (H1 free cash flow was -₹263 cr, with operating cash flow at -0.04x PAT) and a slow Europe business. Analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS down 2.3% over 90 days) even though 4 of 5 rate it a buy, and rising crude in a risk-off market is a headwind for auto demand.

fundamental.thesis: HFCL makes telecom and networking equipment (optical fibre, cables, telecom gear, defence electronics), so it sells to carriers rather than being a carrier; the operator-focused telecom card fits only loosely, and I graded it on EV/EBITDA as a capital-intensive equipment maker. fundamental.thesis: Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

fundamental.thesis: ICICI Bank is India's second-largest private-sector bank, with a large retail and business-banking franchise and subsidiaries in life and general insurance. Following the sector card, I value lenders on price-to-book against ROE: P/B of 2.48x with a 16.4% ROE is fair for a top-quality bank, even though it ranks P93 (expensive) on P/B among its 15 bank peers, and the stock sits at 22% of its 52-week range, which makes for a reasonable entry point. The biggest risk is that management expects two more 25bp repo hikes and says NIM will only bottom after Q3, so margins could compress further before they recover.

fundamental.thesis: Infosys is India's second-largest IT services exporter, a debt-free, cash-generative tier-1 franchise now caught in the sector's AI reset, where productivity gains are shrinking legacy time-and-materials revenue. H1FY27 revenue was ₹97,454 cr, up only +1.9% YoY (Q2 constant-currency growth +1.5%, down from +2.4% in Q1 and +3.1% for FY26). Using trailing P/E as the yardstick for an asset-light IT services firm, 15.8× sits well below the 22–30× sector range and 36% below the peer median of 24.7× (P12), so the stock grades cheap, at about 10–18% of its 52-week range. The offsets are $5.2B of H1 large-deal TCV (62% net new), AI revenue at 10.5% of total and FCF at about 113% of PAT. The biggest risk is that the discount is a value trap: shrinking legacy revenue, a guidance cut and small but steady estimate cuts (-0.3% over 30 days) may mean the low multiple reflects a lasting slowdown rather than a mispricing.

IRCTC is the government-backed monopoly for railway e-ticketing, onboard catering, Rail Neer bottled water and rail tourism, and its ticketing arm has an unusually high 82.4% segment margin. Revenue growth sped up from +3.8% YoY in Q1FY26 and +11.6% in FY26 to +18.1% in Q1FY27 and +17.2% in H1FY27 (₹2,703 cr), led by catering (+30.1%) and tourism (+21.2%). Profit did not keep up: ticketing grew only 0.8%, Rail Neer swung to a ₹95 cr loss, and profit before tax fell 11.3% YoY to ₹798 cr after a ₹116 cr exceptional provision. H1 PAT was not in the extracted data, so the PAT margin is null. Under the sector card's yardstick for a non-platform cash-generating franchise (P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers), the stock is fair: trailing P/E is 30.1x, P41 in the broad market and about 14% below the 35.2x median, while EV/EBITDA of 23.4x sits right at the median (P50). That is well below the sector card's 60–100x norm for consumer discretionary. The stock is at only 10% of its 52-week range, but analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 8.8% over 90 days, which argues for caution rather than calling it cheap. The main risk is the GSTAT profiteering order: it says ₹5,041 cr plus 18% interest since 2019 (about 12% of market cap and more than the ₹3,709 cr net cash), while only ₹116 cr has been provided. That amount looks large next to Rail Neer's roughly ₹215 cr half-year revenue and may be an extraction error, but until it is checked it is a serious open liability.

fundamental.thesis: CG Power is a leading Indian maker of power transformers, switchgear and industrial motors, positioned in the transmission and data-centre capex upcycle, with a loss-making semiconductor venture (Axiro) on the side. Per the official filings, Q2FY27 revenue rose +30.0% YoY to ₹3,802 cr and PAT rose +44.0% to ₹409 cr, a clear acceleration from Q1FY27's +14% revenue and +16% PAT (the pre-computed 'decelerating' label reads the rows in reverse order; the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,586 cr does not match the PDF and is ignored). PAT margin improved to 10.8% from 9.4% and EBITDA margin to 16.3%, while the order backlog of ₹23,646 cr (+58% YoY, about 6.2x sales) on order intake of ₹8,485 cr (+78% YoY) gives more than two years of revenue visibility. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for order-book industrials, the stock trades at 90.2x against a peer median of 34.0x (P100 in sector), with trailing P/E at 122x and forward P/E at 68x, at 97% of its 52-week range; that is clearly expensive even after allowing for the electricals premium. The biggest fundamental risk is weak cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT of 0.43x, FCF of -₹290 cr, receivables up ₹788 cr) combined with widening semiconductor losses (₹84 cr in H1), at a valuation that leaves no room for an execution slip or a capex-pause de-rating.

Tata Steel is one of India's largest integrated steelmakers, with a high-margin India business (Q2FY27 India EBITDA ₹17,790/t, about 25% margin) and loss-prone European operations in the Netherlands and UK. It operates inside a steel upcycle protected by safeguard duties. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹65,436 cr, up 11.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,700 cr, up 16.3%. Revenue growth slowed slightly from +14.3% in Q1. Consolidated EBITDA margin rose from 15.4% to 16.3% and EBITDA/t from ₹12,898 to ₹13,462. However, India margin slipped from 26.8% to 25.0%, and Q2 profit may include a ₹3,457 cr one-off accounting gain from revaluing the TMILL stake. If so, underlying PAT quality is much weaker than the headline. Management says H2 should be stronger than H1: India realisations up ₹3,500–3,600/t in Q3 and cost savings of ₹7,000 cr targeted for FY27, of which ₹1,800 cr is delivered so far. Sell-side FY-EPS estimates are rising (+4.9% FY, +8.9% next FY over 30 days). On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for steel cyclicals, the stock trades at 10.45×. That is cheap against the Materials median of 17.9× (P13) and forward P/E of 10.8× is P6. But the median is inflated by paint makers, and 10.45× is above the 5–8× mid-cycle range for steel, with net debt at ₹91,423 cr (2.4× net debt/EBITDA). So I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is Tata Steel Nederland. Regulators have signalled they may revoke its coke/gas plant permits, the auditor has issued a modified opinion over doubts about its ability to keep operating (going concern), and a large unrecognised impairment of its assets is possible.

fundamental.thesis: Bharat Electronics is India's leading defence-electronics PSU (Navratna), with a ₹68,717 cr order book, about 5.3x annual revenue, giving roughly five years of revenue visibility. The standalone Q2 row is missing, so this uses the half-year (H1FY27) figures: revenue grew +25.8% YoY to ₹12,875 cr, faster than +15.9% in H1FY26. PAT grew only +15.0% to ₹2,595 cr, and margins are shrinking: PAT margin fell to 20.1% from 22.1% and EBITDA margin fell to 29.4% from 32.0%. Also, the order book has shrunk every quarter from ₹74,453 cr to ₹68,717 cr, because work is being completed faster than new orders arrive, and only about 57% of H1 profit turned into operating cash. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for order-book industrials: at 36.0x it is close to the peer median of 34.0x (P65), and trailing P/E of 49.8x is below the peer median of 53.8x but above the static 28–45x sector range, so the grade is fair, with the stock mid-range at 41% of its 52-week band. The main risk is that order inflows stay weaker than execution while margins keep slipping, and analysts' earnings estimates are already being trimmed slightly (FY EPS -1.0% over 30 days) even though 31 of 32 rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Mankind Pharma is a mainly India-focused branded drug maker, ranked #1 by prescriptions for nine straight years with a 15.2% share and limited direct exposure to US tariffs. Q2 FY27 is not reported separately in the data, but H1 less Q1 implies revenue of about Rs 4,337 cr (about +17% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 716 cr (about +38%), with quarterly revenue growth accelerating from +11.5% in Q3 FY26 to +11.8%, +12.9% and about +17%, and H1 PAT margin up 210 bps to 15.4%, backed by cash generation of 1.41x CFO/PAT. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, the stock is expensive: the listed 50.5x P/E appears to use FY26 EPS and is about 43x on my trailing-12-month estimate, still above the 28-40x sector range, while EV/EBITDA of 28.0x is 31% above the peer median (P77); I ignored the implausible 8.0% dividend yield and used net debt of 1.1x EBITDA (FY26) rather than the 38.11 debt/equity flag, which looks like a percentage. The biggest risk is that this premium assumes the Q2 jump will last, yet the source of the step-up is not visible in this data, Consumer Healthcare grew only 2.6% in H1, and FY26 volume growth was just 2.3%.

fundamental.thesis: Thermax is a mid-cap capital-goods company selling boilers, heating, cooling, water and environmental systems, plus a growing green-energy and renewable-utility arm, and it benefits from India's industrial capex cycle. Consolidated revenue growth picked up to +11.4% YoY in Q2FY27 (Rs 2,756 cr), from +6.7% in Q1 and about +3-4% through FY26, but profit has not followed: Q2 PAT fell 5% YoY to Rs 113 cr (4.1% margin vs 4.8% a year ago), Q1 PAT collapsed 85% to Rs 22 cr, and Q2 was propped up by Rs 20 cr of one-off PSI incentive income alongside a Rs 15 cr Green Solutions impairment, so the core margin trend is contracting. Grading on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book industrial, the stock trades at 53.5x, 57% above the 34x peer median and at the 82nd percentile, with trailing P/E of 76x well above the 28-45x sector band; that is expensive, especially with the price at about 91% of its 52-week range and sell-side FY EPS estimates cut about 14% over 30-90 days (the quoted +40% upside looks erroneous, since a Rs 3,900 mean target sits below the current price). The biggest risk is that order momentum is fading: consolidated order booking fell 8% YoY to Rs 3,259 cr, the Rs 14,250 cr backlog covers only about 1.3x annual revenue, and free cash flow was negative (FY26 FCF -Rs 411 cr, CFO/PAT 0.75x), which leaves little room for a multiple this rich.

Mphasis is a mid-tier Indian IT services company that earns most of its money from banking and insurance clients, mainly in the US. In the latest quarter we have extracted (Q4 FY26), revenue grew +7.1% YoY in constant currency and +2.5% QoQ, but growth has slowed from +11.6% to +6.7–7.1% across recent periods. FY26 full-year PAT rose +9.4% on a PAT margin of 11.7%, operating margin held at 15.3–15.4% inside the 14.75–15.75% target band, and deal wins look strong for future revenue: FY26 TCV of $2.1B (+68% YoY), BFSI +15%, insurance +46.5%. On valuation (P/E checked against EV/EBITDA and peer rank), the trailing P/E of 24.7x sits inside the 22–30x IT range and exactly at the peer median (P50), EV/EBITDA of 14.7x is also at the median, and the forward P/E of 18.3x is below trailing, so the market expects earnings growth; this makes the stock fair, not cheap. The biggest caveats are cash conversion and stale data: CFO/PAT is only 0.67x and DSO rose from 76 to 90 days, and the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 are not in our extracted data, so this view rests on numbers two quarters old.

fundamental.thesis: Glenmark is a mid-cap pharma company. Its main businesses are branded medicines in India (it ranks as the 2nd fastest-growing among India's top 15 drug companies), US generics including 20 commercialised injectables, and a global specialty franchise led by the nasal spray Ryaltris, whose secondary sales grew 50% across 55 markets. Its in-licensing deal with AbbVie (USD 700M upfront, up to USD 1,925M in total) also inflates reported earnings with one-off income that will not repeat. The trend data is not reliable. Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-05 but have not been extracted, and the figures we have mix standalone and consolidated numbers (FY26 revenue shows as Rs 1,698 cr but Q4FY26 alone as Rs 3,771 cr). The cleanest consolidated-looking quarter, Q4FY26, grew revenue +15.8% YoY at a 7.6% PAT margin, and the reported growth path (+27.3% → +15.8% → +15.1%) points to slowing growth. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 37.85x sits inside the 28-40x pharma range and at P62 among peers, and the forward P/E of 24.7x (P46) suggests earnings growth is expected. EV/EBITDA of 14.0x is 35% below the peer median (P15), but one-off AbbVie income may be inflating EBITDA, so overall the grade is fair rather than cheap. With the stock at 83.5% of its 52-week range and the average analyst target (Rs 2,660) roughly equal to the current price, upside looks limited. The biggest risk is that analysts are cutting their estimates (FY EPS -5.9% over 30 days, -6.6% over 90 days) while 10 of 12 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower, and the US is still reviewing whether to extend tariffs to generics.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant FoodWorks runs India's largest QSR network: Domino's India, a fast-growing Popeyes, and DP Eurasia (Domino's and Coffy in Turkey), with 3,820 stores across the group. In Q2FY27, consolidated revenue rose 11.8% YoY to ₹2,608 cr, but revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% to +14.1% to +11.8% over three quarters. Reported PAT fell 42.7% to ₹111.6 cr (4.3% margin) because Dunkin was moved to discontinued operations. Profit from continuing operations grew only 0.5% to ₹113.9 cr. EBITDA grew 7.3%, slower than revenue, and EBITDA margin fell 83 bps to 19.7%. On the positive side, Domino's India like-for-like sales growth improved from 0.2% to 2.5% to 4.1% over the last three quarters, Popeyes grew revenue 122%, and cash generation is strong (H1 CFO is 4.6x PAT, though lease accounting inflates this ratio). Valuation, judged on P/E and P/B against sector peers with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check (the sector card's multiple-based yardstick for retailers): trailing P/E is 83.7x (P82 among peers, 111% above the 39.7x sector median), forward P/E is 52.1x (P90) and P/B is 13.6x (P79), so the stock is expensive. EV/EBITDA of 21.9x sits exactly at the peer median, but lease accounting flatters that number. The biggest risk is that ~200 bps of input-cost inflation (cheese, dairy, LPG, wages) keeps continuing-ops profit flat while analysts cut estimates (FY EPS down 3% in 30 days), leaving no room in a top-quartile multiple.
