fundamental.thesis: GIC Re is India's dominant state-owned reinsurer. It takes on risk from domestic insurers across fire, motor, health, agriculture and other lines, and AM Best rates it A- (Excellent) with a stable outlook. In H1 FY27, gross written premium grew 11.7% year on year to ₹24,713 cr, faster than the +5.8% to +6.4% of FY26 and H1 FY26. Profit fell the other way: consolidated PAT dropped 12.8% to ₹4,709 cr, PAT margin shrank from 26.8% to 19.1%, and the combined ratio worsened slightly from 106.36% to 106.79%. That means the company loses money on underwriting and relies on ₹5,015 cr of investment income. Q2 alone (about ₹2,966 cr of PAT, implied by H1 minus Q1) was much better than Q1, whose PAT fell 31%. For an insurer I grade value on price-to-book against ROE, not P/E. At 0.62x book, the cheapest in the peer set and near the bottom of its 52-week range, the stock is cheap even for a below-par 9.1% ROE, and the 4.18x solvency ratio gives a large capital buffer. The trailing P/E of 6.8x supports this but is not my yardstick. The ROE gap is the main reason the market keeps this PSU at a discount to book. The biggest risk is that underwriting losses stay above 100% of premium while estimates keep being cut (FY EPS down 10% over 90 days), so earnings would depend on volatile investment gains.

fundamental.thesis: Dr. Lal Path Labs is India's leading organised pathology diagnostics network — 300+ labs and ~2,000 collection centres — serving a structurally underpenetrated preventive-testing market with no US tariff exposure (pure domestic revenue). Q1FY27 revenue grew 19.1% YoY to ₹798 cr, accelerating sharply from the 10.6–10.7% band seen in Q2–Q3FY26; PAT grew faster at 28% YoY to ₹170 cr with EBITDA margin expanding to 35.0% (from a prior-quarter range of 26.6–30.7%), confirming that operating leverage is kicking in as volume scales over a relatively fixed cost base. At a trailing P/E of 59.2× against the Healthcare sector benchmark of 28–40× (pharma), and sitting at P77–P89 versus 473 broad-market peers on every major multiple, the stock is unambiguously expensive — the forward P/E of 43.85× shows the market has already priced in a robust earnings catch-up, and at 88.8% of its 52-week range there is minimal margin of safety. The single biggest risk is the ₹380 cr acquisition of Sunshine Healthcare in Ghana (a frontier market) via a Dubai subsidiary, which introduces material execution, currency, and governance complexity at exactly the point where a stretched valuation tolerates no negative surprises.

Aster DM Healthcare is a multi-specialty hospital chain. Its merger with Quality Care India closed on 1 July 2026, giving it 38 hospitals and 10,840+ beds across 27 cities under the Aster, CARE, Evercare and KIMSHEALTH brands, which puts it among India's largest hospital networks. Q2 FY27 was the first full quarter as a merged company: revenue rose 19.0% YoY to ₹2,829 cr and normalised PAT rose 34% to ₹281 cr (9.9% margin). Occupancy improved 335 bps to 68%, patient volumes grew 12%, and medical value travel revenue grew 36%. There is only one clean quarter, though, so we cannot yet see a trend, and the FY26 row (₹3,739 cr revenue) does not match the merged entity's scale. For valuation we used EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital business: it is 45.9x, the 87th percentile of the broad market. Trailing P/E is 123x but distorted by the merger, forward P/E is 41x, and P/B is 8.9x against a TTM ROE of only 10.1%. With the stock at 85% of its 52-week range, we grade it expensive. The biggest risk is that analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by about 18% in the last 30 days while all 12 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating if merger synergies come slowly.

fundamental.thesis: Syngene is a mid-sized Indian contract research and manufacturing company serving global pharma, with capacity in India and a newly acquired US biologics site. H1FY27 revenue rose 13.1% YoY to Rs 1,629 cr and PAT rose from Rs 46.6 cr to Rs 140 cr (8.6% margin), but this followed a Q1 revenue decline of 17.1% and a small loss, while FY26 revenue grew only 2.6% and PAT fell 36.1%; the implied Q2 rebound is unproven because the mixed-period trend table, the yfinance rows and the implied H1FY26 base do not reconcile, so the table's 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are unreliable. The biggest risk is that the price near its 52-week low (2.9% of range) is a falling knife rather than value: FY EPS estimates were cut 21.1% in the last 30 days, H1 operating cash flow was -Rs 143 cr, FCF was -Rs 363 cr, and restructuring costs and a management change add execution risk.

Caplin Point is a debt-free, mid-sized generics maker: about 79% of its business is selling formulations into Latin American and African markets, and its US injectables arm (Caplin Steriles) is growing fast. Revenue growth has sped up from about +11% YoY through H1 FY26 to +18.8% in H1 FY27 (₹1,240 cr), and the implied Q2 FY27 shows revenue of about ₹630 cr (+18.0%) and PAT of about ₹182 cr (+15.2%). US segment revenue grew +23.5% and EBITDA margin held steady at 38.5%. PAT margin, however, slipped about 60 bps to 27.7% as depreciation from new capacity rose about 30%, and management raised its outlook by saying it expects the own-label US business to double revenue and profit over FY26. Judged on P/E and EV/EBITDA (this is a healthcare company, not a lender or platform), the trailing P/E of 28.0x is at the bottom of the 28–40x pharma range and the forward P/E of 22.1x points to expected earnings growth. It ranks P37–P53 against broad-market peers on every multiple, so the stock is fairly valued, but at 90.7% of its 52-week range much of the good news is already in the price. The main concern is cash conversion: operating cash flow to PAT fell to 0.57x, free cash flow dropped about 56% YoY to ₹70 cr, receivables stretched to 129 days and inventory rose to ₹544 cr, all while a capex programme of more than ₹1,000 cr is ramping up.

ABFRL is a multi-format fashion retailer (Pantaloons value retail, ethnic brands including TCNS, the TMRW digital-brand platform, and luxury retail) with about 1,286 stores. It is no longer the parent of Madura brands like Louis Philippe and Van Heusen, so the remaining portfolio is still loss-making and growing its footprint. The trend is getting worse: Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,030 cr, up only 2.4% YoY. Growth has slowed from about +11% in FY26 and Q1 FY27 to +6.4% for H1 and +2.4% for Q2. H1 operating margin fell to -7.3% from -2.5% a year ago, and H1 free cash flow was -₹288 cr, so the business is still burning cash. Small bright spots, such as TMRW cutting its EBITDA loss by ₹21 cr in Q1 and luxury growing 30%, do not offset this. P/E means nothing for a loss-maker, so I graded valuation on EV/sales, EV/EBITDA and the direction of unit economics, as the sector card says to do for pre-profit names. Price/sales of 0.92x and P/B of 1.28x (P7 vs the broad market) look cheap on paper. But EV/EBITDA of 18.2x rests on a very thin and shrinking EBITDA base, and ROE is -12.7%, so overall I call it fair, not cheap. The stock is near its 52-week low (19% of range), which may be a value trap rather than a good entry. The biggest risk is that losses keep widening while growth stalls, forcing another round of fundraising or equity dilution.

The biggest risk is that growth keeps slowing from the 40%s toward the 20%s while the stock is priced for perfection, which could cut the multiple by 25–40%, the typical reset for this sector.

The biggest risk is that a premium valuation leaves little room for error if margins keep slipping while cash conversion stays weak, with H1 operating cash flow of only Rs 358 cr after Rs 3,352 cr of financing-arm loan disbursements and net debt up from Rs 2,159 cr to Rs 3,470 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Siemens is one of India's leading electrical, automation and mobility equipment makers, with a net cash position of about ₹8,113 cr. That positions it squarely in the transmission, data-centre and rail capex cycle. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹5,734 cr, accelerating from +14.6% and +14.8% in the prior two periods, and new orders jumped 37.8% to ₹6,228 cr, with the order backlog up 12% to ₹47,034 cr (roughly 2x annualised revenue). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this order-book business, 52.8x is about 55% above the 34x peer median (around the 76th percentile), and trailing P/E of 76.5x sits at the top of even the 50–80x electricals band. With full-year EPS estimates cut 4.5% over 90 days, the stock looks expensive, and the biggest risk is that orders keep growing but margins don't, leaving the premium multiple to de-rate.

LIC is India's largest life insurer, mostly government-owned, and still holds the leading share of the market even as private insurers keep gaining ground. For H1 FY27 (filed 2026-11-05), gross premium income grew 11.6% YoY to ₹275,423 cr and PAT grew 22.1% to ₹25,699 cr. That is faster growth than H1 FY26's +4.8% revenue, but PAT margin slipped slightly from 9.8% to 9.3%. Two data caveats: the two revenue figures in the table actually imply about +27.6%, not +11.6%, so the comparison basis is unclear; and the quarterly rows in between are blank. The right yardstick for a life insurer is P/EV, backed by new-business value margin (VNB) and new-premium growth (APE), but none of these are in the data. On the fallback multiples LIC is the cheapest of its 4 life-insurance peers on every measure: trailing P/E 8.7x vs a peer median of 53.7x, P/B 2.0x vs 6.8x. The stock sits at 30% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates were raised 2.9%. So I grade it cheap, but part of that discount is long-standing (state ownership, a book weighted toward traditional participating policies, and PAT reported under Indian GAAP because Ind AS adoption was deferred). The biggest risk is that LIC keeps losing new-business share to private insurers while margins on that business stay low, and without VNB/APE data this cannot be checked. A 'Change in Management' filing on 2026-11-05 also needs a follow-up.

fundamental.thesis: Marico is a leading Indian FMCG company built on Parachute coconut oil, Saffola and value-added hair oils, with growing foods, digital-first and international businesses (international was about 24% of FY26 revenue); 96% of its business is gaining or holding market share. Revenue growth has slowed sharply from about +20-23% in Q1FY27/FY26 to +8.4%, and the profit jump comes after exceptional items that were not broken out, so the margin expansion should not be treated as recurring. fundamental.thesis: Lupin is a large Indian generics maker with a broad US business (3rd by prescriptions, about 5% of US generic prescriptions) and a chronic-led India franchise that is growing slightly faster than the market (India Rx +14.4% vs market +14.3%, chronic +19.5% vs +17.2%). Growth has slowed while margins are shrinking: Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹7,827 cr (derived as H1 ₹16,104 cr minus Q1 ₹8,277 cr) grew +14.0% YoY, down from +32.1% in Q1. Q2 PAT of about ₹1,186 cr (derived) fell roughly 22-25% YoY, and H1 PAT fell 10.9% even as H1 revenue rose 20.9%, as EBITDA margin slipped from 31.5% in FY26 to 29.5% in H1 and to about 25% in Q2, the pharma operating margin fell to 22.9% from 26.5%, and the tax rate rose to 26.7% from 13.4%. On the business-model yardstick for generics (EV/EBITDA cross-checked with P/E), the stock looks cheap: EV/EBITDA is 12.4x (P8 among 13 peers, 42% below the 21.4x median) and trailing P/E is 19.4x, the cheapest in the peer set and below the 28-40x sector band. However, forward P/E of 22.1x is above trailing, and next-year EPS estimates have been cut 4.6% over 90 days, so the market expects earnings to fall from FY26's elevated base. The biggest risk is that FY26's +62% PAT jump included US windfalls that are not repeatable, which would mean the low multiple reflects falling earnings rather than mispricing; the pending US tariff review of generics and ₹5,817 mn of remaining antitrust provisions add further risk.

fundamental.thesis: Berger Paints is India's number-two decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemical and international businesses, and it says its market share stayed stable through Q2 even as Birla Opus pushes into the market. Revenue growth has sped up from +0.4% YoY in Q3FY26 to +6.7% in Q4FY26, +12.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.2% in Q2FY27. H1FY27 revenue was ₹6,784 cr (+12.5%) and PAT ₹622 cr (+19.3%). Margins are moving the other way: subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 revenue of about ₹3,200 cr and PAT of about ₹217 cr, a PAT margin near 6.8% against 11.3% in Q1. Q2 operating profit grew only 5.2% and standalone EBITDA margin fell 4.4pp because of sharp raw-material inflation and higher ad spend. Because paints are a consumer franchise, I graded valuation on P/E against the sector card's 30–60× band rather than against steel and metals stocks: a trailing P/E of 50.9× (38.7× forward) is fair, though top quartile within Materials (P87), and it sits below the priciest peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND. The biggest risk is that management sees no easing in input costs and is relying on further price increases from November, while a new entrant makes it harder to pass costs on. fundamental.thesis: Colgate-Palmolive India is the dominant oral-care franchise, with the number one toothpaste brand at roughly three times the size of the second player, 69-70% gross margins and an 81.6% ROE. Revenue growth has picked up from flat in FY26 to +9.0% in Q4FY26 and about +12% for the last two quarters, reaching Rs 1,706 cr (+12.4% YoY) in Q2FY27 on high-single-digit toothpaste volume growth, but PAT growth slowed from +10.6% to +4.3% (Rs 342 cr). PAT margin fell from 22.3% to 20.0% and EBITDA margin from 32.2% to 29.0% because ad spend rose 39.8% YoY to 18.4% of sales, while gross margin held flat. On the FMCG yardstick of P/E cross-checked with EV/EBITDA, trailing P/E of 41.1x sits at the low end of the 40-60x sector band and 6% below the peer median of 43.8x (P40), EV/EBITDA of 28.3x is at P20, and forward P/E of 34.1x implies earnings growth, so the stock grades fair with the price at 33% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that the heavy ad spending does not turn into lasting volume and premium-mix gains, leaving profit growth stuck in low single digits while revenue grows double digits.

fundamental.thesis: M&M Financial Services is Mahindra group's rural and semi-urban vehicle-finance NBFC, lending mainly for tractors, utility vehicles and used vehicles, and growing into SME loans (+32%) and loans against property (+41%). H1 FY27 revenue rose 16.3% YoY to ₹11,654 cr and PAT rose 67.9% to ₹1,838 cr. From the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 revenue was about ₹5,936 cr (+18% YoY) and PAT about ₹911 cr (+61% YoY). Part of that PAT jump comes from a weak, high-provision H1 FY26 base. PAT was roughly flat quarter on quarter (₹927 cr to ₹911 cr), and FY26 AUM growth (12%) and disbursement growth (6%) were modest. As an NBFC this is judged on price-to-book versus ROE, not P/E. At 1.52× book with a TTM ROE of 11.9%, it sits just outside the 'cheap' rule (below 1.5× book with ROE above 12%) and at P22 on P/B among credit-services peers, a 50% discount to the sector median. That discount looks justified by ROE below peers, so the grade is fair, leaning cheap. The main worries are FY and next-FY EPS estimates cut about 5–6% over the last 90 days while 24 of 35 analysts still rate it buy, and no fresh Q2 asset-quality data. Stage 3 was 3.4% and Stage 2+3 8.2% at FY26, with ₹1,196 cr of impairment charges in H1.

Page Industries holds the exclusive Jockey and Speedo licences in India. It is a premium innerwear and athleisure franchise that needs little capital, with about 52% ROE, ₹436 cr of H1 free cash flow (CFO/PAT 2.36x) and a net cash balance sheet. Revenue growth sped up from +5.6% to +7.9% to +11.5% YoY over the last three quarters (₹1,440 cr in Q2 FY27), but PAT grew only +4.0% to ₹203 cr because EBITDA margin fell 134 bps YoY to 20.9%. Margins are being squeezed, not expanding. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against ROE, since the business is asset-light: trailing P/E of 56.2x is 41% above the 39.7x sector median (P71), and forward P/E of 44.9x (P79) and EV/EBITDA of 37.0x (P78) are both in the top quarter of peers. That is expensive for a company growing profit in single digits, even though it sits below the 60-100x paid for TITAN/TRENT and in the middle of its 52-week range. The main risk is that higher labour-code costs and the inventory build (₹1,160 cr, 81% of quarterly revenue) keep margins under pressure. The sell-side has cut FY EPS estimates 4.9% over 90 days, and the unresolved FEMA e-commerce compounding issue adds headline risk.

fundamental.thesis: Poonawalla Fincorp is a fast-scaling NBFC backed by the Poonawalla group, focused on consumer and MSME lending with an AUM of ₹74,008cr in Q2FY27 (up from ₹60,348cr in Q4FY26, a 22.6% HoH increase). Q2FY27 shows compelling sequential improvement across all key NBFC metrics: NII grew 12.3% QoQ to ₹1,589cr, PAT rose 21.8% QoQ to ₹375cr (PAT margin expanded sharply to 23.6%), NIM improved 16bps QoQ to 9.26%, GNPA declined to 1.2% from 1.44%, and RoA strengthened to 2.18% — with H1FY27 revenue up +73.5% YoY and the multi-quarter trajectory firmly accelerating; the sector card yardstick for NBFCs is P/B vs sustainable ROE: at P/B 3.06× against an H1FY27 annualised ROE of ~11.3%, the stock grades expensive (P/B >3 with ROE <12% = expensive per house calibration), and the trailing P/E of 57.7× is P100 vs 9 NBFC peers at a 187% premium to the sector median of 20.1×; the forward P/E collapsing to 16.5× (below the NBFC sector lower bound of 18×) signals consensus has priced in rapid earnings normalisation that still needs to execute. The principal risk is that credit costs remain elevated at 2.19% and cost of borrowing continues to tick higher (7.76%, +4bps QoQ), delaying the RoA/ROE recovery the premium forward multiple demands and risking a sharp de-rating from an already near-52-week-low price.

fundamental.thesis: Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, mid-sized Chennai NBFC focused mainly on vehicle finance, with housing finance, asset management and a general-insurance JV (Royal Sundaram) under the group; it is known for steady growth and clean asset quality. H1FY27 consolidated PAT rose 20% to Rs 1,153 cr, and standalone Q2 PAT grew 21% to Rs 475 cr on 28% disbursement growth and 19% core AUM growth, with Gross Stage 3 improving to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rising to 51% from 45%. However, momentum slowed within the half: consolidated PAT growth fell from +33.9% in Q1 to roughly +9% implied for Q2 (Rs 517 cr vs Rs 474 cr), and Q2 standalone profits from operations grew only 11%, partly because of a Rs 66 cr Supreme Court-driven motor third-party provision at Royal Sundaram. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, valuation looks fair to full: 3.5x book for a 16.75% ROE sits at P67 of peers on P/B and at P100 on forward P/E (21.2x vs a 14.6x median), so the quality premium is already priced in, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 1.4-1.8% over 90 days. The main risks are that this premium unwinds if the slower Q2 profit growth persists, and leadership transition after the chairman's resignation on 2026-11-05.

fundamental.thesis: Persistent Systems is a Pune-based mid-tier IT services company (~₹10,700 cr estimated FY26 revenue) specialising in digital engineering and cloud transformation for BFSI and Hi-Tech verticals, and one of the fastest-growing Indian IT mid-caps by revenue trajectory. Q1FY27 revenue grew +24.3% YoY to ₹2,866 cr (stable vs multi-quarter trend of +21–25%), and deal TCV has nearly doubled from $0.33B in Q4FY25 to $0.67B in Q3FY26 — a strong pipeline leading indicator that supports above-sector growth for at least 2–3 quarters ahead; PAT margin at ~16.9% (Q1FY27 per yfinance) shows modest compression vs prior year's 18%+ levels, suggesting cost build-up offsetting revenue scale. At trailing P/E 45.1× versus the IT sector median of 22–30×, and ranked P100 (most expensive in sector) across trailing P/E (+82.9% premium), forward P/E (+77%), P/B (+102%), and EV/EBITDA (+108%), the stock is unambiguously expensive with a significant premium that is only defensible if 23–25% revenue growth proves durable in a sector undergoing AI-driven deflation. Note: the multi-quarter trend table shows revenue in units inconsistent with yfinance quarterly figures (growth rates match but absolute levels diverge ~14×), reducing confidence in PDF-sourced absolute numbers; data_quality is therefore partial.

fundamental.thesis: Biocon is India's largest biosimilars company, selling insulins, oncology and immunology biosimilars mainly in North America (~40% of revenue) and Europe (~35%), with a generics arm and a stake in Syngene (CRDMO). Growth has slowed: H1FY27 revenue was Rs 8,725 cr, up 5.9% YoY, after growth of 17.3%, 14.0% and 10.0% in earlier periods. Biosimilars grew 9% and generics 15%, but services fell 12%. EBITDA margin dropped from 22% to 20%, and PAT of Rs 182 cr is only a 2.1% margin because Rs 453 cr of half-year interest absorbs most operating profit. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, because heavy debt makes the P/E misleading. At 23.3x, EV/EBITDA is exactly the sector median (P50), so the grade is fair. The earnings-based multiples look much worse: trailing P/E is 147.6x (the most expensive of 17 Healthcare peers), forward P/E is 35.5x (P69), and a P/B of 2.0x is backed by only 1.1% ROE, so a median multiple is not cheap for a business growing about 6%. The biggest risk is that sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut about 18% in 30 to 90 days while most ratings stay bullish, a classic pattern before a stock re-rates lower. The H2 pickup management talks about (Pertuzumab launch in Europe, extra Malaysia insulin capacity, Yesafili/Yesintek ramp-up) has no numbers attached.

fundamental.thesis: Fortis Healthcare runs a large hospital network of about 6,300 operational beds plus a diagnostics arm of about 400 labs, and it grows through occupancy, revenue per patient and adding beds. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 17.3% YoY to Rs 2,735 cr, with growth essentially flat over five periods (17.3% to 17.8%, with only a slight recent easing), helped by 72% hospital occupancy and about 7% growth in revenue per patient, but PAT fell 2.5% to Rs 320 cr and PAT margin dropped from 14.1% to 11.7%; lower exceptional gains (Rs 3 cr vs Rs 24 cr) explain only about 1 point of that drop, and even excluding them PAT grew only about 4% by my pre-tax-unadjusted estimate. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock is expensive at 35.6x vs a sector median of 23.3x (P81), and a trailing P/E of 69.3x vs a forward P/E of 40.9x implies about 69% EPS growth, although the mostly pharma peer set makes the comparison imperfect and the 34% consensus upside looks overstated because the 52-week position implies a price near Rs 957, or about 15% upside to the Rs 1,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit while FY EPS estimates, already cut 5.8% over 90 days, fall further against a valuation that needs a sharp earnings rebound.

fundamental.thesis: Balkrishna Industries is a global niche maker of off-highway tyres for farm, construction and mining vehicles. Most of its sales are exports to Europe and the Americas, so demand depends on overseas farm and industrial cycles rather than Indian auto volumes. The latest official numbers we have are for full-year FY26: revenue of ₹10,823 cr grew only +3.6% while PAT fell -24.9% to ₹1,243 cr (11.2% margin), and growth has hovered between 0% and +4% for four straight periods. The Q2FY27 results filed on 4 Nov have not been extracted, and the unverified yfinance rows do not hang together (Q2FY27 revenue ₹1,957 cr against a FY26 run-rate near ₹2,700 cr a quarter, and an outlier Q1FY27 PAT of ₹451 cr), so the current trajectory cannot be confirmed. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-heavy manufacturer, 19.5x sits at the peer median (P60), while trailing P/E of 29.7x is just above the 18–28x auto band but cheap against auto-parts peers (P20). Forward P/E of 21.5x assumes an earnings recovery, yet consensus EPS has been cut 3.1% over 90 days, so overall it grades as fair. The biggest risk is that heavy capex (₹2,600 cr FY26 guidance, free cash flow of -₹754 cr) runs ahead of flat export volumes, while euro/forex swings and freight costs keep squeezing margins.

fundamental.thesis: Tube Investments of India is a high-ROIC diversified engineering conglomerate (core segment ROCE 44–49%) spanning precision tubes, metal-formed products, industrial chains, a 56.3% stake in CG Power (power equipment), and a nascent EV mobility business — positioning it across India's capital-goods and energy-transition cycles. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +17.1% YoY to ₹6,215 cr (consistent with FY26's +17.5%), but PAT declined -3.0% YoY to ₹294 cr as PAT margin compressed to 4.73% from 5.71% YoY — EBITDA margin has contracted sequentially from 12.6% (9M FY26) to 11.6% (FY26) to 10.6% (Q1FY27), driven primarily by the EV segment's ₹147 cr PBT loss in the quarter. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive conglomerate (27.4× vs sector peer median 34.0×, P29 percentile), the stock grades fair; trailing P/E of 84.75× sits at P88 vs peers and well above the Industrials ceiling of 45×, but this is inflated by EV-loss-suppressed current earnings, and forward P/E of 35.05× (near sector median) implies the market is already pricing in meaningful earnings recovery — leaving limited valuation buffer if that recovery is delayed. The biggest near-term risk is the EV segment burning roughly ₹147 cr in PBT per quarter with no stated path to breakeven, while sell-side EPS estimates have been cut -12% over both 30 and 90 days — a warning that consensus may need further downward adjustment before a re-rating.

Bharat Forge is a global forging and auto-components maker that is shifting toward defence and aerospace. Its overseas auto operations in Germany (BF CDP) and the US are struggling, with EBITDA margins of about 3.5–4%. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue grew 19.8% YoY to ₹9,510 cr, up from roughly +7–11% in FY26, helped by defence revenue up about 47%. But PAT fell 67.7% to ₹189 cr (2.0% margin, against about 7.3% a year ago) because of large exceptional charges, mainly the restructuring provision for the German unit. Backing out Q1, the Sep quarter alone made about ₹279 cr of PAT on about ₹4,870 cr of revenue (around 5.7% margin), so EBITDA margin of about 15.3% is holding but has slipped from 17.4% in FY26. Because this is a capital-intensive business I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, and it looks expensive. EV/EBITDA of 33.4x is about 75% above the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x, trailing P/E of 86x and forward P/E of 39.6x are the highest among peers, and P/B of 9.7x is paired with only an 11.6% ROE. The stock is also at 88% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the price already assumes a smooth defence ramp and a recovery in Europe and the US, while analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS down 11.3% over 90 days) and H1 free cash flow was negative at ₹-616 cr.

fundamental.thesis: MRF is India's largest tyre maker, with a strong brand in both replacement and OEM channels, an AAA credit rating and net cash of about ₹1,850 cr. Sales are growing faster but profits are shrinking: H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.4% YoY to ₹17,076 cr, which implies Q2 revenue of about ₹8,660 cr (+17.4% YoY, up from +9.6% in Q1). Over the same period, H1 PAT fell 14.3% to ₹882 cr, and implied Q2 PAT of about ₹387 cr is down roughly 26% YoY with only a 4.5% margin. EBITDA margin has dropped every quarter, from 17.8% in Q3 FY26 to 14.1% in Q1 and about 10% in the implied Q2, because raw materials now take 72.7% of revenue. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-heavy business, the stock trades at 11.1x and 22.5x trailing P/E, which sits inside the 18-28x Auto band, so I grade it fair rather than cheap. It looks cheap against the auto-parts peer set (P0 on P/E and EV/EBITDA), but that set has a different business mix, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 8.3% over 90 days, so the 19.2x forward P/E probably overstates the earnings recovery. The 22.5x P/E will also rise as weaker quarters enter the trailing figure. The stock is near its 52-week low (15% of range), but with no turn in margins yet, it could be a falling knife.

fundamental.thesis: Dixon Technologies is India's largest contract electronics maker (EMS). It assembles smartphones, TVs, lighting, IT hardware and telecom gear, and is building camera-module and display capacity under the PLI scheme and the China+1 shift. The filed H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹37,938 cr and PAT of ₹1,129 cr, with PAT up 51% YoY. That leaves an implied Q2 of about ₹21,900–22,400 cr revenue and ₹411–466 cr PAT, which is only about a 2% PAT margin against 4.3–4.5% in Q1 FY27. Q1 revenue grew +21% to +25% (the two extracted Q1 rows disagree). The reported +147% H1 revenue growth and the ₹4,959 cr FY26 row do not reconcile with the quarterly figures, so the growth rate cannot be trusted. Margins are being diluted as volume grows faster than profit. Because this is an assembly-heavy, low-margin business, I graded on EV/EBITDA plus trailing P/E. EV/EBITDA is 32.3x, and trailing P/E of 42.9x sits at the top of the 28–45x Industrials range, so I grade it fair-to-full rather than cheap even though the stock is only 22% up its 52-week range. The peer-rank block compares Dixon with IT-services companies (WIPRO, INFY, PERSISTENT), which are not real peers, so I gave its 'P100 expensive' verdict little weight. The forward P/E is above the trailing P/E, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7% over 30 days and 10% over 90 days while ratings stay 22 buy. That pattern often comes before a de-rating. FY26 cash conversion was also weak: cash from operations was only 0.22x PAT and free cash flow was -₹271 cr.

Astral is one of India's leading makers of plastic (CPVC/PVC) pipes and fittings, and it also sells adhesives, bathware and paints; the data feed tags it as Industrials, but it behaves more like a building-materials company. The trend table cannot be trusted this time: H1 FY27 revenue of ₹1,413 cr with a ₹15 cr loss, Q4 FY26 revenue of ₹17,347 cr and full-year FY26 revenue of ₹657 cr cannot all be right for a company of Astral's size, so this looks like an extraction error and no real quarterly growth or margin trend can be read from it. Since earnings figures are unreliable, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names: 35.7x is only 5% above the peer median of 34.0x (P59). Trailing P/E of 68.2x (P62) and forward P/E of 43.3x look fair against peers but rich against the static Industrials range of 28–45x, and the stock sits at 32% of its 52-week range. The biggest warning sign is that analysts have cut their FY EPS estimates by about 7% over the last 90 days while 23 of 28 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating at a premium multiple.

fundamental.thesis: BHEL is India's dominant PSU power equipment and heavy engineering manufacturer, with leading exposure to thermal power, defence, and T&D — a direct beneficiary of the government-led capex upcycle in power and infrastructure. Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. The most critical data gap is the absence of current order-book and book-to-bill figures, which are the primary leading indicator for any capital-goods name; without these, it is impossible to confirm that the execution ramp is sustainable, and any government capex pause could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is historically prone to from near-highs.

fundamental.thesis: SRF is a diversified Indian chemicals and packaging-films maker; most of its profit comes from refrigerant gases and specialty chemicals for agrochemical and pharma clients. The SECTOR CARD places it in specialty chemicals, with the ref-gas cycle turning up. The latest quarter in the official trend table is Q1FY27, which showed revenue of ₹5,033 cr (+31.8% YoY) and PAT of ₹759 cr (+75.5% YoY), with EBITDA margin rising to 25.2% from about 18-20% through 9MFY26 and FY26 (FY26 revenue grew only +7.5%, so growth has re-accelerated sharply). However, the Q2FY27 results filed on 21 Oct are not yet in the extracted table, the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,600 cr looks inconsistent with that run-rate (likely standalone or partial), and the H1FY26 row appears mislabelled, so the newest quarter is unverified. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the card names for chemical cyclicals: 19.2x EV/EBITDA, 34.6x trailing P/E and 27.9x forward P/E sit well above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle EV/EBITDA and the 12-22x Materials P/E band, so it grades expensive. The 'cheap vs peers' verdict is not usable because the peer set is capital-goods names (ABB, CGPOWER, HAL) after a yfinance Industrials mis-tag; the stock sitting near its 52-week low (19% of range) only partly offsets this. The biggest risk is earnings quality and cycle dependence: H1 cash conversion was weak (CFO/PAT 0.63x, FCF -₹180 cr) during a heavy capex phase (₹974 cr in H1), with ₹165 cr of forex losses, so any cooling in refrigerant-gas pricing would hit a peak-margin earnings base.

Tata Chemicals sells soda ash, which makes it a global price taker, with plants in India, the US, the UK and Kenya; it also has a smaller consumer and specialty arm (Living Essentials, Rallis). Sales are recovering, with growth of +13.9% in Q1FY27 and +11.0% for H1FY27 (₹8,432 cr), after -1% to -2% across Q3FY26 to Q4FY26. Profit has not followed: H1 PAT fell 98% to ₹10 cr (₹535 cr a year ago), and Q2FY27 alone was an estimated loss of about ₹50 cr on about ₹4,177 cr of sales, against a ₹219 cr profit in Q2FY26. EBITDA margin also slipped from 13.0% in Q1 to an implied ~9.2% in Q2, hurt by UK gas costs, the Kenya suspension and weak soda ash prices. There is no trailing P/E because profits are negative, so I graded on the sector card's yardstick for commodity chemicals (EV/EBITDA plus balance sheet). At 14.5x EV/EBITDA the stock costs roughly double the 5–8x mid-cycle norm, though that is partly because EBITDA is at a cyclical low. P/B of 0.82x is the cheapest in the sector (P0), so overall I call it fair, not a clear bargain. The main reason for caution is that analysts have cut this year's EPS forecasts by 55% in 90 days and their ratings lean sell (4 sell vs 2 buy).

fundamental.thesis: PI Industries is an agrochemical custom-synthesis exporter that also has a domestic crop-protection brand business and a small but fast-growing pharma CDMO arm, with an order book of about $1.1bn and roughly ₹3,500 cr of net cash. Revenue has now shrunk year on year for several periods in a row: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹3,529 cr (-10.4% YoY) and PAT was ₹366 cr (-54.7%). Splitting H1 into quarters, Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹1,763 cr (-9.8% YoY) and PAT only about ₹122 cr (around -70%), so PAT margin fell from 13.8% in Q1 to about 6.9%, and EBITDA margin has dropped from 25–27% in FY26 to 17.2% in H1. We graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for specialty chemicals: at 22.1× it is 23% above the Materials peer median of 17.9× (P60), and far above the 5–8× the card treats as normal for a mid-cycle chemicals business. The trailing P/E of 29.4× looks moderate only because it still includes stronger earlier quarters (on the Q2 run-rate it would be about 70×), and the 21× forward P/E depends on a recovery that has not shown up yet, so we grade it expensive even though the stock sits near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that China's price war keeps squeezing realisations and customers keep cutting inventory, so profit falls further before new molecules (such as Pioxaniliprole) and pharma growth can make up for it; weak cash conversion (FY26 CFO/PAT 0.48×, FCF -₹2,692 cr) adds to this risk.

fundamental.thesis: Coromandel International is India's second-largest phosphatic fertiliser company, with about 17.5% of the phosphatic market, and it has a growing crop-protection arm after buying 53% of NACL Industries. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 6.6% YoY to ₹10,294 cr, but PAT fell 34.0% YoY to ₹523 cr (5.1% margin). This is the third quarter in a row of falling profit (-80.1% in Q4FY26, -23.9% in Q1FY27, -34.0% now), while revenue growth has slowed from +30.7% to +19.0% to +15.9% to +6.6%. The fertiliser business is subsidy-driven and does not match the sector card's steel/cement/paints yardsticks, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 17.3x it is close to the peer median of 17.9x (P47). Trailing P/E is 31.6x, below the peer median of 37.3x but above the 12–22x Materials benchmark, so overall it is fair, not cheap. The bigger warning is earnings estimates: analysts have cut this year's EPS forecast by about 23% in 30 days, yet 8 of 9 still rate it a buy. Profits are also not turning into cash: H1 operating cash flow was only ₹54 cr against ₹1,220 cr of pre-tax profit, as working capital and subsidy receivables absorb cash. Note that the snapshot's 56% dividend yield and 11.47x debt/equity are almost certainly data errors. Filings show net debt of ₹574 cr against ₹14,010 cr of equity, which is low leverage.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Birla Capital is a diversified financial-services holding company with an NBFC, a housing finance arm, an AMC, life and health insurance, and a growing digital platform; lending AUM is ₹2.34 lakh cr, up 32% YoY. In Q2 FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹16,545 cr (+31% YoY) and PAT was ₹1,288 cr (+38% YoY), with PAT margin at 7.8% versus 7.0% for FY26. The Q1 FY27 row (₹316 cr revenue) looks like a standalone figure, so I am not reading the 'accelerating' signal as a real quarter-on-quarter pattern; the cleaner signals are NBFC PBT +41%, HFC PBT +73%, NBFC ROA up 25bps to 2.45%, Stage 2+3 assets improving 72bps YoY to 2.31%, and life VNB margin up 447bps to 16.1%. Because this is a lending-led holding company, I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, as the sector card says, and called it fair: P/B is 2.82× on a modest 11.2% TTM ROE, which is close to the 'expensive' line, but forward P/E of 15.1× (down from 26× trailing) shows earnings growth is expected and estimates were raised about 2.8% over 90 days. The stock sits at 96% of its 52-week range with all 14 analysts rated buy, so much of the good news looks priced in; the AMC is barely growing (QAAUM +4%) and health insurance is still losing money on underwriting (combined ratio 107%).

Voltas is India's largest room-AC (RAC) brand, with a 17.4% market share and a 4.2 pp lead over the No. 2 player; RAC volumes grew 32% in Q2 FY27, and its Voltbek appliance venture is also gaining share (washing machines 8.8%, refrigerators 7.0%). Revenue has recovered from falling 8-12% in FY26 to growing 17.4% in H1 FY27 (₹7,380 cr), but growth is already slowing: Q1 grew 18.6%, and our estimate for Q2 alone is about ₹2,706 cr, up roughly 15%. Q2 profit of about ₹47 cr is a 1.7% margin. That includes a ₹63 cr one-off write-back from the Sidra bank guarantee case and ₹25 cr of PLI incentive income, so the core business was likely close to breakeven or loss-making in Q2. The projects (EMP) segment shrank 21% in H1, and operating cash flow was negative. We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA because profit margins are thin and distorted by one-offs. At 47.8x it is more than double the sector median of 21.9x (89th percentile), and the 86x trailing P/E is at the 94th percentile. So the stock is expensive even though it trades near its 52-week low, and even the 36x forward P/E is above the peer median. The biggest risk is that the rebound is low-quality: analysts have cut FY EPS estimates 16.5% over 90 days, commodity and currency costs are squeezing margins, and EMP keeps shrinking, which could force another de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Petronet LNG runs India's largest LNG import and regasification terminals (Dahej and Kochi), and it earns mostly from volumes and tariffs, so the price of LNG itself matters little to its profits. H1 FY27 revenue fell 44.3% YoY to ₹12,760 cr, because the Middle East Force Majeure (from Feb 28, 2026) and the suspension of all three dedicated LNG vessels since March 2 cut the LNG it passed through. Even so, PAT rose 43.1% YoY to ₹2,394 cr, EBITDA margin went from 13.2% to 30.4%, and operating cash flow was ₹2,984 cr, 1.25x PAT. Some of that profit jump comes from pass-through revenue shrinking and from Use-or-Pay timing, and only one extracted period is available, so the direction of the business cannot be confirmed over several quarters. On EV/EBITDA, the right measure for an infrastructure business like this, the stock trades at 6.1x, in line with the Energy sector median of 6.1x. Trailing P/E is 10.3x, at the low end of the sector range and at P67 among peers, so the valuation looks fair rather than cheap. Some live data does not add up: a 372% dividend yield, a D/E of 10.51 that contradicts the reported net cash, and a consensus target 1.7% below a price that seems to sit near or above the 52-week high. Also, FY-EPS estimates have risen 31% over 90 days while the next-year estimate barely moved, which suggests the market sees this year's profit jump as a one-off.

fundamental.thesis: Bandhan Bank is a mid-size private bank with roots in microfinance, now serving 3.2+ crore customers through 6,400+ outlets, with lending still concentrated in high-yield, unsecured-style segments. Q2 FY27 PAT was ₹620 cr (+455.7% YoY on a very weak base) on revenue of ₹3,670 cr (+16.9% YoY), up from ₹502 cr PAT in Q1 (+34.9%); ROA has climbed from 0.6% in FY26 to 1.2%, and credit cost fell sharply from 2.84% in FY26 to 1.8%. Using the P/B-plus-ROE yardstick for lenders, the stock trades at 1.35x book against a trailing ROE of only 4.9%, so it does not meet the cheap bar (ROE above 12%) despite a low multiple. Forward P/E of 9.9x versus trailing 28.2x prices in a strong recovery, and the stock sits at 95% of its 52-week range, so I grade it fair with limited room for error. Quality signals are weakening: provision coverage fell from 85.9% to 71.2% in one quarter, CASA slid from 29.4% to 26.7%, deposits (+9.2%) are growing slower than loans (+13.1%), and next-year EPS estimates are down 4.2% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Aptus Value Housing Finance is a mid-sized affordable-housing lender focused on self-employed, lower-income borrowers in South India, and it earns unusually high returns for a lender (ROE 20.1%, ROA about 7.7%). In H1FY27, revenue grew 15.0% YoY to ₹1,224 cr and PAT grew 18.4% to ₹528 cr (43.2% margin). However, growth has slowed steadily, from +30.4% in H1FY26 to +25.2% in FY26 to +15.0% now, and FY26 loan/AUM growth was only about 12%. Using the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE), P/B of 2.69x for a 20% ROE is fair, and trailing P/E of 14.5x (forward 10.5x) is below the 18–28x NBFC range, so the stock leans cheap but not clearly mispriced. The main risk is asset quality: gross NPA has climbed from 1.19% to 1.42% to 1.52% over three periods while provision coverage stays thin at about 25%, so further slippage would hit profits directly.

fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. That makes it a high-beta bet on market activity, not a lender. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. For a fee-based broker I graded on P/E cross-checked with P/B against ROE: trailing P/E of 35.8x is above the 18–28x NBFC/capital-markets band and in line with the broad market (P52), while forward P/E of 20.3x prices in a further earnings recovery. P/B of 5.25x against only 15.5% ROE is rich, so overall this is fair at best, with the stock at 97% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 3.5% in 30 days and 4.8% in 90 days. The biggest risk is regulatory: further SEBI tightening of retail F&O, or a drop in market activity in this risk-off tape, would hit volumes directly. Cash flow from operations was also deeply negative in FY26 (-4.5x PAT) because the borrowed-money margin-funding book grew about 39%, which adds leverage (debt/equity about 1.0–1.3x).

Using P/B plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, the stock is fair at 2.07x book against ROE of 14.4% (H1 annualised) to 16.1% (TTM); its cheap rank on trailing P/E (13.9x) is against the broad market rather than lending peers, so I gave it little weight, and I also ignored the +64.9% target upside because the ₹15,315 cr market cap implies a price near ₹519, or about +25% to the ₹651 mean target. The biggest risk is asset quality: gross NPA rose from 2.46% to 3.18% between Q1 FY26 and 9M FY26 while provision coverage fell from 44.7% to 39.0%, and no newer readings were available to show whether this has stabilised.

fundamental.thesis: Go Digit is a digital-first general insurer with about 3.9% motor market share, a book that is roughly 62/38 third-party/own-damage in motor, and a solvency ratio of 2.4x. On the official H1 FY27 filing, insurance revenue was ₹5,386 cr (+4.5% YoY) and PAT was ₹521 cr (-3.2% YoY), after Q1 premiums fell 8.4%; growth has slowed from mid-teens in FY26. Underwriting has clearly worsened: the combined operating ratio rose to 94.1% from 83.9%, the claims ratio to 60.9% from 53.2%, and the expense ratio to 33.3% from 30.7%, which is above IRDAI limits and has led to a forbearance application. Using price-to-book against ROE as the yardstick for financials, as the sector card directs, the stock looks expensive at 4.95x P/B for an H1 ROE of 6.6% (down from 17.7% for FY26), and a 47x trailing P/E adds to that. It is near its 52-week low, but sell-side EPS estimates were cut 10.7% in 30 days and 14.1% in 90 days, so the low price does not yet look like value. Some figures do not reconcile: the H1 profit level does not square with the Q1 and yfinance Q2 figures after the Ind AS restatement, so growth and margin numbers should be treated with caution.

fundamental.thesis: IDBI Bank is a government- and LIC-controlled mid-size lender with a 69:31 retail-to-corporate loan mix and an unusually strong deposit base: CASA is 43.82%, well above the 35-38% sector norm, though it is down 197 bps YoY. In Q2FY27, reported total income rose only +2.8% YoY to ₹9,865 cr and PAT fell -39% to ₹2,205 cr (PAT margin 22.3% vs 62.8%), but that drop mostly reflects a ₹1,699 cr one-off NSDL stake-sale gain in Q2FY26. The underlying business is growing well: net interest income +29% to ₹4,228 cr, NIM up 40 bps YoY to 4.11%, advances +18%, deposits +17%, gross NPA down 53 bps to 2.12%, net NPA 0.17%, provision coverage 99.24% and capital adequacy 27.1%. Valued on price-to-book plus ROE, the yardstick the sector card names for lenders (P/E ignored), it looks cheap at 1.33× book with a 14.2% ROE, mid-way in its 52-week range. The main risks are the NIM jump, which runs against the easing cycle, internally inconsistent prior-quarter figures (Q1 NIM shown as 2.5% while the 50 bps QoQ change implies ~3.6%), and uncertainty around the government divestment process flagged in the October 14 exchange clarification.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Real-Time Market volumes have grown from 20% of its electricity volumes in FY23 to 41% in H1 FY27. In Q2FY27 revenue rose +10.8% YoY to ₹203 cr and PAT rose +12.9% to ₹139 cr, a 68.5% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. Part of that discount is fair given the regulatory overhang, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, so the stock is not mispriced beyond doubt.

fundamental.thesis: IIFL Finance is a mid-size NBFC with a diversified lending book spanning home loans, gold loans, SME credit, and microfinance, recovering from an RBI embargo on its gold loan business imposed in early FY25 that drove PAT to near-zero. Q3FY26 (latest extracted official data) showed revenue of ₹3,427 cr (+40.4% YoY) and PAT of ₹464 cr (+1,040% YoY off a severely depressed Q3FY25 base of ₹82 cr), with PAT margin expanding from 6.4% (Q3FY25) to 13.5% (Q3FY26) and GNPA improving from 2.4% to 1.6% — but Q2FY27 results filed October 15 remain unextracted, leaving a ~9-month data gap that materially limits current visibility. On the appropriate lender yardstick (P/B + ROE), IIFL trades at 1.62× P/B with a 12.3% ROE — borderline cheap — confirmed by a P11 broad-market percentile rank on trailing P/E and a forward P/E of 7.66× (vs trailing 13.65×) that implies strong consensus earnings growth priced in at a meaningful discount to NBFC sector median of 18–28×. The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

HUDCO is a government-owned NBFC (NBFC-Upper Layer) that lends mainly to state agencies for housing and urban infrastructure. Its loan book is ₹1.87 lakh crore, up about 29% YoY. In H1 FY27, total income rose 25.7% YoY to ₹7,789 cr and PAT rose 31.5% to ₹1,762 cr, so the PAT margin widened to 22.6% from 21.6% a year ago. Growth has eased only slightly from the +28-29% pace of FY26, and asset quality is very clean: net credit-impaired assets are 0.04% with provision coverage of 93.8%. We grade valuation on price-to-book versus return on equity, the right measure for a lender, not P/E. P/B is about 2.35x against an ROE of roughly 16-20%, which is fair for a government lender; the low trailing P/E of 10.5x (forward 8.5x) adds some comfort but does not make it outright cheap. The main risk is concentration: borrowing is 7.2x equity and the book depends heavily on state-government infrastructure borrowers, so a slowdown in state spending or slow government repayments (such as the ₹743 cr Andrews Ganj claim on the housing ministry) would quickly squeeze growth and margins.

fundamental.thesis: Jio Financial Services is a Reliance-group holding company whose value sits mainly in its Reliance Industries stake, with a fast-growing lending arm (Jio Credit), an asset-management joint venture (JioBlackRock), payments and insurance businesses. Consolidated total income for H1FY27 grew 136% YoY to Rs 3,195 cr, but this is inflated by consolidating RSHL from April 2026, and PAT grew only about 15% (Rs 1,171 cr vs roughly Rs 1,020 cr in H1FY26), so the PAT margin fell to 36.6% from 47.7% in FY26 and around 60% in H1FY26. Underneath that, Jio Credit AUM rose 154% YoY to Rs 37,320 cr, credit cost is a low 0.48%, and the capital adequacy ratio is 18.5%. I graded valuation with the lender and holding-company yardstick (P/B against ROE), not the 71x trailing P/E: P/B of 1.09x looks low, but ROA is only 0.95% and the equity base is dominated by a low-yield strategic stake, so the low multiple fits a holding-company discount and I rate it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that borrowings grew about 250% YoY to Rs 42,000+ cr and finance costs reached Rs 578 cr in Q2 to fund a young, untested loan book, so asset quality could weaken as the book ages, even with Bank of America's planned Rs 18,000 cr equity infusion.

fundamental.thesis: Info Edge runs Naukri, India's leading online jobs platform, along with 99acres, Jeevansathi and Shiksha, and recruitment remains its main profit engine with a 58.7% H1 operating margin, up 448 bps. RITES is a government-owned (PSU) transport infrastructure consultancy and engineering firm, focused mainly on railways. Its business is asset-light: most of its revenue comes from consulting, project management, exports and leasing, not heavy construction. The latest extracted numbers are stale and come from mixed periods: FY26 revenue was ₹2,415 cr (+10.0% YoY) with PAT of ₹454 cr (+7.3%, 18.8% margin), and Q3FY26 revenue was ₹609 cr (+5.7%) with a flat 18.9% margin. The Q2FY27 results, filed on 2026-11-04, have not been extracted from the PDF, and Q1FY27 is blank. The yfinance Q2FY27 row (₹261 cr revenue, ₹86 cr PAT) is less than half the usual quarterly run-rate, so I treat it as suspect and do not use it. On valuation, trailing P/E is 24.85x and EV/EBITDA is 16.9x. Both are below the 28-45x Industrials range and around the 31st percentile of the broad market, but against low-to-mid single-digit growth, weak cash conversion and sell-side estimate cuts this looks fair rather than cheap. The main risk is that growth stays slow without order-book visibility, while consensus FY EPS has already been cut 6% over 90 days even though all 3 analysts rate it a buy, which is a classic setup for the stock to re-rate lower.

fundamental.thesis: Newgen is a mid-cap Indian software product company that sells low-code and AI-led process automation platforms (NewgenONE), mainly to banks, insurers and governments. It is not a headcount-driven services firm. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹422 cr (+5.0% YoY) and PAT was ₹87 cr (+6.0% YoY, 20.6% margin). Headline growth has slowed from +11.2% in Q1FY27, so the pre-computed 'accelerating' label is wrong because the table is ordered newest-first. Underneath, quality is better: annuity revenue grew 15% to ₹268 cr (63.5% of revenue), SaaS grew 36% (down from 40%) and subscription grew 18% (down from 21%), while lumpy licence and implementation revenue dragged the total. On the IT yardstick of trailing P/E, the stock trades at 22.6×, the bottom of the 22–30× IT band, with forward P/E of 17.1×, EV/EBITDA of 14.8× (P25 vs the broad market) and price at 15.7% of its 52-week range, so I grade it fair-to-cheap and call it fair. The biggest risk is that headline growth stays in single digits while the founder CMD, Diwakar Nigam, remains unavailable due to ill-health. That combines with next-FY EPS estimate cuts (-2.5% over 90 days) and middling cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.72×).

Bombay Burmah is a Wadia group holding company rather than a pure FMCG business: almost all its revenue comes from its controlling stake in Britannia (the bakery segment earned ₹10,605 cr of revenue at a 16.2% margin in H1), with tea plantations and auto-electrical parts as small side businesses that are losing money. Consolidated H1 FY27 revenue grew 11.7% YoY to ₹10,787 cr, up from about 6–7% growth through FY26, and PAT grew 12.1% to ₹1,192 cr (11.1% margin). However, 55% of that PAT (₹656 cr) belongs to Britannia's minority shareholders, and the 'expanding PAT margin' trend is not reliable because it mixes H1, 9M and full-year periods that don't line up. I used EV/EBITDA and P/B together with peer rank, since P/E alone misleads for a holding company, and the stock looks cheap on every one: trailing P/E 7.8x against an FMCG norm of 40–60x, EV/EBITDA 3.1x (P0 among peers), P/B 1.4x (P9), and the price sits at 15% of its 52-week range. But the sector card warns that 'cheap FMCG' usually means a structural problem, and here it is a lasting holding-company discount, so a re-rating is not a given. Governance is the biggest risk to this view: the CFO and Company Secretary both resigned on results day, short-term debt doubled to ₹2,612 cr from ₹1,270 cr, cash conversion fell to 0.63x CFO/PAT, and SEBI's appeal in the Supreme Court against associate Bombay Dyeing is still pending.

fundamental.thesis: Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation, now Adani-promoted) is a mid-sized EPC contractor in marine, foundation, tunnelling and urban infrastructure work, with a record order book of ₹32,715 cr at Sept 30, 2026, up about 58% from ₹20,646 cr a year earlier and roughly 3.0x trailing-twelve-month revenue of about ₹10,800 cr. Execution has sped up: Q2 FY27 revenue rose 25.2% YoY to ₹2,749 cr, after +5.6% in Q1, and H1 revenue grew 14.6% to ₹5,470 cr. Profit quality is weaker than the topline: Q2 PAT rose 21.3% to ₹131 cr, but EBITDA margin slipped from 11.1% to 10.2% YoY, PAT margin is down to about 4.8%, and H1 operating cash flow was negative (CFO/PAT -0.29x) as contract assets rose by ₹474 cr. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 19.9x, 15% below the broad-market median, and its trailing P/E of 34.3x sits inside the 28–45x Industrials range, so the grade is fair; however, the price is at 91% of its 52-week range and consensus EPS estimates have been cut 7% in 30 days and 12% in 90 days, which caps near-term upside. Note: yfinance shows Q2 revenue of ₹2,034 cr against ₹2,749 cr in the filing, and its 26% dividend yield and 37.7 debt/equity figures are clearly data errors; the filing figures are used throughout.

fundamental.thesis: Cochin Shipyard (COCHINSHIP) is India's largest PSU shipyard executing defence (Navy/Coast Guard) and commercial vessel contracts, backed by an order book of ₹21,100 cr (~5× annualised revenue) that provides multi-year execution visibility — structurally the most compelling asset on the balance sheet. Revenue growth has decelerated from +38.5% YoY in Q1 FY26 to +15.5% for 9M FY26, but more critically, PAT has swung sharply negative (-18.5% YoY in 9M FY26 vs +7.8% in Q1 FY26) as EBITDA margins compressed from 28.0% to 21.3% — a classic fixed-price-contract cost-creep pattern, likely driven by ISRF ramp-up overheads and higher input/subcontracting costs; cash conversion is deeply negative (CFO/PAT -2.40×, FCF -₹812 cr in H1 FY26), which is the most immediate red flag. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive model per the sector card, 45.51× sits at the upper bound of the 28–45× Industrials range and at P86 in the broad market (95% premium to median), grading expensive; the forward P/E discount (33.25× vs 54× trailing) signals the street is pricing in a sharp earnings recovery — but that recovery has not yet appeared in filed numbers and Q1 FY27 extraction is blank despite the August 2026 filing date. The single biggest risk is that margin compression deepens further on the ISRF ramp and rising crude-linked operating costs, in a RISK_OFF macro with D/E at 28.47 — any slippage in earnings recovery would unwind the current rich valuation quickly.

Usha Martin is one of the world's leading makers of specialty wire ropes and wires. It has been reshaped into a focused wire-and-rope business after selling its steel and bright-bar unit to Tata Steel Long Products and its cables business to RR Kabel for ₹77 cr (effective 31 Oct 2026). H1FY27 revenue rose 14.8% YoY to ₹2,021 cr and PAT rose 28.2% to ₹271 cr, with PAT margin up to 13.4% from 12.0%. However, the Q2FY27 figures implied by H1 minus Q1 show a slowdown: revenue of about ₹988 cr is up only about 9.5% YoY, against +16.4% in Q1, and PAT of about ₹129 cr is up about 17%, against +41% in Q1. So the 'accelerating' label rests mainly on Q1, while margins have held at about 13%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive manufacturer. EV/EBITDA of 19.4x and trailing P/E of 28.3x sit at the low end of the Industrials range (28–45x), above the plain Materials range, and about 17–19% below the broad-market median (P38–P40). That makes it fair, not cheap. The forward P/E of 21.2x and small upward estimate revisions point to some expected earnings growth. The weak spots are cash generation and governance: H1 operating cash flow fell 18% YoY even as profit rose 28% (CFO/PAT 0.78x, down from 1.42x in FY26), and ED/CBI proceedings over ₹190 cr of attached Ranchi land are still pending, with hearings on 28 Nov and 4 Dec.

fundamental.thesis: Delhivery is India's largest independent third-party logistics company, earning most of its revenue from e-commerce express parcels and part-truckload (PTL) freight. It does not run on an order book, so the card's order-book yardstick does not fit and it is judged here on volume growth, margins and EV/EBITDA. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹3,066 cr, up 20.0% YoY, a slowdown from +27.8% in Q1 (the pre-computed 'accelerating' label reads this backwards). EBITDA margin fell from 8.6% to 6.7% quarter-on-quarter, and PAT was only ₹41 cr, a 1.3% margin, after Q1 PAT dropped 65% YoY. Parcel volumes grew 32% but parcel revenue only 22%, so the company is earning less per shipment; PTL is healthier, with tonnage up 14% and revenue up 23%. On valuation, EV/EBITDA of 111x (P98 vs the market) and trailing P/E of 231x make it expensive even after the cash cushion of about ₹4,676 cr. Forward P/E of 41x still assumes a big profit ramp that analysts are cutting: FY EPS estimates are down 14% in 30 days and 26% in 90 days, while 18 of 20 ratings stay at buy. That gap is a classic setup for the stock to re-rate lower.

Aditya Infotech sells video-surveillance and security products under the CP PLUS brand, a leading name in India, and makes its own hardware through the AIL Dixon manufacturing joint venture. It is a product and distribution business, not an order-book contractor, so the usual Industrials order-book measures do not apply. The filings only give the latest period as a half-year (the data table labels it H1FY26, but the QIP and fire dates in the notes put it in H1 FY27, the half ended September 2026). In that half, revenue rose 89.7% YoY to ₹3,148 cr and PAT rose 218% to ₹328 cr, a 10.4% PAT margin and 16.4% EBITDA margin, even after a ₹34 cr exceptional fire loss. Two caveats: the table's 'accelerating/expanding' trajectory labels look wrong because the period labels are mislabeled and inconsistent, and the profits are not turning into cash (operating cash flow was -₹67 cr, CFO/PAT -0.20x, free cash flow -₹180 cr, as inventory and receivables piled up). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E. The stock is clearly expensive: trailing P/E of 109.5x against the 28–45x Industrials range, EV/EBITDA of 70x, forward P/E still 51x, around the 95th percentile of the broad market on every multiple, and trading at 92.6% of its 52-week range. Rising analyst estimates (+12% over 90 days) support the growth story, but the average target price is only about 4% above the current price. The biggest risks are a de-rating if the cash drain continues while growth slows, plus a ₹308.6 cr customs penalty still under CESTAT appeal.

fundamental.thesis: eClerx is a mid-sized data, analytics and business-process services firm whose clients are mostly in North America (78% of revenue, top 10 clients about 60%). The pipeline tags it as Industrials, but it is really an IT/BPM services business, so we value it on IT-services yardsticks rather than the order-book lens on the sector card. Revenue still grew a healthy +18.3% YoY to Rs 1,189 cr in Q2 FY27 (PAT Rs 180 cr). However, revenue growth has slowed from +25.4% in Q3 FY26 to +18.3%, and margins are shrinking: PAT margin fell from 17.9% to about 15%, EBITDA margin from 27.7% to 25.4%, and H1 EPS grew only +8.4%, so profits are lagging revenue. On valuation we used trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against IT-services benchmarks. A trailing P/E of 19.5x is below the 22-30x IT range, forward P/E is 14.7x and EV/EBITDA is 12.0x (P18 vs the broad market), with 29% ROE and a 3% dividend yield. The stock sits at 11% of its 52-week range, so it grades cheap. The main risk is that this is a value trap: analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7.9% over 90 days while margins keep shrinking, and the stock may keep de-rating until margins stop falling.

fundamental.thesis: Emmvee is an integrated solar module and cell maker with 10.3 GW of installed module capacity, 2.94 GW of TOPCon cell capacity and an order book of 10.4 GW. It is tagged Industrials/IT in our data, but it really trades on the solar-manufacturing cycle. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 45.1% YoY to ₹3,132 cr and PAT rose 79.1% to ₹762 cr, a 24.3% PAT margin. Growth is clearly slowing from the +116% revenue growth of FY26. EBITDA margin is flat at around 35%, and new orders in Q2 were only 1.5 GW against 10.3 GW of module capacity running at 44% utilisation. No separate quarterly breakdown was available, so these are half-year figures. On the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, it looks cheap: EV/EBITDA is 13.4x (P21, 42% below the broad-market median of 23.3x), trailing P/E is 19.5x (below the 28–45x Industrials range) and forward P/E is 13.7x. That multiple is being applied to what look like peak-cycle 35% EBITDA margins, and the stock is already at 90% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is earnings quality. Cash from operations covered only 0.54x of PAT in H1 and 0.18x in FY26, free cash flow in FY26 was -₹453 cr, and analysts have cut next-year EPS estimates by 12.5% in the last 30 days. Together these suggest margins may fall back as module supply catches up.

fundamental.thesis: GMR Airports is India's largest private airport operator, running Delhi, Hyderabad, Goa (Mopa), Medan, and newly Nagpur and Vizag. Its earnings depend on regulated aero tariffs plus a fast-growing non-aero business (retail, F&B, real estate, hotels). Revenue growth has slowed sharply: from +48.6% YoY in Q3FY26 to +23.0% in Q1FY27, and to about +11.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹4,188 cr, from H1 ₹8,273 cr minus Q1 ₹4,085 cr). EBITDA margin has slipped from 43.8% to 37.9% and passenger traffic grew only about 1%, so growth now rests on tariffs and non-aero income. Implied Q2 PAT is only about ₹65 cr (1.6% margin) after ₹1,931 cr of H1 interest, and yfinance shows a ₹15 cr loss, so profit quality is thin. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-asset business and P/E is not meaningful: at 25.1x EV/EBITDA, 82.6x forward P/E (P98 among peers), negative book value and 98% of the 52-week range, it is expensive. Sell-side EPS estimates have also been cut 37–42% over 90 days while 7 of 8 ratings stay Buy, a classic sign of a possible de-rating. The biggest risk is that weak traffic (Hyderabad -11.7%, Mopa -14.4%) plus a heavy debt load leaves the stock leaning on the Delhi CP-4 tariff being implemented on time.

fundamental.thesis: Graphite India makes graphite electrodes for electric-arc-furnace (EAF) steelmakers. It runs 80,000 tpa of capacity at 97% utilisation, and that demand depends on the steel cycle and on EAF adoption, not on an order book, so the Industrials order-book framework fits poorly. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 34% YoY to Rs 1,871 cr and PAT rose 26% to Rs 265 cr; subtracting Q1 (Rs 842 cr / Rs 171 cr) implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 1,029 cr (+41% YoY vs Rs 729 cr) and PAT of about Rs 94 cr (+24% vs Rs 76 cr). However, the implied Q2 PAT margin fell sharply to about 9.1% from 20.3% in Q1, so revenue is accelerating while profitability per rupee is slipping. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, and the signals conflict, so the grade is fair: EV/EBITDA of 51x (P89, +119% vs median) and a trailing P/E of 72x look expensive because trailing earnings come from the FY26 trough (PAT -62%), while a forward P/E of 12.5x (P16), P/B of 2.2x, and a mid-range 52-week position price in a sharp earnings recovery that the 30-day sell-side EPS upgrade (+8.3%) supports. The main risk is that the recovery stalls as margins compress, global steel output stays flat (-0.2% YoY, China -1.6%), and Chinese electrode pricing pressure persists; the reported debt/equity of 6.27 also conflicts with the company's historically low leverage and is probably a units error, but it should be verified.

Finolex Cables is a leading Indian maker of electrical wires and cables (about 88% of revenue) and optical fibre cables (about 9%). It has net cash (debt/equity 0.31 including treasury holdings) and is adding capacity in fibre draw and preform. In the latest verified quarter (Q1FY27) revenue was ₹2,013 cr, up 44.2% YoY, and PAT was ₹249 cr, up 53.1%, with a 12.4% PAT margin. fundamental.thesis: NBCC (India) is a Navratna PSU operating primarily as a Project Management Consultant (PMC) on government construction projects, with smaller EPC and real estate segments — a near-debt-free government-backed execution engine whose revenue visibility depends almost entirely on public-sector order flow. Q1FY27 revenue contracted 5.5% YoY to ₹2,260 cr (sharply reversing the +11–13% growth seen through FY26), while PAT grew 17.9% YoY to ₹159 cr on expanding margins (7.0% vs 5.5% a year ago) — however this PAT growth is of questionable quality: FY26 FCF turned deeply negative at -₹280 cr (CFO/PAT: -0.36x vs a healthy 2.20x in FY25), the EPC segment collapsed 63.4% YoY and turned loss-making, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut -7.4% in the last 30 days. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (per sector card guidance for capital-intensive industrials), NBCC trades at 22.4x EV/EBITDA — roughly at the sector peer median (P48) and within the industrials benchmark range — making it fairly valued, with forward P/E of 35.5x at a meaningful 52.9% premium to the market forward median, reflecting priced-in government-capex optionality. The biggest risk to the thesis is sustained working-capital deterioration (FY26 FCF -₹280 cr, CFO/PAT -0.36x) alongside EPC segment losses and Supreme Court-related regulatory uncertainty on the Kochi housing project, which could keep revenue under pressure and undermine the credibility of reported PAT growth.

fundamental.thesis: Waaree Energies is India's largest solar module maker. It is integrating backward into cells, inverters, BESS and polysilicon, and it now runs India's largest retail solar distribution network, with 700+ franchises. In Q2 FY27 revenue grew +23.9% YoY to ₹7,518 cr, but growth has slowed sharply from +118.8% in Q3 FY26 to +79.2% in Q1 FY27 and +23.9% now. PAT fell -14.2% YoY to ₹754 cr as operating EBITDA margin dropped 540 bps to 17.8%. The positives are that management held its FY27 operating EBITDA guidance of ₹7,000–7,700 cr, cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 2.1x, net cash ₹3,224 cr) and the order book of ₹59,200 cr covers 2.2x revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials. At 11.3x it is about 50% below the broad-market median (P15). Trailing P/E is 19.8x (P22) and forward P/E is 15.9x, both far below Industrials norms, so the stock is optically cheap. The discount is partly earned: margins are shrinking, sell-side EPS estimates were cut about 6-7% over 90 days, and new order inflow fell to ₹7,300 cr from ₹20,500 cr. The biggest risk is a global module glut (utilisation fell to 45% from 71%) combined with US Section 232 and AD/CVD duties, which cut the overseas mix from 47% to 18.5%. Together these could keep pushing margins and the multiple lower.

MMTC is a state-owned former trading company with almost no operating business left: H1 FY27 operating revenue was only ₹1.95 cr. Its profits come almost entirely from interest on about ₹1,926 cr of net cash and ₹111 cr of dividend income from investments. Operating revenue fell 20.7% YoY (₹2.46 cr to ₹1.95 cr), down from +12.9% in Q3 FY26, and consolidated PAT fell 42.1% YoY to ₹124.41 cr. Last year's figure was flattered by a ₹378 cr exceptional item, and operating cash flow was negative at ₹179 cr, so reported profit is not turning into cash. The sector card's order-book yardstick does not fit a company with no order book, so we valued it on net cash and assets: a ₹11,242 cr market cap is about 5.8× net cash, with P/B of 5.3× and a meaningless P/S of about 3,300×. The trailing P/E of 29× looks fair against peers (P39) only because the earnings are passive income, and with the stock at 88% of its 52-week range we grade it expensive. The biggest risks are that the price rests on PSU or revival hopes rather than any business, plus the unresolved Anglo Coal liability (₹82.82 cr not recognised, hearing on 03.12.2026) and the CBI case over the liquidated Singapore subsidiary.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Stainless (JSL) is India's #1 stainless steel producer and #5 globally ex-China, operating 4.2 MTPA capacity across 120+ product grades on a ~₹44,000 cr TTM revenue base, with strong structural demand from government infrastructure programmes (railways, highways, airports). Q1FY27 revenue grew +10.5% YoY to ₹11,279 cr (stable, not accelerating from FY26's +9.3%), but PAT margin has contracted from 7.4% in FY26 to 6.8% in Q1FY27 as raw material costs at ~70% of revenue compress the spread; PAT growth has decelerated sharply from +27.4% in FY26 to +7.7% YoY in Q1FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (the correct metric for capital-intensive steel, per sector card), JSL trades at 6.59× — inside the 5–8× mid-cycle cyclical range and at the 4th percentile vs 473 broad-market peers — grading CHEAP, corroborated by forward P/E (13.68×) sitting at a discount to trailing P/E (18.27×), pricing in continued earnings growth. The biggest risk to this thesis is raw material cost volatility (nickel, ferro-alloys at ~70% of revenue) combined with structural Chinese overcapacity, which could further erode the already-contracting EBITDA margin (13.1% Q1FY27 vs 13.7% peak in FY26).

Anupam Rasayan is a mid-cap Indian specialty-chemicals maker that does custom synthesis for global agrochemical, pharma and polymer customers, so it is a beneficiary of the China+1 shift. In the latest quarter with usable numbers (Q1FY27), revenue was ₹655 cr, up 34.8% YoY, but growth has slowed from +149% (Q2FY26) and +64.6% (FY26). PAT grew only 5.7% to ₹51 cr, so the PAT margin is stuck around 7.2–7.7% even though EBITDA margin rose from 19.0% to 26.2%. Interest and depreciation are eating most of the operating gains, and FY26 free cash flow was negative at ₹-221 cr. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, which fits a capital-intensive chemicals business: at 32.6× it is well above the cyclical-chemicals norm and at P68 vs the broad market. Trailing P/E of 83.7× (P89) and P/B of 4.4× against an ROE of only 5.8% also point to expensive, and even with forward P/E falling to 42× and next-year estimates raised 25.7% over 90 days, the mean analyst target (₹1,263) is flat to the current price. The biggest risks are that the Q2FY27 results were filed but not extracted (and a corrected version was issued), and fresh promoter share-encumbrance disclosures on 2026-11-09 raise a governance flag.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Copper is India's only vertically integrated copper miner, a state-owned company whose earnings move with the global copper price, so it should be valued as a commodity cyclical and not as a franchise business. Taking H1FY27 and subtracting Q1FY27 gives a Q2FY27 estimate of about ₹1,176 cr revenue (roughly +64% YoY) and ₹518 cr PAT (about +180% YoY). H1FY27 revenue rose 71% to ₹2,112 cr and PAT rose 174% to ₹870 cr, and EBITDA margin widened from about 41% to 58%; operating cash covered 0.97x of profit, leaving ₹601 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for commodity cyclicals, and it is expensive: 33.4x against the 5–8x mid-cycle norm, with trailing P/E of 53.5x against a Materials range of 12–22x and P/B of 14.8x (92nd percentile in the market), though forward P/E of 25.6x and rising analyst estimates (+10% over 90 days) show the market expects strong profit growth to continue. The biggest risk is that margins are probably near the top of the copper-price cycle, so any fall in copper or the LME price would hit profits hard while the stock is still priced for growth.

fundamental.thesis: Indiamart runs a large Indian B2B online marketplace, with 8.9 million supplier storefronts and 217 thousand paying suppliers, and earns mainly from advance-paid supplier subscriptions, which makes it a platform rather than a typical consumer company. Comparing like quarters (the pre-computed trend signals mix quarterly and full-year figures), Q2 FY27 revenue rose 9.7% YoY to Rs 429 cr, slowing from +12% a year earlier, while PAT rose about 10% to Rs 91 cr, EBITDA margin improved from 33% to 37%, and PAT margin stayed flat near 21%; however, paying suppliers fell 2% and collections grew only 9%, so growth depends on higher revenue per supplier rather than more customers, though cash conversion is strong at 1.48x CFO/PAT. Valuation is fair using a platform yardstick of EV/EBITDA and unit economics: EV/EBITDA of 18.1x and trailing P/E of 27.1x sit below the broad-market medians of 23.3x and 35.2x (no close peers are available), and cash of Rs 3,234 cr is about 25% of market cap, but trailing P/E rests on FY26 PAT of Rs 475 cr, while annualising the latest quarter gives about 35x, and the 20.7x forward P/E assumes a profit recovery that the Rs 91 cr quarter does not yet show. The biggest risk is that a shrinking paying-supplier base eventually limits pricing power and pulls revenue growth down toward or below the current 9% collections growth; the Rs 1,939 consensus target is also not relied on because its stated +23% upside conflicts with a price of about Rs 2,137 implied by the 52-week range.
