fundamental.thesis: PVR INOX is a leading Indian multiplex operator whose results depend on film releases and cinema footfall, and it sold its Zea Maize food business in January 2026. H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

Lemon Tree Hotels is India's largest mid-priced hotel chain, and it is shifting toward an asset-light model by splitting the hotel-owning business from the management and brand business (CCI, NSE and BSE have approved the scheme; NCLT sanction is still pending). H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹706 cr, which works out to about ₹361 cr in Q2, up roughly 18% YoY, but growth across the trend window has slowed from +20.1% in FY25. EBITDA margin has held at about 44.5%, while reported H1 PAT of ₹89 cr (12.6% margin) is mixed up with large and inconsistently stated one-off items, and Q2 PAT by subtraction (about ₹32 cr) is below last year's roughly ₹35 cr. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hotel owner, the stock trades at 16.1x, 31% below the broad-market median (P29); trailing P/E is 39x and forward P/E is 22x. Near its 52-week low, that makes it fair to slightly cheap, but the leverage, the pending restructuring and steady small cuts to sell-side estimates (FY EPS -2% over 90 days) argue against a strong call.

fundamental.thesis: Swiggy is India's number-two food-delivery and quick-commerce (Instamart) platform, with a small but fast-growing out-of-home dining segment. Revenue keeps growing in the mid-30s: H1 FY27 rose 36.7% to ₹14,383 cr, and the implied Q2 is about ₹7,571 cr, up roughly 36% YoY, slower than FY26's +51.4%. The trend-table label 'accelerating' mixes half-year, full-year and quarterly periods and overstates the move. Losses are narrowing on a YoY basis: the H1 EBITDA loss fell to ₹997 cr from ₹1,606 cr and H1 net loss to ₹1,713 cr from ₹2,289 cr. Sequentially, however, the Q2 loss widened to about ₹922 cr from ₹791 cr in Q1. Food delivery is close to breakeven at a -7.65% margin, but Instamart still lost ₹1,415 cr at a -55.9% margin. Because P/E and EV/EBITDA are meaningless while the company is loss-making, I graded valuation on EV/sales plus unit-economics delivery, as the sector card prescribes for platforms. Price/sales of 2.89x (about 2.3x on annualised H1 revenue) and P/B of 3.35x (P37 vs the broad market) look fair, not stretched, for ~36% growth with improving margins. Sell-side estimates have been revised sharply upward (FY EPS +50.7% over 90 days), but there is no formal management guidance, and the main risk is that the Instamart cash burn in the quick-commerce price war delays group profitability.

fundamental.thesis: Apollo Tyres is a mid-cap tyre maker with its main earnings base in APMEA (Asia Pacific, Middle East and Africa, including India) and a smaller, weak Europe business that it is restructuring. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue rose 12.8% YoY to Rs 7,398 cr, up from +3.6% in Q1FY26, but the +2609% PAT growth to Rs 349 cr is flattered by a Rs 13 cr base, and EBITDA margin fell from 13.2% to 11.7% (the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trend signals mix cumulative periods, so I relied on like-for-like quarters, and PAT implied by those cumulative figures fell from about Rs 631 cr in Q4FY26). On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business, 7.0x looks low, and the 19.8x trailing P/E sits at the low end of the 18-28x Auto range, but I grade it fair rather than cheap because the peer ranks compare it with the broad market rather than tyre makers, ROE is only 8.7% at 1.62x book, and I disregard the snapshot's implausible 204% dividend yield and treat its 21.99 debt/equity as a likely percentage given 0.75x net debt/EBITDA. Q2FY27 results are due at the 4 November board meeting, so this view rests on data one quarter old, and the main risk is that rising crude ($96) squeezes margins further while the Europe restructuring is still incomplete.

fundamental.thesis: Minda Corporation is a mid-cap auto-component maker supplying mechatronics, security and access systems, wiring harnesses and a growing range of electronics and EV systems to Indian two-wheeler, passenger-vehicle and commercial-vehicle makers, with some export business. Revenue growth has picked up sharply, from +10.3% in FY25 and +22.3% in FY26 to +33.2% in Q1FY27 and a record Rs 2,189 cr (+42.6% YoY) in Q2FY27. H1FY27 revenue was Rs 4,036 cr (+38.1%). Much of this jump comes from consolidating Minda-VAST from April 2026 rather than organic demand, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 14.2% in FY25 to about 11.6-11.8%. Reported H1 PAT of Rs 349 cr (+132.9%) includes a one-time Rs 106 cr gain, so underlying Q2 PAT is about Rs 143 cr, a 6.5% margin. Using P/E as the auto yardstick, the stock is expensive: trailing P/E is 43.3x against an 18-28x auto benchmark (and the one-time gain flatters even that number), forward P/E of 29.2x is still at the top of the range, and it trades at 88% of its 52-week range. EV/EBITDA of 23.3x is only in line with the broad market, so the call rests mainly on P/E; analysts have nudged estimates up (+3% FY EPS over 90 days), but the price already reflects much of that.

Tenneco Clean Air India makes exhaust after-treatment and emission-control systems for Indian passenger-vehicle and commercial-vehicle makers, so it gains from tighter emission rules and richer vehicle mix. In the latest quarter with full numbers (Q1 FY27), revenue grew 20.2% YoY to ₹1,545 cr, up from 10.5% growth for FY26, but PAT fell 1.7% YoY to ₹165 cr and PAT margin slipped to 10.7% from 11.2% in FY26. H1 FY27 PAT of ₹339 cr implies Q2 FY27 PAT of about ₹174 cr, but the Q2 revenue figures filed on 2026-11-04 are not yet in the extracted data. Cash conversion is strong: H1 FY27 operating cash flow was 1.38x PAT and FY26 was 2.37x. Judged on P/E against auto-component peers, a trailing P/E of 38.2x is above the 18–28x sector range, so the stock is expensive on trailing earnings. The forward P/E of 27.7x and EV/EBITDA of 24.3x (in line with the broad-market median, P53) are less stretched. The main risks are faster sales growth not turning into profit growth, and analysts cutting next-year EPS estimates by 4.0% over 90 days even while 6 of 7 rate the stock a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Ola Electric makes electric two-wheelers and is building its own cell business; it has lost market share in a segment where the sector card says e-2W penetration is still rising (~6.5%), so its weakness is company-specific rather than an industry slump. In the latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, revenue was ₹455 cr, down 45.0% YoY, with a PAT loss of ₹-336 cr. The revenue decline has eased only slightly from -49.7% in Q1FY26, while PAT margin worsened from -51.7% to -73.8% and EBITDA margin from -20.4% to -29.9%, and CFO/PAT is a weak 0.64x. P/E is meaningless for a loss-making company, so I graded valuation on EV/sales, growth delivery and the unit-economics trend: at 8.29x price-to-sales for a business whose sales are shrinking about 45% with widening losses, plus P/B of 5.58x against ROE of -43.2%, the stock is expensive, and 7 of 8 analysts rate it sell with FY EPS estimates cut 11.9% over 90 days. The biggest risk is continued cash burn on a leveraged balance sheet (debt/equity 82.45 as reported) before volumes recover. Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-12 but are not yet extracted, so this view rests on Q1 data and the Q2 print could change it.

fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini is one of India's largest integrated sugar makers: 80,000 TCD crushing, 1,050 KLPD distillery for ethanol, 175.7 MW saleable co-generation, and a new 80,000 TPA PLA bioplastics plant. That makes it a regulated, seasonal, capital-intensive commodity business rather than a true FMCG compounder, so the FMCG sector card and its 40-65x P/E norms do not fit here. In Q2FY27 revenue grew +12.3% YoY to ₹1,876 cr and PAT rose +81.6% to ₹104 cr (5.5% margin). That rebound follows a weak Q1FY27 (+6.1% revenue, PAT -14.4%), and H1FY27 shows revenue +9.3% and PAT +38.9%, but revenue growth has slowed from the +18-22% pace of FY26 and the Q2 EBITDA margin of 9.1% is below the FY26 full-year 13.0% (seasonal, but worth watching). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 25.0x and a trailing P/E of 38.0x look rich against the 12-22x Materials-style range. The forward P/E of 18.5x, sell-side FY EPS estimates raised +18.7% over 30 days and +29.4% over 90 days, and a P/B of 3.4x (P38 vs the broad market) pull the overall verdict back to fair, with the stock already at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is government policy on sugar export quotas, minimum sale price, and ethanol procurement pricing, together with negative free cash flow (FY26 FCF -₹349 cr) from PLA and distillery capex, which together could leave the forward earnings that justify the multiple undelivered.

UNO Minda makes auto components for Indian OEMs, including lighting, switches, alloy wheels, acoustics, sunroofs and EV parts. It is a domestic-focused ancillary that benefits from premiumisation and the shift to EVs, and it announced a sunroof capacity expansion with its results. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 27.2% YoY to ₹8,937 cr and PAT rose 19.7% to ₹756 cr, an 8.5% PAT margin. The Q2 press release reports record growth of 38% YoY in both revenue and PAT, so momentum is speeding up from the roughly 18-20% growth seen in FY26 and Q3 FY26. Cash backing is good: FY26 operating cash flow was 1.44x PAT. The quarter-by-quarter split in the trend table does not add up, though (the Q1 row of ₹5,557 cr cannot be reconciled with H1), and EBITDA margin slipped from 12.6% to 11.2%. Valuation is expensive: P/E is 53x trailing and 35.5x forward against an Auto-ancillary median of 18-28x, EV/EBITDA is 29x and P/B is 10x on a 19% ROE. All of these sit at the 64th-82nd percentile of the broad market, and the mean analyst target is only 2.4% above the price, even though analysts have raised EPS estimates by about 6% over the past 90 days. The main risk is that minority shareholders in subsidiaries take a growing share of profit: EPS grew only 3.6% against 19.7% PAT growth, which leaves little room for any slowdown after the festive season at this multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Bikaji is a fast-growing branded ethnic-snacks maker (bhujia, namkeen, sweets) with a strong base in Rajasthan and the north-east, and it has been adding capacity and small acquisitions to expand nationally. Sales are still growing, but profits are lagging behind. H1FY27 revenue rose 13.1% YoY to ₹1,642 cr, down slightly from +14.4% for FY26 and +14.9% in Q1FY26, while H1 PAT fell 5.7% to ₹128 cr. PAT margin has narrowed from 9.4% to 8.3% to 7.8%, and Q2 profit appears to have fallen about 10% YoY. FY26 volume growth was a healthy 9.5%, so demand looks real, but no current-period volume figure was given. On P/E, the yardstick for FMCG, the stock trades at 54.9x trailing (39.3x forward) and 34.5x EV/EBITDA, which sits inside the 40–65x FMCG band, so I grade it fair. Being near its 52-week low gives some cushion, but analysts have cut FY EPS estimates about 10% over 90 days, which means the forward P/E is less comforting than it looks. The biggest risk is that profits keep shrinking while capex is high: H1 free cash flow was -₹48 cr and net debt jumped from ₹172 cr to ₹323 cr, so a slowdown could hit the multiple hard.

fundamental.thesis: Affle 3i is a mobile ad-tech platform that sells cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) advertising, mainly in India and emerging markets; it is a platform business, not a headcount-based IT services firm. Growth is steady but not speeding up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 20.8% YoY to ₹1,531 cr and PAT rose 19.5% to ₹258 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹784 cr (around +21% YoY) and PAT of about ₹130 cr (about 16.6% margin), so YoY growth has held in a tight 19–21% band for six periods with PAT margin flat at 16.6–17.2%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA (31.6x) plus forward P/E (29.7x), not the static IT-services P/E table, because Affle is a platform business. Trailing P/E of 46x is above the 22–30x IT range and about 31% above the broad-market median (P66). Forward P/E is at the top of that range, and the stock sits at 25.5% of its 52-week range. For a business growing about 20% with a ₹1,752 cr net cash cushion, I grade it fair, not cheap. Several things just added risk. The company agreed to acquire Israel-listed Perion Network, cancelled its earnings call citing a 'material development', and still has a ₹1,358 cr Bobble investment caught in insolvency, with a Supreme Court hearing on 25 Nov 2026. Cash conversion has also weakened to 0.65x CFO/PAT in H1.

fundamental.thesis: Cyient is a mid-cap engineering-services firm with three businesses: design and engineering services (DET, about 74% of revenue), electronics contract manufacturing (DLM), and a loss-making semiconductor unit, and it recently bought TAO Digital for about ₹2,156 cr. H1 FY27 revenue grew 23.4% YoY to ₹4,311 cr, but that growth is largely acquisition-driven, and PAT fell 19.7% YoY to ₹241 cr, so the PAT margin dropped from 8.6% to 5.6%. Profit has now fallen in every reported period (-24.9% in Q3FY26, -32.3% in Q1FY27, -19.7% in H1FY27), and the semiconductor unit lost ₹58 cr at a -16.5% margin. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA together, and the stock looks fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the 22–30x IT range, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x ranks P16 against the broad market, but ROE is only 7.8%. The low 11.9x forward P/E rests on analyst estimates that were cut 18% over the last 90 days, so it should not be trusted yet. The biggest risk is that semiconductor losses and integrating TAO keep eating into the steady DET profits, and the data has gaps: the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹1,498 cr conflicts with the filings, Q1FY27 shows two different growth rates, and the reported debt/equity and dividend-yield figures look like data errors.

Travel Food Services runs airport food and beverage outlets and lounges in India, operating at 22 airports with about 541 outlets, and has net cash of ₹451.5 cr with no traditional debt. In H1FY27, consolidated revenue rose 20.1% YoY to ₹878 cr and PAT rose 43.1% YoY to ₹276 cr. The Q1FY27 rate of +20.6% implies Q2 revenue of about ₹426 cr (+~20%) and PAT of about ₹147 cr, so growth is holding steady and PAT margin widened to 31.4% from 26.4%, with strong cash backing (CFO/PAT 1.57x). Much of that growth comes from new outlets (23 added in Q1) rather than existing ones: same-store sales grew only 4.2% while passenger traffic is falling. I used EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this concession-based business: at 23.3x it sits exactly at the broad-market median (P50), trailing P/E of 34.8x is also at the median and far below the 60–100x multiples typical of premium consumer names, and forward P/E of 29.5x implies further earnings growth, so with the stock mid-way through its 52-week range the grade is fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the Delhi Terminal 3 subsidiary (60% owned and material to the group): its licence expired on 30 Sept 2026, and losing or re-pricing that concession would hit both revenue and margins.

fundamental.thesis: Honasa Consumer, the owner of Mamaearth, The Derma Co and other brands, is a mid-cap personal-care company that started online (D2C) and is fast growing its share in a crowded category. Revenue growth has sped up from about +16% in FY26 to +32% YoY in Q1FY27 and +31.2% in H1FY27 (Rs 1,487 cr). The implied Q2FY27 figures, worked out as H1 minus Q1, are revenue of about Rs 607 cr (around +30% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 74 cr. This growth is mostly real demand: Q1 volume growth was +30.5% against only +1.5% from price/mix. H1 EBITDA margin widened about 450 bps to 16.7% and PAT more than doubled (+103%). I graded valuation using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA, both expensive: trailing P/E of 66.3x is above the FMCG card's 40-65x range, EV/EBITDA of 62.4x sits at P93 against peers, and the stock trades at 83% of its 52-week range. Forward P/E of 42.6x shows strong growth is already priced in, although analysts' estimates have risen 24% over 90 days. The biggest risk is weak conversion of profit into cash (H1 CFO/PAT of 0.57x, FY26 FCF of -Rs 84 cr) while working capital grows, so any growth slowdown could cut the high multiple quickly.

fundamental.thesis: Intellect Design Arena is a mid-cap banking and insurance software maker. It sells licences, platform subscriptions and maintenance (AMC) to more than 500 financial institutions in 62 countries. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹855 cr, up 13.0% YoY, and growth has slowed over the trend window from +36.2% (Q2 FY26) to +20.6% (Q1FY27) to +13.0%. PAT was ₹104 cr, up only 1.8% YoY, and the PAT margin fell to 12.2% from 13.5% a year ago. EBITDA margin was 23.2% vs 24.3% a year ago, while LTM EBITDA margin fell about 344 bps to 22.4%, and LTM PBT is down 6.2%; management puts over ₹100 cr of that on AI investment. On the main IT yardstick, trailing P/E is 31.2×, just above the 22–30× sector range. The forward P/E of 18.4× and EV/EBITDA of 17.0× sit well below the broad-market median (P31–P43), so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The forward P/E leans on earnings growth that analysts are now cutting: FY EPS estimates are down about 10% and next-year estimates about 13% over 30–90 days. The biggest risk is that the heavy AI spending (the MSOCK platform) keeps squeezing margins while revenue growth keeps slowing, so revenue growth stops turning into profit growth.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Energy Solutions is India's largest private power-transmission company, with about 30% share of recent transmission bids, 29,802 circuit km of lines, a Mumbai distribution business, a fast-growing smart-meter business and a newly consolidated energy-trading platform. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 47.5% YoY to ₹19,787 cr and PAT rose 137% to ₹2,600 cr, a 13.1% PAT margin, after Q1 FY27 grew revenue 42.4% and PAT 124%. Two caveats apply to that growth: the H1 figures restate prior periods to include the energy-trading platform, and they count ₹4,961 cr of construction revenue (SCA, up from ₹3,692 cr). The extracted H1 rows also conflict (₹14,351 cr vs ₹19,787 cr). We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/B against ROE, the yardstick for capital-intensive utilities: EV/EBITDA of 25.1x, P/B of 7.2x on a 9.7% ROE and trailing P/E of 81.7x are far above the 10–18x utilities range, and the stock sits at 89.5% of its 52-week range. Analysts raising FY EPS estimates by about 16% in 30 days and a ₹87,222 cr transmission order book give good visibility, but the price already assumes flawless delivery. The main risks are leverage and execution: debt/equity is 1.84x, net debt is ₹41,067 cr, free cash flow is negative (₹-3,185 cr in H1), capex guidance is ₹21,000–25,000 cr a year, and Adani group news can move the stock regardless of results.

fundamental.thesis: NHPC is India's largest hydropower company, a state-owned utility that earns a regulated return on the plants it commissions, so its profits grow as new capacity comes online (Subansiri Lower is now at 1,250 MW of a planned 2,000 MW). In H1 FY27 revenue rose 26.0% YoY to Rs 8,291 cr and PAT rose 20.6% to Rs 2,836 cr, a 34.2% margin, up from +14.5% and +8.6% in H1 FY26. However, Rs 918 cr of that revenue is provisional Parbati-II income still awaiting CERC tariff approval, and without it revenue growth is closer to +12%. The trend table mixes half-year, nine-month and full-year periods, so only the H1-vs-H1 comparison is reliable. On valuation (using EV/EBITDA and P/E against the utilities benchmark), EV/EBITDA of 25.5x and trailing P/E of 27.4x are well above the 10-18x utility P/E band, and P/B of 1.85x is rich for a 9% ROE, so the stock looks expensive even though it sits low (24%) in its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that debt-funded capex is outpacing earnings: finance costs more than doubled (+115%), net debt is Rs 56,674 cr, and consensus FY EPS has been cut 20% in 30 days.

fundamental.thesis: Anant Raj is an NCR-focused mid-cap developer that is building a data-centre and cloud business alongside its residential projects; a Board-approved demerger of the data-centre arm into a subsidiary is awaiting NCLT approval. Growth has slowed sharply: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,293 cr (+5.7% YoY), down from +24-26% through FY26, and the implied Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹662 cr was only about +5% YoY. PAT still grew faster than revenue, reaching ₹306 cr (+15.8%), because EBITDA margin widened to 32.3% from about 27-29%. On the sector card's yardstick valuation looks fair: P/E is not meaningful for developers and pre-sales/bookings data was not provided, so I graded on P/B 3.2x against an annualised ROE of about 10-11% (a rich pairing) and EV/EBITDA 28.6x (P63 vs the broad market), offset by a forward P/E of 18.5x and P/B at P36. The biggest risk is weak cash conversion: H1 operating cash flow was only about ₹32 cr against ₹306 cr of PAT (0.10x), and FY26 free cash flow was -₹693 cr, so reported profits are not yet turning into cash while capex and inventory of about ₹1,507 cr keep rising.

Bharti Hexacom is Bharti Airtel's listed subsidiary covering the Rajasthan and North-East telecom circles, with about 30 million customers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,582 cr, up 11.4% YoY, a slight pick-up from 10.9% in Q1 and 9.4% for FY26. PAT was ₹566 cr, up 34.4%, with PAT margin widening to 21.9% from 19.2% in Q1. EBITDAaL rose 14.2%, cash generation is strong (FY26 CFO/PAT of 2.6x) and net debt is low at 0.31x EBITDAaL. The weak spot is ARPU, the sector's key number: it grew only 5.2% to ₹264, which suggests growth is coming more from data usage and broadband than from pricing power. On that basis it trades at 53.9x trailing earnings (P73 against broad-market peers, 53% above the 35.2x median) and 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81). The forward P/E of 33.6x shows strong earnings growth is already priced in. A P/B of 17x is supported by a 37.9% ROE and almost no debt (debt/equity 0.11). Overall the stock is fair to stretched rather than cheap, with the price about 1% above the mean analyst target of ₹3,674. The main risk is that exchange volumes are cyclical and the business is exposed to regulatory or fee changes, and at this multiple the stock has little room to absorb any slowdown in trading activity.

P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. On valuation, the quoted trailing P/E of 27.3× sits just below the 28–45× Industrials band and EV/EBITDA of 19.3× is about 17% below the market median. VRS costs continued in H1FY27 (₹13 cr) along with a ₹5.8 cr forex loss, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-03 are not yet in the extracted data. Franchisee like-for-like growth in the high single digits is the one positive KPI. I graded valuation on P/E plus ROE, because the low 13.7× EV/EBITDA is inflated by lease accounting. On that basis the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E is 75.6× (P86 vs the broad market, +115% vs the 35× median) and P/B is 6.4× on an ROE of only 8.5%. That is a premium-retailer multiple for a business growing revenue in low single digits. The forward P/E of 37× assumes a profit recovery that has not shown up yet. Sell-side views are bearish (8 sell out of 14), and FY EPS estimates have been cut 8.2% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the margin recovery story keeps slipping while estimates keep being cut, which would push the multiple down further.

BLS International runs outsourced visa and consular processing for foreign governments, plus a fast-growing but lower-margin digital and e-governance services arm; it does not fit the premium consumer-discretionary template in the sector card. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 32.0% YoY to ₹973 cr, up from +25.3% in Q1FY27, but PAT rose only 8.6% to ₹202 cr (Q1: +11.4%). PAT margin has contracted from 25.2% a year ago to 20.8%, and from 24.1% for FY26. The main cause is mix: digital services (H1 revenue ₹793 cr, +50% YoY) earns a 6.2% segment margin against 39.7% in visa, and acquisition costs from Atyati and the Trefeddian hotel add to the pressure. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA and P/E together with cash conversion, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 13.8x and EV/EBITDA is 10.2x, both around the 11th percentile of the broad market (median 35.2x / 23.3x). It also has ₹1,665 cr net cash and CFO/PAT of 1.37x, though the price sitting at 11% of its 52-week range shows the market is pricing in a de-rating as profits grow far slower than sales. The biggest risk is that the shift toward digital services keeps diluting margins, so strong revenue growth fails to turn into earnings growth.

fundamental.thesis: Crompton is one of India's largest fan, pump and small-appliance makers. It leads the market in ceiling fans, reaches about 2.5 lakh retailers, and gained share across most categories between FY23 and FY26 (water heaters +200 bps, residential pumps +180 bps). In Q1 FY27 revenue rose 11.8% YoY to ₹2,235 cr and PAT rose about 15% to ₹143 cr (PAT margin 6.4%), up from +7.3% revenue growth in Q3 FY26. But EBITDA margin slipped from about 11% to about 10%, because the company passed on only about 80% of cost inflation despite 10–15% price hikes, and it lost roughly ₹200 cr of primary sales to supply disruption. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because FY26 swung to a ₹-242 cr loss. On the yardsticks I used instead, the stock looks fair to slightly cheap: forward P/E is 23.9x, close to the broad-market median of 23.2x and well below the 60–100x the sector card cites for consumer names, and EV/EBITDA is 20.0x, 14% below the median. JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India; JSW Group took control in Dec 2025) is a decorative and industrial paints maker that sold its Powder Coatings and IRC divisions and is now chasing market share. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,927 cr, up only 5.8% YoY as reported, but up 20% on a comparable retained-business basis with 23% volume growth, and the latest single quarter improved from Q1 FY27's -2.8%. Profitability is moving the wrong way: gross margin fell 1,180bp from 47.2% to 35.4%, EBITDA margin slipped to 13.2% from 14.4%, and PAT margin dropped to 7.8% from 12.1% on an operating basis, while cash conversion is weak (CFO/PAT 0.42x, FCF about ₹-8 cr). On valuation I used forward P/E and ignored the 7.45x trailing P/E, because the ₹1,874 cr one-off divestment gain inflates it; at 31.3x forward and 6.0x P/B the stock is cheap against the card's 60-100x discretionary norms, but analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (-5.8% over 90 days), so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that volume-led growth is being bought with price and margin under a new promoter, and the price increases do not restore gross margin before earnings estimates are cut further.

It is a cyclical, capital-heavy textile business rather than a premium consumer brand, so the Consumer Discr. sector card's 60–100× multiple norms do not apply. Growth has turned sharply upward. Revenue growth accelerated from about +1% through FY26 to +13.3% in Q1FY27 and about +15.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹2,866 cr vs ₹2,480 cr). Implied Q2 PAT nearly doubled to about ₹358 cr (+91% YoY), and EBITDA margin expanded from 13–17% to 21.5% in H1FY27, with cash conversion strong at 1.48x CFO/PAT. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, 15.2× is about 35% below the broad-market median, and forward P/E of 14.6× vs trailing 25.3× prices in further earnings growth. But P/B of 1.85× against a TTM ROE of only 7.3%, with the stock at 98.4% of its 52-week range, makes this fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the margin jump reflects a favourable cotton-yarn spread cycle rather than structural gains, and next-year EPS estimates are already being trimmed (-2.8% over 30 days).

PAT fell 9.0% to ₹284 cr, and PAT margin compressed from 17.9% to 13.1% (EBITDA margin 25.6% → 22.6%) as acquisition costs and finance charges (₹5.1 cr → ₹11.7 cr) hit profits, so growth is being bought, not earned organically, and the filings give no volume-growth figure to check real demand. On P/E plus EV/EBITDA, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.5× and forward P/E of 18.5× are far below the 40–65× FMCG norm, EV/EBITDA is 17.7× (24% below the broad-market median), it trades at only 9% of its 52-week range, and ROE is 27.6% with a net-cash balance sheet (₹78 cr); however, the sector card warns that cheap FMCG usually signals a structural problem, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 2.8–3.0% over 30–90 days. The biggest risk is that the acquired businesses keep diluting margins while the core franchise shows little organic volume growth, which would justify the de-rating rather than reverse it.

fundamental.thesis: SAIL is a large government-owned integrated steel maker, with Bhilai, Bokaro and Rourkela contributing about 81% of revenue, and it benefits from India's protected steel upcycle. H1 FY27 revenue rose 10.7% YoY to Rs 58,243 cr, improving from about +8% in H1 FY26, while EBITDA margin edged up from 10.9% to 11.5%; PAT jumped about 192% to Rs 3,395 cr, but EBITDA rose only about 14% (roughly Rs 840 cr against a PAT gain above Rs 2,200 cr), so the jump is not explained by operations, and the missing Q1 FY27 row means Q2 momentum cannot be isolated. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive steel, the 8.84x snapshot is slightly above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, while the 22.3x trailing P/E looks stale because filing-based trailing PAT of about Rs 5,516 cr implies about 13.6x, so I grade it fair: P/B of 1.3x with about 10.9% annualised ROE is not a clear bargain, the broad-market peer ranks are a weak comparison, and rising estimates (FY EPS +18.5% over 30 days) are offset by little upside, since the Rs 185 mean target is only about 2% above the roughly Rs 182 price implied by the 52-week position, not the stated 13.2%. The biggest risk is that the PAT surge proves non-recurring or steel spreads narrow, and no spread or EBITDA-per-tonne data was available to test this, with Rs 23,457 cr of provisionally priced government sales and a 0.79 current ratio adding balance-sheet risk.

Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 34.6× against the sector card's 5-8× mid-cycle range for chemical cyclicals and a 23.3× broad-market median (P73), with trailing P/E of 41.9× also above the 12-22× Materials range; there are no tight industry peers, and the feed's 27% dividend yield, 1.86 debt/equity and +54% target upside look wrong because the ₹494 mean target is only about 2.5% above the roughly ₹482 price implied by market cap. fundamental.thesis: Piramal Pharma is a loss-making midcap pharma company (market cap about ₹21,256 cr) with a contract drug manufacturing (CDMO) business, recently expanded by raising its stake in vaccine and biologics CDMO Yapan Bio to 74%; the filings data provided does not establish its market position. Valuation is fair on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick used here for a capital-intensive building-materials maker: 20.4x sits at P44 against the broad market, trailing P/E is 36x versus a 35x median, but P/B of 6.5x is rich and the stock trades at 88% of its 52-week range, which leaves limited upside. The biggest risk is that a ₹340 cr+ three-site capacity expansion and rising working-capital days land just as a risk-off, crude-inflated macro squeezes housing demand and gas-linked kiln costs.

fundamental.thesis: Urban Company is India's largest online platform for home services such as beauty, cleaning and repairs, and it also sells its own water purifiers and smart locks (Native), runs international operations and has a Saudi joint venture. It is now funding a heavily loss-making quick home-help business called InstaHelp. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹537 cr, up 41% YoY, faster than FY26's +36%. Orders rose 103% and Net Transaction Value (NTV, the total value of services booked) rose 39% to ₹1,432 cr. Profit went the other way: consolidated adjusted EBITDA was -₹144 cr, a -26.8% margin, against +6.8% for FY26. That is because InstaHelp lost ₹174 cr, which wiped out a core business that is profitable and improving (core EBITDA ₹30 cr, up 213% YoY; India consumer margin 3.5%, up 110 bps). Since the business is pre-profit, P/E means nothing here, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales and unit economics instead. At 12.3x sales and 8.6x book value (76th percentile of the broad market), the price is reasonable for 40% growth only if InstaHelp's losses keep shrinking. InstaHelp's loss per order did improve 19% from the previous quarter but is still ₹279. I rate valuation fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: JK Tyre is one of India's largest tyre makers, with 11 plants (9 in India, 2 in Mexico), about 38 million units a year of capacity, and a strong truck/bus and OEM franchise. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue hit a record ₹4,841 cr, up 20.7% YoY (a rebound from -6.6% in Q1), helped by 32% domestic sales growth and 65% OE growth after GST 2.0. Profits have not kept up. EBITDA margin has roughly halved, from 13.3% in Q2FY26 to 7.1%, Q1 PAT fell 75% YoY to ₹44 cr (1.1% margin), and Q2 free cash flow was -₹447 cr. On the usual EV/EBITDA yardstick for a capital-intensive auto ancillary, the stock looks cheap at 7.7x EV/EBITDA and 14.6x trailing P/E against an Auto sector range of 18–28x (P6–P14 vs the market). However, those trailing multiples still include the high-margin quarters, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 57% over 90 days, and annualised current-run-rate PAT would put the stock well above sector P/E, so we grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is further margin squeeze: about 70% of raw materials are petro-based, crude is above $102, debt is meaningful and cash flow is negative, so volume growth may not turn into earnings.

fundamental.thesis: CCL Products is one of the world's largest private-label instant coffee makers, with plants in India and Vietnam (Ngon Coffee, which earned ₹53 cr PAT in Q2 alone), plus a small but growing branded domestic business; it trades as FMCG but is mostly a B2B coffee processor exposed to green-coffee price swings. Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +44.5% (H1FY26) and +38.5% (Q3FY26) to +13.7% in Q1FY27 and +10.5% for H1FY27 (₹2,411 cr). That implies Q2FY27 grew only about +7–8% (≈₹1,211 cr vs ≈₹1,127 cr), most likely as coffee-price pass-through fades. Profits are still growing much faster than sales: H1 PAT is up 42.5% to ₹247 cr, PAT margin has widened from 8.0% to 10.2%, and cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 1.78x, FCF ₹414 cr). Valuation is fair rather than cheap. I used EV/EBITDA because this is a capital- and working-capital-heavy processor, not a classic staples brand: EV/EBITDA is 21.6x (P46 vs market) and trailing P/E is 38.9x, at the bottom of the FMCG 40–60x band but rich for a commodity-linked exporter. Forward P/E of 24.1x already prices in strong earnings growth, and the stock sits at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits as coffee prices normalise, while margin gains, which drove most of this year's profit growth, become harder to repeat.

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive regulated utility, at 15.88× SJVN sits within the regulated-utility peer range and at P28 vs broad market, while P/B at 1.86× (P16 vs peers) and forward P/E at 14× (P22 vs peers, deep discount to trailing 38×) reflect market pricing in earnings recovery — grading overall as fair, but the 52-week position at 12.8% of range and ongoing sell-side EPS cuts of -13.3% over 30 days caution against treating the cheapness as a catalyst. The DSCR of 0.60 combined with a current ratio of 0.54 means near-term liquidity is structurally stressed, and the NJHPS tariff determination pending since April 2024 (₹3,200+ cr billed provisionally under an expired 2019 tariff) creates a binary earnings event with no resolution timeline visible.

Bajaj Holdings is a near-debt-free holding company: its earnings come from dividends, interest and its share of profits from its large stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv, so revenue (₹576 cr in H1FY27) is a small figure next to profit. Reported H1FY27 PAT fell 6.7% YoY to ₹4,845 cr and revenue fell 20.1%, but that is mainly because last year included a one-off ₹1,522 cr gain from selling Bajaj Finserv shares. Without that gain, PAT rose about 37%, and the share of associate profits grew 32% to ₹4,626 cr, helped by Bajaj Auto Q2 PAT up 62% and Bajaj Finserv up 23%. Reported growth has slowed sharply, from +65.6% to -6.7% half-year on half-year, but the underlying associate engine is accelerating. Using the holding-company yardstick (discount to NAV, not P/E or EV/EBITDA, which mean little here), the stock trades at about a 52% discount to the reported NAV of ₹21,578 per share (estimated price around ₹10,300). That sits in the middle of the usual 40–60% holdco discount band, and peer P/E of 11.4x (P33) and P/B of 1.5x with ROE of 12.6% back a 'fair' grade, with the stock in the lower third of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is concentration: value depends almost entirely on Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv share prices, and the holdco discount may not narrow, so this is a leveraged-looking proxy on two group stocks rather than an independent earnings story.

Its continuing operations shrank after the demerger: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹59,872 cr, down 22.9% YoY, and Q2 revenue fell to ₹26,356 cr from ₹33,515 cr in Q1. Forward P/E of 12.7x vs trailing 17.75x, and analysts raising FY EPS estimates by 25% over 90 days, point the same way. The main risks are that Q2 revenue and profit both fell from Q1, and that several data points don't reconcile (yfinance Q2 revenue ₹11,229 cr vs ₹26,356 cr in the filing, a 1038% dividend yield, and a 52-week range distorted by the demerger), so the inputs carry real uncertainty.

Solar Industries makes commercial explosives for coal miners such as CIL and SCCL, and it is now growing fast as a defence ammunition and energetics supplier. It sits under the Materials label, but it is really an explosives and defence business, so steel and chemical multiples do not apply. In the half-year to September 2026 (HY27, from the official filing), revenue grew +69.7% YoY to ₹7,187 cr and PAT grew +84.3% to ₹1,316 cr. That is faster than FY26 (+30.0% revenue) and Q3FY26 (+29.0%), and defence revenue more than doubled (+109% to ₹1,935 cr). EBITDA margin widened about 140 bps to 28.4%, so the pre-computed 'contracting' margin flag looks like a period-ordering artefact. The ₹20,178 cr order book (87% defence) covers roughly 2 years of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business. At 65.8x EV/EBITDA, 101.7x trailing P/E and 32x P/B, the stock is at P93–P99 versus the broad market, well above the 12–22x Materials range and rich even for a defence name. The forward P/E of 63x and estimate upgrades (+11% FY-EPS over 90 days) show strong growth is already priced in, and the price is at 97% of its 52-week range. So: expensive. The biggest risk is that the defence order flow is lumpy and largely export-driven, so any slip in orders or execution would hit a stock priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: NTPC is India's largest power generator. For a capital-intensive utility I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, backed by P/B with ROE. On that basis it looks cheap against peers: EV/EBITDA is 8.4x against a peer median of 11.6x (cheapest in the peer group) and trailing P/E is 11.9x against 14.7x. P/B is 1.7x with ROE of 13.7%. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, valuation is expensive: trailing P/E is 33.4x vs a 26.9x peer median (P82), forward P/E is 26.3x vs 17.9x (P82) and EV/EBITDA is 23.7x vs 15.2x (P78), with the stock at 88% of its 52-week range, although the trailing P/E appears to use FY26 earnings and would be about 25x on my rough trailing-12-month PAT of ₹3,569 cr, so the premium is less clear-cut if H1 profits prove durable. The biggest risk is that H1 was lifted by lumpy or one-off items, which the mere +1.9% to +2.4% rise in estimates from two analysts could hint at, leaving little room for disappointment at this price.

IPCA Laboratories is a mid-sized Indian pharma maker with a chronic-therapy branded business at home (about 45% of revenue, ranked 16th in India) plus formulation and API exports through its Unichem subsidiary. Profit has risen faster than sales over the last six periods: H1 FY27 revenue grew 17.1% YoY to ₹5,698 cr and PAT jumped 50.7% to ₹814 cr, with EBITDA margin up 280 bps to 22.9%, ahead of the 22-22.3% FY27 guidance. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹2,910 cr (+14% YoY), slower than Q1's +20.8%, at a PAT margin of about 13.4%. Domestic formulations grew 13% and export formulations 33%. Using P/E with an EV/EBITDA cross-check, the stock looks fair: trailing P/E of 38x sits at the top of the 28-40x pharma range and at the 69th percentile of its peers, forward P/E is 28x and EV/EBITDA is 22.6x, about 6% above the peer median. With the price at 96% of its 52-week range and the average analyst target only about 5% above it, the earnings growth is mostly priced in.

fundamental.thesis: United Breweries is India's largest beer maker, owning Kingfisher and selling Heineken, with growth increasingly led by premium brands. fundamental.thesis: Anand Rathi Wealth is a capital-light HNI/UHNWI wealth management distributor earning trail commissions and distribution fees on a growing AUM base — an asset-light model that structurally warrants premium P/E multiples over traditional lenders. H1FY27 revenue grew +17.4% YoY to ₹646 cr (decelerating from FY26's +22.3%), while PAT surged +26.4% YoY to ₹322 cr with PAT margin expanding sharply to 49.8% from 34.5% in FY26, suggesting strong operating leverage — though this margin step-up from ~34% to ~50% in a single half-year warrants scrutiny for one-off items and seasonal AUM tailwinds. The stock trades at a trailing P/E of 80.3× and P/B of 36.78× — at P88 and P100 respectively vs the broad 499-stock market — with sell-side mean targets implying −26.8% downside and zero buy recommendations from only 2 analysts, while the 52-week position at 95.1% of range signals the stock is priced for near-perfection; using EV/EBITDA of 56.3× as the primary yardstick (per sector card for capital-light/platform-adjacent names), this is unambiguously expensive versus any reasonable comparable. The single largest risk is valuation derating from extreme multiples if AUM growth decelerates or equity markets correct, compounded by recent promoter pledge disclosures (SAST Reg 31 filings on Oct 16) which are a governance flag for a MIDCAP, thin sell-side coverage, below-1.0 CFO/PAT ratio (0.71×), and a high reported D/E of 8.25 whose nature warrants clarification.

fundamental.thesis: BSE is India's oldest stock exchange and a capital-markets infrastructure monopoly, earning revenues through transaction charges, listing fees, clearing/settlement, and investment income — it is not a traditional bank, so the relevant yardstick is P/E and EV/EBITDA (not P/B+ROE). Q1FY27 revenue grew +63.5% YoY to ₹1,566 cr and PAT grew +62.1% YoY to ₹873 cr at a 55.7% margin; while the absolute growth rate is still exceptional, the trajectory has decelerated from +116% in FY25, and PAT margins are broadly stable (55.7% vs 56.3% a year ago) rather than meaningfully expanding. At 48.1× trailing P/E (P68 vs broad peers) and EV/EBITDA of 28.4× (P63), the stock screens as fair against headline P/E metrics, but the forward P/E at 37.8× sits at P78 (expensive), P/B at 17.4× is at P94 (extremely elevated even for an asset-light exchange model), and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut sharply over the past 90 days (FY-EPS −6.6%, next-FY −9.8%) — a classic pre-derating signal that makes the 'fair' grade conditional on growth sustaining. The single biggest risk is that BSE's transaction-charge revenues are directly levered to equity market volumes and IPO activity, both of which face acute pressure from FII outflows of ₹44,000+ cr over 30 days, a RISK_OFF macro regime, and rising regulatory contribution costs (₹193 cr, +66% YoY), which could compress earnings faster than consensus currently models.

fundamental.thesis: CreditAccess Grameen is India's largest pure-play microfinance lender, with a gross loan book of about ₹29,294 cr that grew 21.5% YoY as of H1 FY27 and 2,276 branches lending mostly to rural women borrowers. Earnings are recovering sharply from last year's microfinance stress: Q2 FY27 PAT, derived as H1 ₹995 cr minus Q1 ₹493 cr, is about ₹502 cr on total income of about ₹1,904 cr. That is roughly 7-8x the year-ago quarter, but off a provisioning-hit base, so the +691% H1 PAT and +144% revenue figures overstate the underlying growth, and the revenue figure also mixes NII with total income across periods. Asset quality is the real story: GNPA improved from 4.04% (9M FY26) to 3.17% (FY26) to 2.18% (Q1 FY27), with collection efficiency at 97.4% and provision coverage holding around 65%. Using the sector card's P/B-vs-ROE yardstick for lenders, a P/B of 2.91x against a TTM ROE of 16.4% (annualised H1 ROE about 24%) looks fair rather than cheap. The low forward P/E of 11x simply reflects the earnings normalisation, and analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by 9.8% in the last 30 days. The main risks are a fresh stress cycle in unsecured rural lending, a borrower count that is shrinking (-2.4% YoY) even as loan size grows, and a risk-off macro backdrop for a leveraged midcap lender.

fundamental.thesis: ICICI Prudential AMC is India's largest listed asset management company, earning fee income on equity and debt AUM; it is a pure-beta play on India's financialisation theme (AUM growth +25.6% YoY as of Q4FY26) with an asset-light model generating 85.8% ROE. Revenue growth has decelerated from +23.5% (Q3FY26) to +16.9% (H1FY27, ₹3,238 cr) while PAT growth slowed to +14.3% YoY (₹1,854 cr); PAT margin at 57.2% in H1FY27 has compressed from the 60–61% range seen earlier, and EBITDA margins are on a contracting trajectory — the direction of change is negative even if absolute levels remain high. Using the sector-card mandated P/AUM-linked earnings yardstick, the stock trades at 51.33× trailing P/E and 35.11× EV/EBITDA (P74 vs broad market peers, +50% premium to median), with forward P/E of 36.77× implying priced-in earnings recovery — graded fair given the ROE-justified premium, but the stock at 83% of its 52-week range with consistently negative estimate revisions (FY-EPS cut –5.8% in 30d, next-FY cut –10.5% in 90d) provides very limited margin of safety. The biggest risk is a classic pre-derating setup: sell-side estimates being quietly cut while ratings remain bullish and the pending PMS acquisition from ICICI Securities adds regulatory and integration overhang.

Valuation is fair but not cheap at about 6x EV/TTM sales (our calculation from market cap, net cash and filed revenue), mid-range in the 52-week band; the 128x trailing P/E and 112.9x EV/EBITDA look stale against about 79x annualised H1 PAT, while the 34.9x forward P/E already assumes about Rs 2,000 cr of PAT, roughly 2.25x the current run-rate. The biggest risk is that earnings fail to reach that level, especially as H1 free cash flow was only Rs 42 cr after Rs 434 cr of capex and cash fell Rs 790 cr, with FEMA and GST matters still unresolved.

fundamental.thesis: Pine Labs is India's leading merchant commerce platform operating ~2.17 million POS/DCP devices with embedded affordability finance, UPI infrastructure, and an expanding international footprint (UAE, Malaysia) — a high-growth fintech rather than a traditional lender despite its Financials sector tag. Q1 FY27 revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹737 cr (stable within the 18-24% band across the last four quarters, showing consistent rather than truly accelerating growth), while PAT surged ~4× to ₹20 cr from ₹5 cr YoY, but EBITDA margin contracted sharply from 23% in Q3 FY26 to 17.1% in Q1 FY27 as technology/cloud spend (+33% YoY to ₹64 cr) and international investments eroded profitability — the trajectory signal of 'EBITDA contracting' is the dominant margin read. Valuation is expensive on most yardsticks: trailing P/E of 147× sits at P98 vs peers and far above any sector benchmark (IT 22–30×, Financials 12–18×); EV/EBITDA of 25.7× is more moderate at P58, and forward P/E of 31.7× (P67) is reasonable IF the earnings ramp materialises, but ROE of only 2.4% with D/E of 7.47 makes the P/B of 2.9× difficult to defend — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card's platform guidance, 'fair-to-expensive' is the honest grade, leaning expensive given the ROE/leverage combination. The biggest near-term risk is that the effective tax rate of 48% (vs guided 28-30%) and persistent EBITDA margin compression prevent the PAT inflection on which the forward multiple entirely depends, exposing the stock — already at its 52-week low — to further de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Saw is a midcap maker of large-diameter line pipe and ductile-iron pipe; it is tagged Industrials but trades on a materials and steel-pipe cycle, and no order-book or book-to-bill data was provided to check pipeline visibility. Revenue has returned to growth (H1FY27 ₹8,924 cr, +7.3% YoY; implied Q2FY27 about ₹4,472 cr, +5.6%) after four periods of falling 14-21%, but profits have collapsed: H1 PAT fell 77% to ₹126 cr, and implied Q2 PAT was only about ₹35 cr, a margin under 1%. EBITDA margin has fallen in every period shown, from 17.1% to 8.0%, which suggests the company is accepting lower prices to win volume or facing cost pressure it cannot pass on. One genuine positive is cash: H1 operating cash flow was ₹1,385 cr, against cash burn a year ago, and net debt fell ₹467 cr. Trailing P/E of 30.5x sits inside the 28-45x Industrials band, so I grade valuation fair rather than cheap. Syrma SGS is a mid-sized Indian electronics manufacturing services (EMS) company that builds products for about 270 customers, and it benefits from China+1 sourcing and the PLI scheme; exports are now 26% of operating revenue and grew 80-91% YoY in H1. Trailing P/E of 79.7x (P87) is far above the 28-45x Industrials range, so the stock is expensive, though a forward P/E of 47x and steadily rising analyst estimates (next-FY EPS +7% over 90 days) show strong earnings growth is already expected. With the price at 99% of its 52-week range, the stock is priced for perfection, and any slowdown in growth or further margin squeeze from component shortages could trigger the 30-50% de-rating typical of this sector.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Elxsi is a Tata Group engineering R&D services company specialising in embedded systems design for automotive, media & entertainment, and healthcare verticals — a niche deep-tech services player distinct from commodity IT outsourcers, with a strong domestic and global client base in high-complexity design programmes. Revenue growth has inflected sharply from a -3.9% trough in Q2FY26 to +14.7% YoY in H1FY27 (₹2,077 cr), with PAT rising +13.9% to ₹341 cr and PAT margin holding steady at 16.4%; the System Integration segment contributed 28.9% YoY growth, signalling service diversification — however, EBITDA margin has contracted ~290 bps from its peak of 28.1% (Q3FY26) to 25.2% (H1FY27), driven by New Labour Code wage provisions and rising employee benefits costs. Trailing P/E of 40.78× is above the IT sector benchmark upper bound of 30× (expensive on that metric alone), but the forward P/E collapses to 26.22× — within the 22–30× sector range, confirming earnings recovery is priced in — and peer-rank analysis places TATAELXSI at P60 on both trailing and forward P/E (fairly valued per the ≥P75 expensive threshold); at 6.7% of its 52-week range the stock appears sentiment-oversold relative to an improving earnings trajectory, consistent with the FY26 exceptional charge now cycling out of the base. The primary risk is sustained EBITDA margin compression from structural wage inflation and New Labour Code costs, amplified by a persistent negative EPS revision trend (-0.9% over 90 days, -1.2% next-FY) that historically flags further analyst downgrades ahead, and a long-run AI-driven structural threat to engineering services demand that the sector card explicitly flags as unproven in revenue terms.

C.E. Info Systems (MapmyIndia) is India's leading digital maps and location-intelligence company, selling map data, APIs and IoT/telematics devices to auto makers, enterprises and government. H1FY27 revenue grew +15.3% YoY to ₹271.5 cr, up from roughly +2-3% through FY26, and consolidated PAT rose +32.1% to ₹85.0 cr; Q2 alone works out to about ₹131 cr of revenue (about +16% YoY) and ₹35 cr of PAT (H1 minus Q1). The growth quality is weak, though: almost all of it came from the device segment (+161% to ₹56.2 cr), while the core map data and services business, about 79% of revenue, grew just +0.7%, and the PAT margin fell to about 27% in Q2 from 35.6% in Q1. On the IT yardstick of P/E, the trailing 36.9x sits above the 22-30x sector band, but forward P/E of 22.5x falls inside it and the stock ranks in the middle of the broad-market peer set (P53 on P/E, P64 on EV/EBITDA at 29.1x), so I grade it fair rather than cheap, even though it trades near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the high-margin core map business has stalled while sell-side EPS estimates keep falling (-3.0% FY over 90 days, -4.1% next-FY), so the low price may be a falling knife rather than a value entry.

fundamental.thesis: Chennai Petroleum is a standalone refiner and IOC subsidiary, so its earnings track gross refining margins (GRM, the profit per barrel of crude processed) rather than administered retail fuel prices. Taking the official H1FY27 filing (₹51,414 cr revenue, ₹3,278 cr PAT) and subtracting Q1 gives an implied Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹22,055 cr, up roughly 10% YoY. Implied Q2 PAT was ₹2,247 cr, a 10.2% margin, driven by GRM rising to $8.78/bbl from $3.22 a year ago and a ₹385 cr one-off retrospective price adjustment, even though crude throughput fell 4.5%. On live ratios the stock looks cheap, using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive refiner: trailing P/E 5.4x, EV/EBITDA 3.8x and P/B 1.5x against a 32% ROE, all bottom-percentile versus the market and below the 8–14x energy band. However, these are peak-cycle refining margins, and next-year EPS estimates were cut 11.6% in the last 30 days, so normalised earnings likely put it closer to fair. The bigger worry is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was only ₹25 cr against ₹3,278 cr of profit (0.01x), receivables jumped from ₹235 cr to ₹2,008 cr, cash fell to near zero after dividends, and the auditor flagged board-composition non-compliance.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Oil is India's largest state-run refiner and fuel marketer, so its earnings depend on government fuel-pricing policy as much as on crude prices: falling crude helps it, rising crude hurts. H1FY27 revenue rose 28.4% YoY to ₹549,972 cr and PAT rose 35.2% to ₹21,362 cr, but the half was very uneven: Q1 was a loss (₹-1,141 cr; EBITDA margin 1.9%), then Q2 PAT jumped to about ₹21,630 cr as refining margin (GRM) rose from $15.59 to $18.52/bbl. Revenue growth looks driven mostly by price rather than volume, since marketing sales fell from 26.2 to 25.2 MMT quarter-on-quarter and diesel sales from 10.9 to 9.0 MMT. On the yardstick the sector card names for oil marketing companies (P/E plus dividend yield, EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock looks low on trailing numbers: P/E 4.4x against a peer median of 9.2x, EV/EBITDA 4.1x against 6.1x, and P/B 0.85x with 21% ROE. Those trailing numbers are inflated by an unusually strong Q2, though. Forward P/E is 7.7x, close to the 8.1x peer median and higher than trailing, which means analysts expect earnings to fall, so I grade it fair: priced for policy risk rather than mispriced. The biggest risk is crude at about $91 and rising while retail fuel prices stay frozen, which could push marketing margins back toward Q1-style losses; earnings are also turning into cash poorly (H1 CFO/PAT 0.48x, free cash flow ₹-1,450 cr).

Authum Investment & Infrastructure is a midcap NBFC and investment holding company. A large part of its earnings comes from investment and treasury income and from distressed-asset acquisitions; the latest is an NCLT-approved resolution plan announced on 2026-10-28. Revenue growth slowed from +21.4% in Q1 to +12.6% in Q2, and H1 PAT is down 10.6%. Cash backing for profits is weak: H1FY27 operating cash flow was -0.49x PAT and free cash flow was -₹763 cr. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for lenders, not P/E. P/B of 2.91x with ROE of 13.1% is roughly fair, since the stock is neither under 1.5x nor above 3x with sub-12% ROE. The headline P/E of 8.95x sits at P5 of the broad market, but it is flattered by lumpy investment gains and should not be read as cheap. The main risk is that profits depend on market-linked and one-off gains that are not turning into cash. Thin lender disclosures (no NIM or GNPA data) and the reported 24.6 debt/equity also need checking against the filings.

fundamental.thesis: IRFC is the Government of India's dedicated financing arm for Indian Railways (82.9% government-owned after the June 2026 OFS). It mainly leases rolling stock and project assets to the Ministry of Railways, so credit risk is quasi-sovereign and gross and net NPA have been 0.0% for every reported period. Revenue is growing fast and the pace is picking up: up 22.8% YoY to ₹16,316 cr in H1FY27, against +0.5% in FY26 and -2.4% in 9M FY26. Implied Q2 revenue is about ₹8,055 cr (+26% YoY). Profit is not keeping pace, though. H1 PAT rose only 10.3% to ₹3,886 cr, the PAT margin slipped from 26.5% to 23.8%, and NIM eased from 1.55% to 1.48%, so earnings are rising more slowly than the loan book. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, which is the right yardstick for a lender, not P/E. At 2.3x book for a 12.8–13.3% ROE and roughly 1.4% ROA, the stock is fair, maybe slightly full, for a low-margin, policy-driven financier. The 'cheap' peer reading (trailing P/E 18.7x, P20) compares IRFC with the whole market rather than with lenders, so I don't rely on it. The biggest risk is that further government stake sales add share supply while thin, shrinking spreads keep EPS growth near 10% even with strong loan growth.

fundamental.thesis: NIACL is India's largest PSU general insurer (85.44% government-owned), writing motor, health, marine, and fire coverage domestically and internationally, with a regulatory solvency ratio of 1.80×; however, the franchise is structurally loss-making at the underwriting level and profits depend entirely on investment income. Q1 FY27 delivered a net loss of ₹244 cr (vs. +₹392 cr in Q1 FY26, –162% YoY) as the incurred claim ratio worsened to 102.97% and the combined ratio deteriorated to 121.14%, confirming that claims and expenses together exceed earned premiums — both motor (–₹126 cr underwriting loss) and health (–₹134 cr) dragged, and net earned premium growth decelerated to just +1.9% YoY. Using P/B + ROE as the correct yardstick for an insurer (not P/E), P/B of 0.76× ranks NIACL at P1 in the broad peer set and appears cheap on its face, but a TTM ROE of only 3.4% fully explains this discount — it is structural cheapness, not mispricing — and analyst EPS estimates have been cut –47% in just 30 days, a classic pre-derating signal that the forward P/E of 9.2× bakes in recovery assumptions the combined-ratio trend does not yet support. The dominant near-term risk is a qualified audit conclusion on unreconciled reinsurance recoverable balances (₹75,490L gross, ₹13,783L doubtful-debt provision), compounded by a new CMD appointment in September 2026 and a mandatory Ind AS accounting transition due April 2027, leaving both governance and accounting transparency materially unresolved.

Pfizer Ltd is the Indian listed arm of Pfizer Inc., selling branded medicines in India, so it has little exposure to the US patented-drug tariff. Stripping it out, underlying PAT grew only about 10%, and EBITDA margin has been choppy in the 38–46% range. On a trailing P/E yardstick (the right one for a branded-formulations business, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock trades at 28.7x, at the low end of the 28–40x pharma band. The biggest risk is the earnings path: cash from operations fell 40% in H1 (CFO/PAT 0.69x), sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut 4.3% over 90 days, and the parent's portfolio rationalisation could keep shrinking the product basket.

fundamental.thesis: Sagility is a mid-cap healthcare outsourcing company. About 90% of revenue comes from US health insurers (payers) and about 10% from hospitals and other providers. It is tagged IT here, but its demand comes from US healthcare operations, not tech spending. In Q2FY27 revenue was ₹2,032 cr, up 22.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹284 cr, up 13.3%. Growth has slowed from +35.7% (Q3FY26) to +29.1% (FY26) to +25.0% (H1) to +22.5%, and constant-currency growth is only about 12%, so roughly half the headline growth comes from the weak rupee. Reported PAT margin fell to 14.0% from 15.1% a year ago, and adjusted PAT grew only 8.1% even though adjusted EBITDA margin reached a six-quarter high of 26.3%. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA, the trailing P/E of 21.5x is below the IT sector's 22–30x range and sits at about the 24th percentile of the broad market (there are no close peers in the universe). EV/EBITDA is 11.4x, forward P/E is 15.4x, and cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x), so the stock looks cheap. The biggest risk is client concentration: the top 3 clients are 60% of revenue and the top 10 are 84%, and voluntary attrition is high at 25.7%. Losing or repricing a single large client could hurt badly. The yfinance dividend yield (44%) and debt/equity (11.5) figures look like unit errors, so I ignored them.

Zen Technologies makes combat-training simulators and counter-drone systems, and is a niche midcap that benefits as India shifts defence buying to domestic suppliers (about 82% of recently approved capital proposals are earmarked for Indian industry). Revenue is very uneven from quarter to quarter: Q2FY27 revenue was a record ₹345 cr, up 98.8% YoY, right after Q1FY27 fell 10.5% to ₹142 cr. That took H1FY27 revenue to ₹487 cr (+46.7%), but H1 PAT grew only 15.7% to ₹124 cr. Margins are shrinking, with H1 EBITDA margin down from 39.0% to 35.1% and PAT margin down from 32.3% to 25.5%, partly because other income fell 24%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for order-book businesses, and the stock is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 68.3x (P94 vs peers, +193% vs the 23.3x median) and trailing P/E is 87x, well above the 28–45x Industrials range. The 32.9x forward P/E already assumes a sharp earnings recovery, and analysts raising estimates by about 4–5% only partly supports that. The biggest risk is that the ₹1,376 cr order book covers only about 1.6x trailing-12-month revenue (about ₹880 cr), and new orders arrive in lumps. That gives only around 1.5 years of visibility, so one slow quarter could hurt a stock priced for steady execution.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

Jubilant Ingrevia is a mid-cap Indian chemicals maker with three segments: Specialty Chemicals, Nutrition (vitamin B3 and feed premixes) and Chemical Intermediates (acetyls). It is now adding CDMO capacity and has bought a 40% stake in ZettaOne, an electronics-materials business. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,394 cr, up 24% YoY and an all-time high, compared with low-single-digit growth through FY26 (+1.3% in Q1FY26, +5.0% for FY26). PAT rose 61% to ₹111 cr, and both PAT margin (8.0% vs 6.1–7.2% across FY26) and EBITDA margin (16.0% vs 13.6–14.8%) widened, but Q1FY27 is missing from the filings data, so the speed-up rests mainly on one quarter. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to for chemicals: at 18.1x it is far above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for commodity chemicals, though that range doesn't fully fit a specialty/CDMO mix; it is 22% below the broad-market median (P35), with trailing P/E of 34.6x at P48 and forward P/E of 22.3x, so I call it fair overall, not cheap. The main risks are muddy cash flow and earnings quality: finance costs jumped 85% YoY on acquisition-related borrowing, H1 FY26 earnings were weakly backed by cash (0.67x CFO/PAT, negative free cash flow), and analysts have trimmed next-year EPS estimates (−2.4% over 30 days, −3.7% over 90 days) even as they raised this year's.

fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. Gases bring in about 71% of segment revenue at a 26.4% segment margin, while project engineering earns only 9.8%. PAT margin has slipped to 15.1% from the low-to-mid 20s in earlier periods, and the H1 EBITDA margin dropped 850 bps to 31.8%. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. fundamental.thesis: Narayana Hrudayalaya runs a large chain of affordable multi-specialty and cardiac hospitals in India and also owns a hospital business in the UK, which makes it a mid-sized hospital operator that grows by adding beds and raising occupancy and revenue per bed. PAT is the cleanest figure we have: Q2FY27 PAT was ₹301 cr, up 16.7% YoY (EPS ₹14.82 vs ₹12.72), faster than Q1FY27's +5.4%. Revenue figures disagree with each other, though: the filings table shows ₹2,896 cr (+73.6% YoY) while yfinance shows ₹1,627 cr, and the prior-year comparison rows look mis-scaled. Margins are clearly falling either way (operating margin down about 500 bps to 19.5%, H1 EBITDA margin 20.1% vs 25.0%), and strong cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT 1.91x, FCF ₹594 cr) is the main support. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital chain, the stock trades at 25.4x, which is at or below where Indian hospital peers usually trade. Trailing P/E is 46.9x, but forward P/E of 26.6x implies earnings growth ahead, and the stock sits at 36% of its 52-week range, so fair overall. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while debt stays high (D/E about 1.2x) and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 3.7% over 30 days even though almost all of them rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Neuland Laboratories makes APIs (active drug ingredients) and does contract development and manufacturing (CDMO) for global drugmakers. About 85% of revenue comes from exports, and it has 77 active US drug master files (DMFs) and a clean FDA record. It should benefit from the China+1 shift, and its export-led model is outside the US tariff on patented drugs. Results are lumpy, though: Q2FY27 revenue fell 11.4% YoY to ₹457 cr and PAT fell 47% to ₹51 cr. That came straight after an exceptional Q1 (revenue +116%, PAT ₹147 cr), and the PAT margin dropped from 22.7% to 11.2% between the two quarters. H1FY27 still looks strong, with revenue up 35% to ₹1,091 cr, PAT up 80% to ₹199 cr and cash flow from operations at 1.8x PAT. On valuation I used trailing and forward P/E and P/B, because the reported EV/EBITDA of 401x and debt/equity of 16x are almost certainly data errors for a company the filings show as net cash. At 60.6x trailing earnings (sector range 28–40x), 11.8x book and the P78 peer percentile, the stock is expensive. The 37.6x forward P/E already assumes the H1 growth rate carries on. The biggest risk is that the Q2 drop marks a pause in big customer orders rather than normal quarter-to-quarter swings, which would leave a premium valuation without the earnings to support it.

fundamental.thesis: ITI Limited is a Government of India-owned telecom equipment manufacturer (PSU under Department of Telecommunications) engaged in defence communication, broadband gear, and telecom network products — a structurally impaired business currently in a BIFR-supervised revival plan, NOT a telecom service operator and therefore the Telecom sector card (ARPU/EBITDA framework) does not apply here. Valuation is strikingly expensive: trailing P/E of 79.4× sits at P87 among 473 broad-market peers (+126% premium to market median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 483× is economically meaningless for a loss-making entity — the ₹25,371 cr market cap is pricing in the ₹8,280 cr ASCON Phase IV defence order optionality and GoI backing, not current earnings power. The single biggest risk is the material audit qualification — auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion citing Ind AS 115 revenue recognition failures on complex engineering contracts, inventory obsolescence, and inadequate internal controls, which means reported numbers cannot be relied upon and could be restated downward.

Brigade Enterprises is a Bengaluru-focused developer with residential projects plus a steady leasing and hospitality annuity business; its leasing segment earns a 67.5% margin and grew 1.3% YoY. H1FY27 consolidated revenue fell 13.2% YoY to ₹2,312 cr, mainly because real-estate segment revenue dropped 26.6% to ₹1,374 cr. PAT still rose 32.7% to ₹436 cr, lifting the PAT margin to 18.9%, and the implied Q2 alone (about ₹1,133 cr revenue, ₹219 cr PAT) was similar to Q1. The forward-looking metrics are thin: Q1FY27 bookings were ₹1,061 cr on 0.74 mn sq ft and collections were ₹1,856 cr, with no year-ago figure to show the trend. Cash conversion weakened to 0.42x CFO/PAT in H1, against 1.63x in Q1. Following the sector card, I judged valuation on bookings, collections and net debt, not P/E. On that basis, net debt/EBITDA of 2.1x, gross D/E of 0.79x, a forward P/E of 17x and a price at 53% of its 52-week range point to fair, not cheap, value. The snapshot's P/B of 30.5x and EV/EBITDA of 143.6x look like data errors, since net worth of about ₹7,155 cr against a ₹20,830 cr market cap implies P/B near 2.9x. The biggest risks are the revoked environmental clearance on a large Chennai project and a ₹860 cr landowner JDA dispute. Analysts also cut current-year EPS estimates by 6.1% in the last 30 days.

fundamental.thesis: Zydus Wellness is a mid-cap consumer wellness company (brands include Glucon-D, Complan, Sugar Free, Nycil and Everyuth). It has recently grown through debt-funded acquisitions: Naturell in India and Comfort Click in the UK for GBP 239 million. The latest extracted figures are stale and look inconsistent. The table labelled FY26 shows revenue of ₹396 cr (+46.2% YoY) and PAT of ₹20 cr (-43.2% YoY), but FY25 shows ₹2,709 cr. That suggests a mix of standalone and consolidated figures, or a quarter labelled as a full year. Even so, the direction is clear: EBITDA margin fell from 18.4% to 12.0% and PAT margin from 14.8% to 5.0%, while finance costs rose 718%. The Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-03 are not yet in the data. Using P/E as the yardstick, as the FMCG sector card does, valuation is expensive. Trailing P/E is 81.7x against a sector norm of 40–65x, EV/EBITDA is 38.5x (80th percentile, where 100 = most expensive), and ROE is only 3.4%. The forward P/E of 28.9x assumes a sharp earnings recovery, yet analysts cut their current-year EPS estimate by 21% in the last 30 days. Price is at 74% of the 52-week range, so the upside looks limited.

fundamental.thesis: Dalmia Bharat is a mid-sized Indian cement maker with 54.7 MTPA installed capacity across 12 states, expanding toward 67 MTPA, including the acquired Jaypee assets in Central India. Q2FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1 because the Q2 row is blank, was about ₹3,563 cr (+4.3% YoY, slowing from +10.7% in Q2FY26), and PAT was about ₹-201 cr after ₹339 cr of exceptional items; volume rose only 3%, EBITDA per tonne fell from ₹1,013 to ₹746, below the ₹900-1,100 healthy range, and management expects more fuel and Central India cost pressure in Q3. On the capital-intensive yardsticks of EV/EBITDA and EBITDA per tonne, I grade valuation fair: 12.3x EV/EBITDA is on depressed earnings, the 35.0x trailing P/E (Materials benchmark 12-22x) is distorted by one-offs, and the P19 EV/EBITDA and P15 P/B ranks are less useful because they compare against the broad market, not cement peers; the 15.7% position in the 52-week range offers some support, but this is not clearly cheap with FY EPS estimates cut about 19% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that fuel inflation and Central India dilution keep margins falling while capex of ₹3,200-3,400 cr continues, leading to further estimate cuts.

GMDCLTD is a Gujarat state-owned miner whose main business is lignite. Mining brings in nearly all its revenue (FY26 mining revenue ₹2,508 cr out of ₹2,653 cr total), and the loss-making power segment adds the rest. In Q2FY27, revenue from the official filing rose 71.2% YoY to ₹903 cr, faster than +23.8% in Q1FY27. Reported PAT fell 63.3% to ₹171 cr, but that is because Q2FY26 included a one-time ₹474 cr GST credit; without it, PAT grew about 27%. The PAT margin is 18.9%, close to Q1's 18.0% and well below FY26's 36% (which was inflated by the one-off). The quarter was strongly cash-backed: operating cash flow was 3.9x PAT and free cash flow ₹376 cr. Because this is a capital-heavy commodity miner, the right measure is EV/EBITDA, and the reported 43.9x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for cyclicals. However, that figure, the 163% dividend yield and the 4.47 debt/equity do not fit with Q1 EBITDA of ₹267 cr and the low liabilities in the segment data, so I treat them as unreliable. On the more dependable cross-check, trailing P/E of 20.6x is at the top of the 12–22x Materials range and P/B of 2.78x with 14.2% ROE is not cheap. Forward P/E (22.0x) is above trailing, which means earnings are expected to fall, so the grade is fair, not cheap, even though the stock ranks low on P/E against the broad market. The biggest risk is that the 71% revenue jump does not match the yfinance figure (₹538 cr), and it brought only modest underlying profit growth while margins shrank.

fundamental.thesis: Abbott India is the Indian listed arm of Abbott. It is a branded-formulations franchise focused on the domestic market (Thyronorm, Duphaston and other women's health, gastro and chronic-therapy brands), so it is in the sector card's 'safe template' group with no US-tariff exposure. The only reliable figures are full-year FY26: revenue of ₹6,929 cr (+8.1% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,552 cr (+9.7% YoY), with a 27.7% EBITDA margin and a stable 22.4% PAT margin. Cash conversion was good but not excellent (CFO/PAT 0.85x, FCF ₹1,278 cr). The Q1FY27 yfinance row does not add up (₹932 cr revenue against a ~₹1,730 cr quarterly run-rate, and a 46% PAT margin), so I ignored it. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet, which means I cannot read the current trend. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 35.8x sits inside the 28-40x pharma range and at P52 against peers, and EV/EBITDA is 28.1x (P62), so I grade it fair. The forward P/E of 28.8x points to expected earnings growth, and the stock trades at 8.4% of its 52-week range, a better entry point if the Q2 numbers hold up. The biggest risk is that the price slide reflects a weaker Q2 or growth slowing to mid-single digits, which this stale data cannot confirm or rule out. Two of the snapshot figures are almost certainly data errors and I ignored them: a dividend yield of 201% and debt/equity of 3.6 for a company that has historically had no debt (the second may be lease liabilities or a unit mismatch).
